objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A marketing coordinator's first attempt at a campaign brief comes back disappointing. She wants to improve the result on her next attempt.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Rewrite her request at much greater length, since more description generally produces a more considered answer.
options.explanation: Length is not the variable. A longer version of an unclear request is still unclear, and padding can bury the one instruction that mattered.

options.text: Send the same request again, on the basis that a second attempt often produces a noticeably better result.
options.explanation: Resending an unchanged request repeats the conditions that produced the weak answer, so any improvement is chance rather than a fix.

options.text: Work out what is actually wrong with the answer, since a vague ask and missing material need different fixes.
options.explanation: The causes call for opposite responses: a vague ask needs a tighter specification, missing source material needs the material supplied, and a wrong task needs restating. Changing something before knowing which it is means guessing.

options.text: Break the brief into four smaller requests, so that each part of the campaign is handled on its own terms.
options.explanation: Splitting up helps when a request is genuinely doing too much, but applied blindly it produces four requests carrying the same original flaw.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: An events officer changed four things about her request at once and the result improved. She now wants to keep improving it over the coming weeks.
question: What is the drawback of working this way?

options.text: She cannot tell which of the four changes helped, so she has learned nothing she can rely on next time.
options.explanation: Bundled changes produce a result but no knowledge. Two of the four may have helped, one may have made no difference and one may have hurt, and she carries all four forward without knowing which is which.

options.text: The four changes together make the request considerably longer than the version she originally started from.
options.explanation: A longer request is a side effect rather than the problem, and length is acceptable when every part of it is earning its place.

options.text: Changing four things at once takes more of her time than changing one thing and reviewing the result.
options.explanation: Changing several things at once is quicker in the moment, so effort is not what she loses by doing it.

options.text: The improvement may not last, because results vary from one attempt to the next even with identical wording.
options.explanation: Some variation between attempts is normal, but that is a reason to check a change more than once rather than an argument against improving the request.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A project administrator's summary of a status report keeps omitting the risks section. Her third attempt reads: 'IMPORTANT: you MUST include the risks. This is CRITICAL.' The risks are still thin.
question: What is a better next change?

options.text: Ask for the summary and then ask, in a follow-up, whether anything important was left out of the first answer.
options.explanation: A follow-up question can surface omissions, but it leaves the original request unimproved and repeats the work every week.

options.text: Move the emphasised instruction to the very top of the request, so it is the first thing that gets read.
options.explanation: Position helps a little with genuinely long requests, but an unspecific instruction at the top is still unspecific.

options.text: State what the risks section must contain, such as each open risk, its owner and the date it was last reviewed.
options.explanation: Emphasis conveys that something matters, not what it should contain. Naming the fields the section must carry turns an insistence into a specification that can actually be followed and checked.

options.text: Add the same emphasised instruction a second time at the very end, so the requirement appears twice in the request.
options.explanation: Repeating an instruction verbatim adds volume rather than information, and the second copy is as vague as the first.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: After five rounds of corrections a policy draft keeps regaining problems that were already fixed, and the chat has become hard to follow. Which two steps should the author take?
question: Select two.

options.text: State plainly which parts of the current draft are settled and must be left untouched.
options.explanation: Protecting the settled sections is a distinct move from restating requirements: it constrains what may change, which is what stops regressions.

options.text: Ask Claude to look back through the chat and remember all corrections made so far.
options.explanation: Asking for recall does not resolve corrections that conflict with each other, and it leaves the requirements spread across many turns rather than stated once.

options.text: Start again with one prompt gathering every agreed requirement in one place.
options.explanation: Consolidating scattered corrections into one clean specification removes the contradictions that accumulate across a long thread of piecemeal edits.

options.text: Carry on with more rounds, since each round has been fixing at least one real issue.
options.explanation: Fixing one thing per round while breaking another is not progress. Continuing the same loop simply repeats the pattern that produced the problem.

options.text: Change to a different topic briefly and then return, to give the draft a fresh start.
options.explanation: A change of subject does not reset anything about the draft. It adds more material to an already cluttered conversation without addressing the cause.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A support team wants to build a comprehensive FAQ from a large set of historical customer tickets.
question: Which decomposition technique is most suitable?

options.text: Employ a third-party FAQ generator instead of using Claude.
options.explanation: Employing a third-party generator avoids the decomposition challenge rather than addressing it, and does not use Claude. The question requires a technique that structures the task for Claude.

options.text: Cluster tickets by topic, generate FAQs per cluster, then merge.
options.explanation: Clustering tickets by topic breaks the large set into manageable sub-problems, enabling focused FAQ generation per cluster. Merging these ensures comprehensive coverage and a well-organized final document.

options.text: Ask Claude to summarize each ticket, then combine into an FAQ.
options.explanation: While summarizing each ticket is a useful preprocessing step, it does not group related issues, so combining summaries still lacks the topic-based organization needed for a coherent FAQ.

options.text: Concatenate all tickets and ask Claude to produce the FAQ.
options.explanation: Concatenating all tickets and asking Claude to produce the FAQ risks exceeding context limits and lacks structured input, making it difficult to identify recurring themes and organize answers coherently.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A business strategist needs to compare three competing products on features, pricing, and market positioning.
question: Which prompt will yield the most useful structured comparison?

options.text: Prompt Claude to compare the three given products, letting the model decide which attributes to cover and how to structure the output, without indicating a preferred format such as a table, bullet points, or paragraph text.
options.explanation: Leaving the attributes and output format entirely up to the model often results in an uneven or incomplete comparison. Without specifying a preferred structure, the output may lack consistency and be difficult to parse for actionable insights.

options.text: Instruct Claude to describe each product in detail covering available features, benefits, and market positioning, then compile a detailed list of similarities and differences drawn from those descriptions.
options.explanation: This prompt asks for detailed descriptions and a list of similarities and differences, but it omits pricing, a key comparison attribute, and does not enforce a structured table. The resulting list may be less precise and harder to interpret quickly than a side-by-side comparison.

options.text: Guide Claude to gather details on features, pricing, and market positioning for each product, then create a comparison table with rows for each product and columns for features, price, positioning, and USPs.
options.explanation: This prompt explicitly defines the key attributes (features, pricing, market positioning) and requests a comparison table with rows for products and columns for features, price, positioning, and USPs. This ensures a structured, consistent, and actionable output that facilitates quick comparison.

options.text: Ask Claude to write an essay comparing the three products, with sections on their development history, market approach, and competitive evolution, rather than providing a point-by-point feature comparison.
options.explanation: An essay format emphasizes narrative over clear, attribute-by-attribute analysis and focuses on development history, market approach, and competitive evolution rather than the requested features, pricing, and positioning. This makes it less suitable for deriving structured business insights.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A finance assistant's variance commentary reads well, but several of the figures quoted in it are wrong. She is about to start rewording her request.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Check the figures she supplied, since a commentary can only be as accurate as the numbers it was given.
options.explanation: When the reasoning and the writing are sound but the numbers are wrong, the input is the first suspect. Rewording the request cannot repair figures that were incorrect before they were pasted in.

options.text: Ask for the commentary to be produced again, this time with each figure checked as it is written out.
options.explanation: A self-check re-reads the same numbers she supplied, so wrong inputs are confirmed rather than corrected.

options.text: Ask for every figure in the commentary to be listed separately, so she can check them all in one place.
options.explanation: A separate list makes checking easier, but it is a step she should take after establishing whether the input data was right.

options.text: Add an instruction that accuracy of the figures matters more than the readability of the commentary.
options.explanation: Instructions about priorities do not correct an underlying number, and they invite more careful presentation of the same wrong values.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A training manager has split a course redesign into four pieces: rewriting the learning objectives, updating the slide deck, refreshing the exercises, and drafting the end-of-course quiz.
question: Which observation should shape the order?

options.text: The quiz is what learners remember most clearly, so drafting it first would set the standard for the rest of the course.
options.explanation: Assessment written before the objectives ends up defining them by accident, so the course is shaped by whatever the quiz happened to test.

options.text: The slide deck is the largest piece, so starting there gets the greatest share of the work out of the way early.
options.explanation: Size is a workload observation. Building slides before the objectives are agreed means rebuilding them when the objectives change.

options.text: The objectives govern the other three pieces, so they are settled first while those three can then run in any order.
options.explanation: Only one real dependency exists here: slides, exercises and quiz all serve the objectives. Once the objectives are fixed, the remaining three are independent of each other and their order is a matter of convenience.

options.text: The exercises take the longest to review by others, so they should be finished ahead of the remaining three pieces.
options.explanation: Review time is a scheduling consideration, and exercises built against objectives that later change will need reworking anyway.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A marketing analyst pastes six months of customer survey comments and asks Claude to summarise the main complaints. She intends to present the result to her director as the complete picture.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The summary will be organised by month rather than by theme, making the leading complaints harder to compare.
options.explanation: Ordering is a presentation issue that a follow-up request fixes in seconds, and it does not mislead anyone about coverage.

options.text: The comments will all be rewritten in fresh wording, so her director never sees any customer's verbatim phrasing.
options.explanation: Losing verbatim quotes weakens the presentation, but she can ask for examples. It does not change what the director believes about the shape of the complaint data.

options.text: A few prominent themes may be reported as though they were everything, hiding complaints that recur less often.
options.explanation: She asked for the main complaints, not for complete coverage, and she plans to present the answer as complete. A low-frequency but serious complaint can be omitted entirely while the summary still reads as authoritative, so the request should state that coverage must be exhaustive.

options.text: Claude will ask which reporting period to cover instead of summarising, delaying the work until she answers.
options.explanation: A clarifying question costs a moment and is easily answered, so it is an inconvenience rather than the risk that matters here.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A grants manager must choose between eleven internal funding applications and plans to work through them in stages with Claude.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Sort the applications by the amount requested, so the largest commitments receive the closest attention first.
options.explanation: Amount requested is one relevant factor among several, and using it to allocate attention first can push a small, strong application aside.

options.text: Ask which of the eleven applications look strongest, and use that shortlist to focus the more detailed stages.
options.explanation: Asking which look strongest outsources the judgement she owns, and it does so before any shared standard exists to justify the ranking.

options.text: Agree what a fundable application must demonstrate, since every later stage compares applications on that basis.
options.explanation: The funding standard defines what every later stage looks for, so summaries, comparisons and the final decision all inherit it. Set afterwards, it simply ratifies whatever the earlier stages happened to surface.

options.text: Ask for a summary of each of the eleven applications, so she has a manageable overview before deciding anything.
options.explanation: Summaries produced before the standard is set capture whatever each application emphasised about itself, which is not a comparable basis for choosing.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A team wants to generate innovative safety features for autonomous vehicles by first brainstorming ways the vehicle could fail or cause accidents, then inverting those to create safety solutions.
question: Which prompt best implements this 'reverse brainstorming' technique?

options.text: Instruct Claude to create a comprehensive list of safety features for autonomous vehicles, drawing from common industry practices, without first systematically identifying specific failure modes or accident scenarios that could be inverted into solutions.
options.explanation: This prompt skips the essential first step of the reverse brainstorming technique, which is to systematically identify failure modes or accident scenarios that could be inverted into solutions. Instead, it directly asks for safety features based on common industry practices, missing the opportunity to generate novel innovations from identified risks.

options.text: Ask Claude to think of potential ways autonomous vehicles could fail and then suggest general safety fixes, without mapping each failure to a specific inverted feature, thereby generating broad advice rather than traceable innovations.
options.explanation: Although it considers potential failures, it only requests general safety fixes without mapping each failure to a specific inverted feature. This approach yields broad advice rather than the precise, traceable innovations that reverse brainstorming requires.

options.text: Direct Claude to examine available accident data for autonomous vehicles and suggest safety features that target the most common accident types, without first brainstorming potential failure modes that could be inverted into solutions.
options.explanation: This prompt relies on existing accident data and targets only the most common types, which is an analytical approach rather than the creative process of reverse brainstorming. It skips the crucial first step of brainstorming potential failure modes that can be inverted into solutions, missing the technique's core.

options.text: Guide Claude to first identify potential failure modes and accident scenarios for autonomous vehicles, then for each, design a safety feature that directly addresses that risk, ensuring each solution is traceable to a specific problem.
options.explanation: This prompt follows the reverse brainstorming technique by first identifying failure modes and accident scenarios, then for each, designing a safety feature that directly addresses that risk. It ensures each solution is traceable to a specific problem, fostering targeted innovation.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A researcher asks Claude to answer a factual question that could be verified from several independent sources before being treated as reliable.
question: Which instruction best supports getting a trustworthy research answer?

options.text: Ask Claude to leave out which sources it consulted so the answer stays concise
options.explanation: Hiding which sources were consulted removes transparency and makes it harder to judge how well the claim was actually verified.

options.text: Ask Claude to answer only from the first source it finds so the reply comes back fastest
options.explanation: Relying on the first source found skips the verification step needed to establish that a research finding is reliable.

options.text: Ask Claude to cross-check the claim against several sources before calling it settled
options.explanation: Encouraging source verification, checking a claim across multiple sources, is a recommended practice for getting reliable results on research tasks.

options.text: Ask Claude to state the answer confidently no matter how many sources were checked
options.explanation: Confident phrasing unrelated to actual verification can misrepresent how well-supported the claim really is.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A press officer is unhappy with a draft announcement and types back: 'This isn't working, make it better.' The next draft is different but no closer to what she wants.
question: What would make her feedback more effective?

options.text: Describing the reaction she wants readers to have, and letting the wording follow from that intended reaction.
options.explanation: Describing an intended reaction is a step up from 'make it better', but it remains an outcome rather than a defect she can point to.

options.text: Pointing at the specific parts that miss, such as an opening that buries the change readers must act on.
options.explanation: Useful feedback identifies what is wrong with this draft and where. Naming the passage and the defect gives a target, whereas a general verdict leaves the next attempt to guess in a different direction.

options.text: Asking for several fresh drafts in different styles, so she can identify which of them comes closest to it.
options.explanation: Generating variety substitutes volume for direction, and she still has to articulate what is wrong once she has picked one.

options.text: Explaining her general preferences in announcements, such as a warm tone and short, uncomplicated sentences.
options.explanation: Stated preferences help across many drafts, but they do not say what this draft got wrong, so the same mistake can recur inside a warm, short-sentenced version.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A market research team has Claude summarise findings from six regional reports and now wants a final recommendation. Which two things should they do before asking for that recommendation?
question: Select two.

options.text: Agree the criteria the recommendation will be judged on, such as cost, risk and timing.
options.explanation: This is an independent point about specification rather than verification: without stated criteria, the recommendation cannot be argued for or assessed.

options.text: Check the summarised findings against the reports so the next step builds on solid ground.
options.explanation: The recommendation inherits every error in the summary stage. Verifying the intermediate output is what makes decomposition safer than one long prompt.

options.text: Paste all six original reports back in again so nothing at all can have been left out.
options.explanation: Re-pasting the full reports discards the work already done and pushes the team back to the single overloaded request that decomposition was meant to avoid.

options.text: Ask for three alternative recommendations at once and pick whichever one reads strongest.
options.explanation: Choosing on how a draft reads substitutes fluency for judgment, and none of the three options has been measured against anything the team actually cares about.

options.text: Move to a faster response setting, since the remaining step is short and mostly writing.
options.explanation: The final step is the judgment-heavy one, so speed is the wrong thing to optimise for here, and it does nothing about unverified inputs.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A prompt for an AI physician's assistant includes patient symptom notes, medical records, and appointment history, and Claude's diagnostic summaries sometimes reference irrelevant details buried in the documents.
question: What technique reduces this noise?

options.text: Ask Claude to first quote the relevant passages in a dedicated tag before writing its summary
options.explanation: Asking Claude to quote relevant parts of long documents before carrying out the task grounds the response in the source material and helps it cut through noise from irrelevant sections.

options.text: Tell Claude to answer the question first and read the documents afterward to check it
options.explanation: Reading the documents only after answering means Claude's initial answer isn't grounded in the source material at all, which is the opposite of the intended fix.

options.text: Instruct Claude to skip the patient records entirely and rely on general medical knowledge
options.explanation: Ignoring the patient records removes the exact source information needed for an accurate, grounded diagnosis and would make the task worse, not better.

options.text: Request that Claude summarize each document in one word before generating a diagnosis
options.explanation: A one-word summary would discard nearly all of the clinically relevant detail rather than helping Claude focus only on what matters.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A technical writer's system prompt says "NEVER use ellipses", but Claude occasionally still uses them in unusual contexts. The real reason for the rule is that Claude's responses are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, and the writer has not told Claude that. The writer wants Claude to generalize the rule reliably.
question: What should they add to the instruction?

options.text: Explain that the text-to-speech engine reading the responses aloud cannot pronounce ellipses
options.explanation: Anthropic's prompting guidance says that providing the context or motivation behind an instruction helps Claude understand the goal, and its own example pairs a bare ban on ellipses with the reason that a text-to-speech engine cannot pronounce them. Knowing the reason lets Claude generalize the rule to cases the writer did not anticipate.

options.text: Add several more exclamation marks to the instruction to emphasize how important the rule is
options.explanation: Adding emphasis through extra punctuation or capitalization does not tell Claude why the rule exists, so it does not help Claude generalize to edge cases the writer never listed.

options.text: Replace the instruction with a much longer list of every punctuation mark Claude should avoid
options.explanation: Listing more banned punctuation marks addresses symptoms rather than the underlying reason, and still would not cover every unanticipated case.

options.text: Ask Claude to run a careful spell-check pass after the response to catch any stray ellipses
options.explanation: A separate post-generation check adds an extra step but does not address why Claude keeps producing ellipses in the first place, because Claude still does not know the purpose of the rule.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A communications manager needs a twelve-page annual review written. She wants to catch problems early rather than after a full draft exists.
question: What should she ask for as the first stage?

options.text: A section-by-section outline naming what each section covers, which she can correct before any prose is written.
options.explanation: An outline is the cheapest artefact that still exposes the decisions that matter: coverage, emphasis and order. Correcting it takes minutes, whereas the same corrections applied to finished prose mean rewriting most of it.

options.text: A list of every source document that the review will need, so that she can gather all of them before writing begins.
options.explanation: A source list is a useful piece of preparation, but it says nothing about what the review will argue or how it will be organised.

options.text: The opening two pages written in full, so she can judge the tone and standard the rest will be written to.
options.explanation: Finished opening pages test tone but not structure, and the review's real risk is that the wrong things are covered in the wrong proportion.

options.text: A full first draft written quickly, on the understanding that she will mark it up heavily on her first read.
options.explanation: Marking up a complete draft is precisely the expensive rework she is trying to avoid, since structural changes at that point mean rewriting whole sections.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A teacher has written end-of-year report comments for every pupil in her class. The school's rule is that no comment may be pasted into Claude until the school office has confirmed that it is cleared for sharing with parents. She wants Claude to turn the cleared comments into short parent-friendly summaries, one pupil at a time, and the office wants every summary written at the same reading level and length.
question: Which sequence should she follow when putting the request together?

options.text: Confirm which comments are cleared for sharing; paste the cleared comments, by pupil; ask for one summary per pupil, leaving the reading level and length for Claude to choose.
options.explanation: The clearance check comes first and only cleared comments are pasted, but the request leaves the reading level and length for Claude to choose. The office wants every summary at the same reading level and length, and Claude's prompting guidance is to be specific about the desired output format and constraints, so those requirements have to be stated in the request.

options.text: Confirm which comments are cleared for sharing; paste the cleared comments in one block, without pupil names; ask for one combined summary of the whole class, stating the reading level and length.
options.explanation: The clearance check comes first, but pasting the comments in one block without pupil names throws away the pupil-by-pupil structure, and a single combined summary of the whole class is not the one summary per pupil the teacher wants. Stating the reading level and length does not repair a request for the wrong deliverable.

options.text: Paste every comment, by pupil; confirm which comments are cleared for sharing; ask for one summary per pupil of the cleared comments only, stating the reading level and length.
options.explanation: Every comment, including any the office has not cleared, is pasted before the clearance check, so the school's rule is already broken. Asking Claude to use only the cleared comments afterwards does not undo that, because the rule governs what may be pasted at all.

options.text: Confirm which comments are cleared for sharing; paste only the cleared comments, by pupil; ask for one summary per pupil, stating the reading level and length you want.
options.explanation: The school's rule says nothing is pasted until the office has confirmed it is cleared, so the check comes first and only the cleared comments go in. They are organized by pupil so each summary can be tied to one pupil, and the request asks for one summary per pupil while stating the reading level and length, which gives Claude the specific output constraints the office wants. Each step follows from the rule or the task in the scenario.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A policy analyst asked for an assessment of a proposed change and received four short paragraphs where she expected several pages of reasoning.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask for the same assessment again and request that this time it should be considerably more detailed.
options.explanation: More detailed is the same instruction the first attempt already implied, so it usually returns the same shape with a few extra sentences.

options.text: Ask what else could be said about this proposal, and add whatever comes back to the assessment she has.
options.explanation: Asking what else could be said produces additional material of unknown relevance, bolted onto an assessment that is still not aimed at her readers.

options.text: Ask for each of the four short paragraphs to be expanded in turn, then join those expansions into one assessment.
options.explanation: Expanding each paragraph inflates the existing structure, which cannot introduce the reasoning the original assessment never attempted.

options.text: State the depth she needs: who reads it, roughly how long it should run, and which questions it must settle.
options.explanation: Shallow output is usually an unstated expectation about depth. Naming the reader, the approximate length and the questions that must be settled converts a vague wish for more into a specification that can be met.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A policy officer must work through a 180-page regulatory guidance document that is too long to handle usefully in one request.
question: How should she divide it up?

options.text: Into the first fifty pages and the last fifty pages, on the basis that the middle is likely to be mostly detail.
options.explanation: Deciding in advance that the middle is unimportant discards material she has not read, and guidance documents commonly place the operative detail there.

options.text: Into as many small pieces as possible, so that each request stays short and every piece is handled thoroughly.
options.explanation: Very small pieces multiply the number of merges and make it more likely that a rule is read without the qualification that governs it.

options.text: Into equal blocks of thirty pages each, so that every part of the work is the same size and easy to plan around.
options.explanation: Fixed page blocks cut through the middle of arguments and definitions, so a part often contains a rule whose scope was set on the previous page.

options.text: Into the document's own chapters, so each part covers one complete topic and can be understood on its own terms.
options.explanation: The document's own structure marks where topics begin and end, so each part arrives complete, carries its own definitions, and can be summarised without depending on material that was cut away.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: An HR officer has spent forty minutes rewording a request for a summary of her organisation's absence policy. Each version comes back generic. She has never pasted the policy itself into the chat.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The successive versions will drift in tone, so the summary reads differently from her earlier internal notes.
options.explanation: Tone drift across versions is visible and easily corrected, and it is not what is keeping the summary generic.

options.text: She will settle on a version whose phrasing suits this policy but works poorly for other documents later on.
options.explanation: Wording tuned narrowly to one document is a genuine limitation, and it presumes the current wording works, which here it does not.

options.text: She keeps refining wording for a problem caused by absent material, so no rewording can produce the answer.
options.explanation: No phrasing can summarise a document that was never supplied. The forty minutes are spent on the wrong variable, and the fix is to paste the policy rather than to rewrite the request again.

options.text: The wording will grow so long over successive attempts that the central instruction is lost among the detail.
options.explanation: Accumulated wording is a real hazard in long iteration, but a shorter request without the policy attached returns exactly the same generic answer.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A project manager pastes her internal meeting notes into the chat and asks for the weekly client update. The notes include unreleased pricing and a blunt remark about the client's own team.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The update may come back shorter than usual, since the notes cover only what was raised in that one meeting.
options.explanation: A shorter update is a quality concern she would spot immediately, not a consequence that reaches the client unnoticed.

options.text: Material she supplied only as background may surface in the client-facing draft and be sent before anyone notices.
options.explanation: Everything pasted is treated as material available for the task unless the request says otherwise. Unreleased pricing and a candid internal remark are exactly the content that must be marked as background only, or removed before pasting.

options.text: The notes may be too long for one message, so part of the week's discussion is left out of the client update.
options.explanation: A set of meeting notes sits comfortably within a single message, and omissions from length are not what makes this situation hazardous.

options.text: The update may adopt a tone that is far too casual for the client, because her meeting notes were written casually.
options.explanation: Tone drift is real but visible on a first read, and it is corrected with one instruction about register.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: An operations coordinator will paste Claude's output straight into a tracking spreadsheet her team already maintains.
question: What should her request specify about the output?

options.text: That the result should be as detailed as possible, so she can delete whatever her tracker has no room to hold.
options.explanation: Maximum detail moves the work rather than removing it, and deleting surplus content by hand is the step she was trying to avoid.

options.text: That the result should be well organised and easy to read, leaving the exact presentation to Claude's judgement.
options.explanation: Easy to read is judged by a human reader, not by a spreadsheet. A well-organised answer in the wrong shape still has to be retyped column by column.

options.text: The exact columns she needs, in the order her tracker uses them, with one row for each item being tracked.
options.explanation: The destination dictates the format, so naming the columns, their order and the row unit produces output that transfers directly instead of output she has to rearrange.

options.text: That the result should be written as short paragraphs, which are simpler to copy across than a formatted table.
options.explanation: Prose is the hardest shape to move into a spreadsheet, because each paragraph has to be split into fields manually.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A grants officer asks Claude to draft the "community impact" section of a funding application, using a one-line prompt that names only the section. The funder publishes its assessment criteria for that section, and the application form strictly enforces a 500-word limit on it. Which two additions to that prompt would most improve the draft?
question: Select two.

options.text: Mention that the submission deadline falls on Friday so the request is urgent.
options.explanation: Deadlines and urgency are information about the officer's week, not about the task. Nothing in the brief becomes clearer, so the draft that comes back is the same draft.

options.text: State the 500-word cap and note that the application form enforces it strictly.
options.explanation: and for a separate reason from the criteria: it supplies a checkable constraint plus the reason behind it. A stated hard cap lets Claude budget the section, and knowing the form enforces it stops it from treating 500 words as a rough target.

options.text: Ask Claude to produce four separate versions and then pick the strongest itself.
options.explanation: Generating four versions from one under-specified brief produces four equally generic sections, and asking Claude to choose does not introduce the missing criteria or word limit. Volume is not a substitute for specification.

options.text: Add that the section should read as compelling and memorable for the reviewers.
options.explanation: "Compelling and memorable" are style adjectives that supply no facts and no measurable target. The draft changes register slightly and stays just as thin on the substance the funder asked for.

options.text: Paste the funder's published assessment criteria for that section.
options.explanation: The funder's criteria are the source material the draft has to satisfy, and pasting the real text beats describing it. Without them Claude writes generically about impact and can only guess what will be scored.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A writer wants Claude to draft technical explanations as flowing prose paragraphs rather than bullet-heavy markdown.
question: Which instruction best achieves this for a drafting task?

options.text: Ask Claude to bullet every key point so the explanation is easy to scan
options.explanation: Requesting bullets for every point produces the opposite of the flowing prose paragraphs the writer is asking for.

options.text: Tell Claude to write flowing prose, reserving markdown for code and simple headings
options.explanation: Telling Claude what to do instead of what not to do, describing the desired prose style directly, is the more effective way to steer output formatting for long-form drafting.

options.text: Tell Claude not to use any markdown, without saying what the response should look like
options.explanation: A bare prohibition without describing the desired prose format is a less effective way to steer formatting than telling Claude what to produce instead.

options.text: Leave the formatting instructions out and hope the default style matches
options.explanation: Omitting formatting guidance leaves the output style to chance rather than steering it toward the flowing prose the writer wants.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: An operations manager is asked to improve her team's onboarding process and wants to work through it with Claude across several stages.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to propose a plan for improving onboarding, and treat that plan as the set of stages to work through.
options.explanation: A proposed plan is a reasonable input, but accepting it as the structure hands over the framing decision before she has said what the work is for.

options.text: Name what the finished work must produce, since that determines how the work divides.
options.explanation: Settling the deliverable is what makes a split meaningful: a revised checklist divides differently from a business case for more headcount. Until the finished product is named, any breakdown is arbitrary.

options.text: Ask for onboarding practices used by similar teams, so the stages can be modelled on what already works well.
options.explanation: Comparative practice is useful later. Gathered first, it shapes the whole exercise around other teams' problems rather than her own.

options.text: Break the work into equal-sized pieces so that each stage can be completed in roughly the same amount of time.
options.explanation: Equal effort is a scheduling convenience, not a structure. It cuts across the natural dependencies in the work and leaves stages that cannot start until another finishes.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A team has revised a customer-facing explanation nine times, each round aimed at making it read better, and they are pleased with the current version.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Nine rounds of rewriting have changed what the text asserts, and nobody has re-checked those claims since.
options.explanation: Rewriting for readability quietly alters meaning: a qualifier disappears, a figure is rounded, a conditional becomes a promise. Because every round was judged on how it reads, nothing in the process re-tested accuracy.

options.text: The nine rounds may have taken longer than writing the explanation from scratch would have taken the team.
options.explanation: Effort spent is a cost the team accepted, and it does not affect what customers are being told.

options.text: The team may have grown so used to the text that they no longer notice awkward phrasing that remains in it.
options.explanation: Familiarity blunting a team's ear is a genuine effect, and it concerns style rather than whether the content is still true.

options.text: The explanation may now be shorter than customers need, since each round tended to remove material from it.
options.explanation: Successive edits do tend to trim, but a shorter explanation is visible to the team and easily restored.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A business analyst is deciding whether to send one large request or break it into stages. Which two features of a request are the strongest signals that it should be decomposed?
question: Select two.(Select 2)

options.text: It bundles several distinct deliverables that are meant for different audiences and uses.
options.explanation: Multiple deliverables with different readers pull the output in different directions, and one response has to compromise. Splitting lets each part be specified properly.

options.text: It concerns a subject area the analyst has not personally worked in for several years.
options.explanation: Unfamiliarity affects how carefully the analyst must review the result, but it says nothing about whether the request itself is structurally overloaded.

options.text: It runs to a long prompt because a good deal of background has been pasted in with it.
options.explanation: A long prompt is not the same as an overloaded one. Pasting rich source material is good practice and often makes a single-step request work better.

options.text: It asks for the final answer to be presented as a table rather than as flowing paragraphs.
options.explanation: Output format is a presentation choice. A table can be produced in one step just as easily as prose, so it is not a reason to break the work up.

options.text: Later parts are only worth producing if the earlier factual work is correct.
options.explanation: Dependency is a separate signal from bundling: when step two builds on step one, a single pass propagates any early error into everything downstream unchecked.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A data team asks Claude to analyze a dataset and wants extended reasoning reserved for questions that truly need multi-step thought, while simple lookups get a direct answer.
question: How should this guidance best be phrased?

options.text: Reserve deeper reasoning for cases needing multi-step thought, answering directly otherwise
options.explanation: Guidance that reasoning adds latency and should be reserved for problems needing multi-step thought, defaulting to a direct response otherwise, matches the recommended way to calibrate reasoning use to task complexity.

options.text: Tell Claude to always reason at the absolute maximum depth no matter how simple the lookup is
options.explanation: Always reasoning at maximum depth adds unnecessary latency for simple lookups that don't need multi-step analysis.

options.text: Tell Claude to randomly alternate between reasoning and direct answers each time
options.explanation: Randomly alternating disconnects the use of reasoning from actual question complexity, which is the opposite of calibrated guidance.

options.text: Tell Claude to never reason through any question so all replies return quickly
options.explanation: Never reasoning would undermine the multi-step analysis the data team wants for harder questions in the dataset.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A learning and development lead needs Claude to gather evidence on training approaches used across the sector, which is a research task rather than a drafting task. Which two prompt elements matter most here?
question: Select two.

options.text: The register and tone the finished piece should adopt for the board reading it later.
options.explanation: Tone is a drafting concern. Deciding the register now shapes how findings are worded before the lead knows what the findings actually are.

options.text: A filled-in template that the returned material should be poured into section by section.
options.explanation: A rigid template presumes the shape of the answer in advance and can push the research to fill boxes rather than report what the evidence supports.

options.text: An exact word count for the output so that it fits the slot in the meeting pack neatly.
options.explanation: A word count constrains presentation, and enforcing one during evidence gathering risks findings being trimmed to fit rather than reported in full.

options.text: The boundaries of the search, such as which countries and which years should be covered.
options.explanation: Research needs a defined scope, otherwise there is no way to say whether the result is complete or merely whatever surfaced first.

options.text: A request that each claim be traceable to a source the lead can open herself.
options.explanation: Traceability is separate from scope and is what makes a research output checkable, since the lead can confirm each claim against its origin.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A developer wants Claude to analyze a dataset and provide a reliable root-cause diagnosis.
question: Which prompt structure is most effective for guiding Claude to systematically analyze the data and avoid premature conclusions?

options.text: Instruct Claude to examine the provided data and give an immediate answer by selecting the most frequent pattern and assuming it causes the observed outcome, without verifying correlation.
options.explanation: This approach prompts Claude to jump to a conclusion based solely on frequency, without establishing a causal link. Anthropic's prompt engineering best practices emphasize giving Claude time to think and verifying its work. Simply assuming the most frequent pattern is the cause ignores the need to correlate patterns with outcomes and test hypotheses.

options.text: Ask Claude to filter the data for entries labeled 'critical' and report the most common entry as the root cause, without verifying its connection to the observed outcome.
options.explanation: This reduces analysis to a keyword filter and frequency count, ignoring the need to correlate patterns with outcomes and test hypotheses. Anthropic best practices warn against shallow heuristics and emphasize thorough, verified reasoning. Simply listing the most common 'critical' entry does not confirm causality and may miss subtle root causes.

options.text: Guide Claude to systematically analyze the data: isolate pattern frequency per category, correlate patterns with observed outcomes, formulate hypotheses, and recommend specific tests to confirm.
options.explanation: This prompt structure aligns with Anthropic's recommended practices for effective prompting. According to Anthropic documentation, Claude should be given clear, step-by-step instructions and a way to verify its work (e.g., recommending tests). This systematic approach—isolating frequencies, correlating with outcomes, formulating hypotheses, and validating—encourages Claude to think carefully and avoid premature conclusions, leading to more reliable diagnoses.

options.text: Prompt Claude to identify the first occurrence of each pattern and then conclude that the pattern that appeared earliest is the likely root cause.
options.explanation: This relies on a temporal heuristic—earliest occurrence—which does not establish causality. An early pattern may be unrelated to the outcome. This method skips systematic correlation and hypothesis testing, which are essential for reliable analysis.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A product manager asks Claude to "Create an analytics dashboard" and receives a bare-bones result with only the most basic charts. The manager wants a fully-featured result on the first try.
question: What should they change about the prompt?

options.text: Lower the temperature setting so that Claude systematically generates more creative dashboard layouts.
options.explanation: Lowering the temperature setting makes outputs more deterministic and less random, not more creative or detailed. This parameter does not compensate for a lack of explicit feature requests—Claude will still lack direction on what constitutes a fully-featured dashboard.

options.text: Repeat the identical short prompt several times; this repetition may signal Claude to add detail on its own.
options.explanation: Repeating the same short prompt adds no new information about the required features or scope, so Claude has no additional guidance to produce a more detailed result. Mere repetition does not signal that it should add detail on its own.

options.text: Ask Claude to first list ten dashboards it admires, then design its own from scratch based on those.
options.explanation: Asking Claude to list admired dashboards introduces an unrelated preliminary step without specifying the desired features or completeness. Even if it then designs based on those, the result may miss the specific elements the manager wants, making it an inefficient approach.

options.text: Explicitly request many relevant features and go beyond basic charts for a fully-featured dashboard.
options.explanation: Explicitly requesting many relevant features and going beyond basic charts directly communicates the desired scope and completeness to Claude. This replaces the vague prompt with clear, detailed instructions, ensuring a fully-featured dashboard on the first attempt.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A legal team needs to compare two lengthy contracts to highlight differences.
question: What is the safest decomposition approach with Claude?

options.text: Ask Claude to output a comparison table with both contracts in a single request.
options.explanation: Asking Claude to output a comparison table with both contracts in a single request risks exceeding the context window limit, leading to truncated input or incomplete comparisons. This approach also makes it harder to manage nuanced differences safely.

options.text: Summarize each contract separately, then compare the two summaries for key differences.
options.explanation: Summarizing each contract separately may omit important legal details and precise wording differences necessary for accurate comparison. Comparing only summaries is less reliable than directly comparing extracted clauses.

options.text: Extract the key clauses from each contract first, then compare them point by point.
options.explanation: Extracting key clauses first reduces complexity, focuses on relevant parts, and minimizes context overflow. This step-by-step decomposition improves accuracy by breaking the task into manageable, point-by-point comparisons.

options.text: Load both contracts into a single context window and ask for a detailed line-by-line diff.
options.explanation: Loading both lengthy contracts into a single context window to generate a detailed line-by-line diff risks exceeding the token limit, resulting in truncated input or an incomplete diff. This approach is less safe than decomposing the task for thorough comparison.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: A training lead asked for a course overview and got four short paragraphs where a detailed document was needed. Which two prompt revisions best address a response that is too brief?
question: Select two.

options.text: Request twice as many overviews so there is more material to choose between later.
options.explanation: Several shallow overviews are no substitute for one adequate document, and comparing them costs time without raising the depth of any of them.

options.text: Ask for the answer as bullet points rather than the paragraphs that were returned.
options.explanation: Bullets change the presentation only. Reformatting thin content tends to make it look even thinner rather than adding what is missing.

options.text: Set out the sections required and what each of them has to cover for this audience.
options.explanation: A required section list converts "more detail" into a concrete specification, and it makes any remaining gap visible when the next draft arrives.

options.text: Ask for the same overview again and add the note "please give me much more detail".
options.explanation: "More detail" without a definition of detail is guesswork. It is the standard weak retry and usually returns a slightly longer version of the same thing.

options.text: Say who will read it and why they need the reasoning as well as the conclusions.
options.explanation: Audience and purpose set the depth from a different direction: they tell Claude which explanations matter, not merely how many headings to fill.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A team lead wants Claude to brainstorm mitigation options for a project risk and then, separately, critically evaluate the feasibility of each option before a final recommendation.
question: Which structure fits this two-part need?

options.text: Ask Claude to evaluate feasibility before any mitigation ideas even exist yet
options.explanation: Evaluating feasibility before any ideas exist reverses the necessary order of brainstorming first and then assessing the generated options.

options.text: Skip generating multiple ideas and produce only the single most feasible option
options.explanation: Producing only a single mitigation option skips the broad brainstorming step meant to surface a range of ideas before evaluation.

options.text: Ask for the brainstormed ideas and the evaluation together in one combined response
options.explanation: Combining both steps into one response does not give the separately inspectable brainstorm and evaluation stages the team lead is asking for.

options.text: Chain two calls: generate mitigation ideas, then evaluate each one's feasibility
options.explanation: Chaining separate calls, generating ideas first and then reviewing them against criteria in a distinct step, fits the self-correction chaining pattern and supports separately inspecting the brainstormed ideas and the feasibility evaluation.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A marketing coordinator asked Claude to "write an email about our new feature" and received a generic announcement that could describe almost any product. Which two changes to the prompt would most improve the next draft?
question: Select two.

options.text: Send the same request a second time in capitals so the requirements are harder to miss.
options.explanation: Repeating an identical prompt with added emphasis is the classic non-fix. Nothing new has been communicated, so there is no reason for the output to improve.

options.text: Say who will receive the email and what they should do after reading it.
options.explanation: Telling Claude who will receive the email and what they should do afterwards defines what the email is for, without assuming anything about who those readers are. This is a separate fix from supplying facts: it constrains framing, emphasis and the call to action.

options.text: Paste in the real release notes rather than describing the feature in a single line.
options.explanation: A generic draft is usually a symptom of missing source material. Pasting the real release notes gives Claude the specifics it otherwise has to invent or gloss over.

options.text: Ask for a much longer draft, on the view that a longer email carries more useful detail.
options.explanation: Length is not the problem. Asking for more words on an under-specified brief produces a longer generic email, and often padding rather than substance.

options.text: Add a sentence asking Claude to write in a warm voice that readers will genuinely enjoy.
options.explanation: Style adjectives such as "warm" and "enjoyable" do not supply any of the missing product facts, so the draft stays generic and simply changes register.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A communications team has a reliable recipe for drafting: name the audience, set the format and attach examples of accepted work. Applied to a question about why complaint volumes doubled, it returns a weak answer.
question: What is missing?

options.text: Examples of complaint analyses that the team has previously accepted, so the shape of a good answer is clear.
options.explanation: Examples convey the shape and register of a finished piece, which is why they work for drafting. They cannot supply the figures this question turns on.

options.text: A stated format for the answer, such as a short summary followed by the supporting detail underneath it.
options.explanation: Format organises an answer, and the problem here is that there is no substance for a format to organise.

options.text: A more precisely named audience, since an answer written for the board differs from one written for the team.
options.explanation: A sharper audience improves how the answer is pitched, and an answer pitched perfectly at the board can still be built on nothing.

options.text: The complaint data itself, along with the specific question about it that the answer is expected to settle.
options.explanation: Drafting is constrained by audience, format and voice; analysis is constrained by evidence and by the question being asked. The recipe supplies all of the first set and none of the second, so it produces well-presented speculation.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: Over eight rounds of revision, a team notices that fixing the newest complaint often brings back a problem they had solved three rounds earlier. Nothing about their requirements is written down.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The team will spend more time on revisions than they would have spent writing the document themselves.
options.explanation: Time spent is a real cost, but the team would accept it if the rounds were converging. The problem is that they are not.

options.text: The wording of the request will become long and repetitive as fixes for each separate complaint accumulate.
options.explanation: An accumulating request is an untidy side effect, and it does not by itself cause earlier fixes to be lost.

options.text: The eighth version will read less naturally than the first, because it has been adjusted so many times over.
options.explanation: Prose quality drifting under repeated revision is worth watching, but it is a milder issue than requirements silently reversing.

options.text: With no record of what the document must satisfy, each round can undo an earlier fix and nobody notices.
options.explanation: Without a written list of everything the document must satisfy, each round is checked only against the latest complaint. Requirements settled earlier are not re-tested, so the work circles instead of converging.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A communications lead has twenty minutes to produce a holding statement about a service outage. Details are still arriving from the operations team and some are unconfirmed.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask what similar organisations usually say during an outage, and adapt the closest example to this situation.
options.explanation: Borrowed wording describes someone else's incident. Adapting it risks asserting a cause or a restoration time that has not been established here.

options.text: Wait until operations has confirmed every detail, then ask for a single accurate statement for publication.
options.explanation: A holding statement exists precisely because confirmation is incomplete, so waiting for certainty means missing the twenty-minute window.

options.text: Write down which facts are confirmed and which are not, and give Claude both lists with the request itself.
options.explanation: Separating confirmed from unconfirmed is the judgement only she can make, and supplying both lists lets the statement assert what is known while explicitly not committing to what is not.

options.text: Ask for a general outage holding statement now, and add the organisation's specific details once they are confirmed.
options.explanation: A generic statement drafted without the confirmed facts has to be rewritten once they arrive, and it invites unconfirmed details to be slotted in under deadline pressure.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A product marketer needs a summary of what three competitors announced during the past quarter.
question: Which addition to the request matters most for this kind of task?

options.text: A request that each announcement carry the source it came from and the date, so recent claims can be checked.
options.explanation: Recent events are exactly where an unsupported summary is most likely to go wrong, so a research task of this kind needs each item traceable to where it was reported and when. Sources and dates are what make the summary checkable.

options.text: A request that the summary be organised competitor by competitor rather than being organised by announcement date.
options.explanation: Grouping by competitor makes the summary easier to navigate, and it does nothing to establish that the announcements listed were real.

options.text: A request that the summary group the announcements by the product area each of the three announcements affects.
options.explanation: Grouping by product area is a useful lens for her team, but it arranges claims that have not yet been shown to be accurate.

options.text: A request that the summary be written in the same style as the internal updates her team already circulates.
options.explanation: Matching house style makes the summary comfortable to read, which is a drafting concern rather than a research one.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: An events team wants a wide field of ideas for a member engagement campaign before narrowing down. Which two prompt choices best suit this brainstorming stage?
question: Select two.

options.text: Ask for the single strongest idea straight away so the team can start work sooner.
options.explanation: Jumping to one recommendation skips the divergent step entirely, and it hides the alternatives the team asked for precisely so they could compare them.

options.text: Provide one finished campaign write-up and ask for close variations on that model.
options.explanation: Anchoring on a finished example narrows the output to near-copies, which is useful when matching a template but counterproductive when seeking range.

options.text: State the limits any idea must respect, such as a small budget and six weeks.
options.explanation: Constraints serve a different purpose from breadth: they keep the wide field usable by excluding options the team could never actually run.

options.text: Fix the tone, house style and final format so every idea arrives ready to publish.
options.explanation: Publication-ready styling belongs to the drafting stage. Applied now it wastes effort on ideas that will mostly be discarded and slows the divergent pass.

options.text: Ask for a spread of clearly different directions, each given a short label and a line.
options.explanation: Brainstorming values coverage over polish. Short labelled options let the team scan a wide field cheaply, which polished prose actively discourages.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: An events lead must recommend a new format for her organisation's annual conference to the board, and plans to work through it with Claude in stages rather than in one request.
question: Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Assemble last year's delegate feedback and the cost figures for each format; compare the candidate formats against those constraints; agree the decision the board must make and the budget and venue constraints; draft the recommendation the board will read.
options.explanation: The constraints arrive after the comparison is already finished, so they cannot shape it.

options.text: Assemble last year's delegate feedback and the cost figures for each format; agree the decision the board must make and the budget and venue constraints; compare the candidate formats against those constraints; draft the recommendation the board will read.
options.explanation: Gathering evidence before agreeing the decision and constraints collects material that may turn out to be irrelevant.

options.text: Agree the decision the board must make and the budget and venue constraints; compare the candidate formats against those constraints; assemble last year's delegate feedback and the cost figures for each format; draft the recommendation the board will read.
options.explanation: Comparing the formats before the feedback and costs are assembled leaves the comparison resting on nothing.

options.text: Agree the decision the board must make and the budget and venue constraints; assemble last year's delegate feedback and the cost figures for each format; compare the candidate formats against those constraints; draft the recommendation the board will read.
options.explanation: The decision and its constraints come first, because they determine which evidence matters; evidence is then gathered, the formats are compared against the constraints, and only then is the recommendation written.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A researcher has produced separate findings for each of five regional markets and now wants them combined into one view.
question: What should the combining request specify?

options.text: That the five regions should each appear in the combined view in order of the revenue they contribute to the business.
options.explanation: Revenue order affects presentation only, and it can bury a serious finding from a small market at the end of the document.

options.text: That the combined view should be shorter than the five sets of findings added together, to keep it readable.
options.explanation: A length target shapes the summary but says nothing about which findings survive, so the reduction happens on unstated grounds.

options.text: How to handle findings that overlap and findings that conflict, so those decisions are made openly and not quietly.
options.explanation: Merging is where a genuine disagreement between regions can be smoothed into a single confident sentence. Saying in advance how overlaps and conflicts are treated keeps those differences visible, since a conflict between regions is often the most useful finding.

options.text: That the strongest of the five sets of findings should be used as the template the other four are all rewritten into.
options.explanation: Forcing four regions into the shape of a fifth discards whatever each of them found that does not fit that template.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: An analyst has refined the wording she uses for supplier reviews across many rounds, using the same supplier's file throughout. She now wants to adopt it as her team's standard wording.
question: What should she do before that?

options.text: Record the reasoning behind each instruction, so that colleagues understand why the wording is written this way.
options.explanation: Documenting the reasoning helps the team maintain the wording later, but it assumes the wording already generalises.

options.text: Shorten the wording so that colleagues who have not followed the refinement can still take it in quickly.
options.explanation: Shortening improves how approachable the wording is, and it may remove instructions whose value has not been established.

options.text: Ask colleagues to read the wording through and confirm that they find the instructions in it clear enough.
options.explanation: A readability check confirms colleagues can follow the instructions, not that the instructions work on a supplier file she never tested.

options.text: Try it on two or three other suppliers' files, since it may have been shaped to fit the one file she used.
options.explanation: Wording refined against a single example tends to encode that example's quirks, such as its headings or its level of detail. Trying it on other files is what separates a genuine improvement from one that only fits the case it was built on.

objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
situation: After four rounds, an internal newsletter item is accurate and well structured, but two headings use the wrong department names. The item is due in ten minutes.
question: What should the editor do?

options.text: Rewrite her original request to include the department names, and produce a fresh version of the whole item.
options.explanation: Regenerating the item risks the accuracy and structure that four rounds established, with ten minutes left to verify them.

options.text: Correct the two headings herself, since the remaining gap is smaller than the effort of another full round.
options.explanation: Iteration is worth continuing while it is cheaper than doing the work by hand. Two headings are a few seconds of typing, so this is the point to stop iterating and finish it herself.

options.text: Publish the item as it stands and issue a short correction about the department names in next week's edition.
options.explanation: Publishing known errors and correcting them later costs the team credibility over a fix that takes moments.

options.text: Run one more round asking for the department names to be corrected, and read the returned version closely.
options.explanation: Another round can fix two words, but it returns a whole document that has to be re-read to confirm nothing else moved.

objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
situation: A prompt describes a multi-step setup process, such as configuring an environment and then running a script, but Claude sometimes performs the steps out of order.
question: What change would make the required order unambiguous?

options.text: Provide the instructions as a numbered list of steps in the exact order they must run
options.explanation: Providing instructions as sequential steps using numbered lists or bullet points is recommended specifically when the order or completeness of the steps matters, removing ambiguity about sequence.

options.text: Combine all of the steps into a single long sentence separated only by commas
options.explanation: A single comma-separated sentence obscures step boundaries and order even more than a plain paragraph would, making the sequence less clear rather than more.

options.text: Describe the steps in a random order and let Claude infer the correct sequence
options.explanation: Describing steps out of order and relying on inference is the opposite of making the required sequence unambiguous.

options.text: Remove the step numbers and rely only on paragraph breaks to imply the correct order
options.explanation: Relying only on paragraph breaks without numbering removes the explicit ordering cue that numbered lists provide for steps where sequence matters.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A researcher has fifteen sets of interview notes and must produce a findings section for a report.
question: Which sequence of stages should she follow?

options.text: Check each theme against the notes; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; write the findings section; group the extracts into themes.
options.explanation: Checking themes that have not yet been formed is not possible, and grouping after the section is written leaves the writing unsupported.

options.text: Group the extracts into themes; check each theme against the notes; write the findings section; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes.
options.explanation: Themes cannot be grouped before the extracts have been pulled, so this ordering starts from material that has not been gathered.

options.text: Pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; group the extracts into themes; check each theme against the notes; write the findings section.
options.explanation: Extracts come out of the notes first, grouping turns them into themes, the check confirms each theme is genuinely supported before it becomes a claim, and the section is written last from verified material.

options.text: Write the findings section; group the extracts into themes; pull the relevant extracts from each set of notes; check each theme against the notes.
options.explanation: Findings written before the extracts exist are assertions in search of evidence, and the checking stage arrives after the section is already written.

objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
situation: A product team is brainstorming new feature ideas and wants Claude to generate a wide range of genuinely different concepts rather than several variations on the same idea.
question: What should the team do when providing example ideas in the prompt?

options.text: Include no examples at all so nothing biases the range of ideas produced
options.explanation: While examples aren't required, omitting them does not itself guarantee variety; well-chosen diverse examples are the recommended way to actively support a broad range of ideas.

options.text: Include a small set of deliberately varied examples so Claude avoids one narrow pattern
options.explanation: Examples should be diverse, covering edge cases and varying enough that Claude does not pick up an unintended narrow pattern, which supports a wide range of brainstormed ideas.

options.text: Include just one example and ask Claude to generate close variations of it
options.explanation: Asking for close variations of one example directly narrows the output to minor tweaks instead of a wide range of distinct ideas.

options.text: Include many examples that all follow the exact same structure as just one clear pattern
options.explanation: Uniform examples that all share the same structure and theme encourage Claude to converge on that single pattern rather than exploring genuinely different concepts.

objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
situation: A team's breakdown of a supplier review ends with a stage described as 'format the findings and add the recommended supplier to the summary page'.
question: What is the greatest concern with this stage?

options.text: Formatting and writing in the same stage makes the stage take longer than the other stages in the breakdown.
options.explanation: Uneven stage durations are a planning detail rather than a risk to the integrity of the review.

options.text: The recommended supplier will appear on the summary page before it appears in the body of the review itself.
options.explanation: Ordering within the document is an editorial choice, and the recommendation appearing early is normal in a review of this kind.

options.text: The summary page may end up formatted differently from the rest of the review, which readers will find jarring.
options.explanation: Inconsistent formatting is a cosmetic defect that a single pass fixes, and it does not affect which supplier is chosen.

options.text: A decision that should be made and reviewed on its own is folded into a step everyone treats as presentation.
options.explanation: Naming the recommendation is the consequential act of the whole review, and burying it in a formatting step means nobody schedules a review of it. Decisions should sit in stages of their own, where they can be challenged.
