options.text: Find each of those statements in the published regulations; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.
options.explanation: She would be looking statements up before deciding which statements matter, so the search has no defined scope and ordinary descriptive sentences get treated as regulatory claims.

options.text: Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.
options.explanation: Singling out the sentences that make a regulatory claim scopes the work; each of those is then traced to the published regulations, which is the authoritative source rather than the draft itself; corrections follow from what that comparison found; and recording the version used makes the check repeatable when the regulations change.

options.text: Correct any statement the regulations do not support; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.
options.explanation: Editing comes first of all, before either the claims have been identified or the regulations opened, so the handbook is changed on no evidence at all.

options.text: Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.
options.explanation: Corrections are made before the regulations have been consulted, which means they rest on what she assumes the rules say. The lookup that should have driven the edits arrives after them.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A manager has fifteen minutes to check a six-page recommendation before a decision meeting. She cannot verify everything in it.
question: What should she concentrate on?

options.text: The passages that are written most confidently, because strongly worded claims carry the most weight in a meeting.
options.explanation: Confidence of expression is unrelated to whether a claim is load-bearing, and a quietly stated figure can be the one the recommendation turns on.

options.text: An even sample drawn from each of the six pages, so that no part of the document goes entirely unexamined.
options.explanation: Even sampling spreads scarce attention across material of very unequal importance, so a decisive figure gets the same scrutiny as background.

options.text: The opening and closing sections, since these are what most attendees will actually read before the meeting.
options.explanation: Checking what will be read protects the meeting's impression of the document but leaves the reasoning behind the recommendation unexamined.

options.text: The few facts the recommendation depends on, since the decision changes if any one of them turns out to be wrong.
options.explanation: With limited time, verification should follow consequence. Identifying the handful of facts that would reverse the recommendation concentrates the check where an error would actually change the outcome.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: A communications officer needs a one-page summary to hand out at an event, with the supporting detail available for anyone who asks afterwards.
question: How should she organise the material?

options.text: Produce one long document containing both the summary and every piece of supporting detail.
options.explanation: A single document that tries to do both is too long to hand out and too summary-led to serve as a reference.

options.text: Produce the handout only, and answer any requests for supporting detail verbally on the day.
options.explanation: Relying on recall leaves the detail unavailable afterwards and inconsistent between conversations.

options.text: Produce a short handout as the deliverable and keep the detail as a separate reference document.
options.explanation: Two audiences with different needs are served by two artefacts, so neither the handout nor the reference is compromised to accommodate the other.

options.text: Produce the supporting detail only, since anyone wanting a summary can read its opening section.
options.explanation: An opening section written for a detailed document is not a handout, and event audiences will not read the rest.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A financial services firm asks Claude to generate personalized investment recommendations for retail clients based on their stated goals.
question: Before any recommendation is sent to a client, what should happen?

options.text: A licensed financial advisor reviews the recommendation for suitability and regulatory compliance
options.explanation: Investment advice is a regulated, high-stakes domain, so a licensed advisor must confirm suitability and compliance before a recommendation reaches a client.

options.text: The recommendation is sent as-is since it was generated from the client's own stated goals
options.explanation: Basing the recommendation on client-stated goals does not eliminate the risk of an unsuitable or non-compliant suggestion reaching the client unreviewed.

options.text: Claude is asked to double-check its own math and confirm the recommendation is internally consistent
options.explanation: Self-checking arithmetic does not address whether a recommendation is suitable for the client or compliant with financial regulations.

options.text: A marketing team member reviews the wording only for tone and readability before sending
options.explanation: Reviewing only tone and readability ignores the substantive suitability and compliance risks that matter most for financial advice.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A workforce planning lead uses Claude to condense several years of performance notes into short profiles, then ranks the profiles to build a promotion shortlist. Reviewing them, she sees that people from one team are consistently described in warmer language than people from another.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The profiles will read inconsistently to the panel, which may find the varying tone across the shortlist distracting during the meeting.
options.explanation: Inconsistent tone is a real presentational flaw, but it is a cosmetic one. It understates what is happening: the tone difference is tracking group membership, and that is what makes it serious rather than untidy.

options.text: The condensing step will have shortened some profiles more than others, so the panel spends unequal reading time on each individual.
options.explanation: Uneven length affects how much attention each profile receives, which is a genuine fairness concern, but it is a second-order effect next to systematically warmer wording being applied to one group of people.

options.text: A skew in the language becomes a skew in the ranking, so a decision about people's careers is shaped by a pattern nobody examined.
options.explanation: Bias in a summary becomes bias in the outcome once the summaries are ranked, and converting it into a shortlist hides the original wording, so an unexamined pattern silently drives a high-stakes decision about people.

options.text: The notes may be old enough that some achievements described in the profiles have since been superseded by more recent work.
options.explanation: Stale source notes would undermine accuracy and are worth checking separately, but they do not explain a pattern that follows team membership, and they are not the greatest risk in a promotion decision.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A team is adding a new Claude-assisted output into an existing process and has to work out how much checking it will get.
question: In which order should these steps be taken?

options.text: Set the level of review that degree of risk requires; judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience.
options.explanation: The review level is being fixed before anyone has worked out the risk, so the assessment that should have driven the decision arrives too late to inform it.

options.text: Release the output to its audience; judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; set the level of review that degree of risk requires; have the named reviewer carry out that review.
options.explanation: Releasing first defeats the whole exercise. Any risk assessment and review that follow publication cannot prevent the harm they were meant to catch.

options.text: Judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; set the level of review that degree of risk requires; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience.
options.explanation: Visibility and reversibility determine how much scrutiny an output deserves, so they are assessed first; that assessment sets the required level of review, the named reviewer then performs it, and only then does the output reach its audience.

options.text: Judge how visible the output is and how easily a mistake in it could be undone; have the named reviewer carry out that review; release the output to its audience; set the level of review that degree of risk requires.
options.explanation: The review happens with no agreed standard behind it, and the level of review is only settled after the output has already gone out, which is the wrong way round.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: A team lead wants a reusable onboarding checklist that colleagues will revise over time.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Share it with the team; agree the steps it must cover; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place.
options.explanation: Nothing exists to share at the first step, which makes the whole ordering unworkable.

options.text: Ask Claude for the checklist as a document; agree the steps it must cover; revise it in place; share it with the team.
options.explanation: The checklist is drafted before anyone has agreed what belongs in it, so the revision step is doing work the first step should have done.

options.text: Agree the steps it must cover; share it with the team; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place.
options.explanation: The checklist is shared before it has been written, and the revision happens after colleagues have already received it.

options.text: Agree the steps it must cover; ask Claude for the checklist as a document; revise it in place; share it with the team.
options.explanation: Content is settled first, a self-contained editable document is the right home for something reused and revised, and it is shared once it is ready.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: An HR team has a Claude-drafted consultation letter that will be sent to forty staff whose roles are at risk, and the wording is governed by employment law.
question: Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Judge the stakes of the letter, then name the reviewer it requires, then have that reviewer check it against the consultation policy, then send it once approval is recorded.
options.explanation: The stakes are high, regulated and irreversible, so the level of scrutiny is decided first, a named person is made accountable for the review, the check is made against the governing policy, and despatch happens only after recorded approval.

options.text: Record who approved the wording, then send the letter to the forty staff, then check it against the consultation policy, then have the HR lead read it.
options.explanation: Recording an approval before anyone has reviewed the letter documents a sign-off that never happened, and the substantive checks still fall after the letter has already gone out.

options.text: Send the letter to the forty staff, then have the HR lead read it, then check it against the consultation policy, then record who approved the wording.
options.explanation: Sending first makes every later step a post-mortem. A consultation letter cannot be recalled from forty recipients, so review carried out after despatch cannot prevent the harm it is meant to prevent.

options.text: Check the letter against the consultation policy, then send it to the forty staff, then judge the stakes of what was sent, then name a reviewer to look over it carefully afterwards.
options.explanation: Checking against the policy first is sensible, but sending before any named person has reviewed the letter or the stakes have been weighed removes the human review gate exactly where irreversibility demands it.

objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
situation: A manager has asked Claude for two different versions of a strategy update and must choose one for a board pack.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude which of its two versions is the stronger and take that recommendation forward.
options.explanation: Claude has not been told what this board needs, so its preference is about writing quality rather than fit.

options.text: Read both versions through carefully and pick whichever one reads more persuasively to her.
options.explanation: Persuasiveness to the writer is not the test; a polished draft can still fail to give the board what it needs to decide.

options.text: Merge the two versions into one document so that nothing useful from either is left behind.
options.explanation: Merging before criteria exist produces a longer document that serves the board less well than either original.

options.text: Write down what the board needs to take from the update before she reads either version.
options.explanation: Without stated criteria a comparison collapses into which draft reads more nicely. Setting the audience's needs down first makes the choice a judgment rather than a preference.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A programme office is setting a policy for how much scrutiny Claude-generated work should receive. Which two factors raise the level of human review required?
question: Select two.

options.text: The prompt that produced the output was long and included pasted background.
options.explanation: Prompt length says nothing about consequence. A well-supplied prompt may even reduce risk, and it certainly does not raise the review bar by itself.

options.text: A large number of people would be affected if the output turned out to be wrong.
options.explanation: Blast radius is independent of reversibility: a mistake that is easy to correct can still reach many people before anyone notices it.

options.text: The action that follows from the output would be hard to undo once taken.
options.explanation: Low reversibility means an error cannot be quietly fixed later, so the check has to happen before the action rather than after it.

options.text: The output arrived in a document format the team has not used very often before.
options.explanation: An unfamiliar file format is a practical inconvenience for the team, not a reason to apply more scrutiny to the content inside it.

options.text: The output was produced faster than the same work would have taken by hand.
options.explanation: Speed of production is not a risk factor. How long the work took has no bearing on what happens if the content is wrong.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A marketing lead asks Claude for a competitor briefing, and the draft states that the competitor won a named industry award last year. She can find no record of that award anywhere.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Establish whether the award claim came from material she supplied or from Claude's general knowledge.
options.explanation: Knowing where a claim originated is what separates a fabrication from a real detail she simply has not located, and it determines every step that follows.

options.text: Ask Claude whether it is confident about the award before she spends any more time on it.
options.explanation: A statement of confidence is generated the same way the claim was, so it adds no independent information about whether the award exists.

options.text: Ask Claude to restate the award claim with more supporting detail so that it becomes easier to check.
options.explanation: Asking for more detail around an unsupported claim usually produces more unsupported detail, which makes the claim harder to dismiss rather than easier to check.

options.text: Delete the sentence about the award and circulate the remainder of the draft to her wider team.
options.explanation: Removing one sentence treats the symptom. If the claim was invented, other statements in the same draft may be too, and she has not yet found out.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: A project manager asks Claude to map out a five-stage approval workflow with branching decision points so the team can reference it during a planning meeting.
question: What is the best way for Claude to present this?

options.text: A JSON object listing each stage as a key-value pair, since structured data is the standard way to represent any multi-step process
options.explanation: Structured JSON is intended for programmatic data consumption, not for a human-facing reference the team will look at during a meeting.

options.text: An inline bulleted list describing each stage in one sentence, since bullet lists are always clearer than diagrams for workflow steps
options.explanation: A text list cannot easily convey branching decision points the way a flowchart can, so it is not the best fit here even though it could work for a simple linear list.

options.text: An artifact containing a Mermaid flowchart, since diagrams are a supported artifact type well suited to visualizing branching workflows
options.explanation: Diagrams and flowcharts are a supported artifact content type, and a branching workflow with decision points is naturally suited to visual representation the team can reference later.

options.text: A strict tool call that returns the workflow stages as validated tool parameters, since tool calls guarantee the stages are correctly ordered
options.explanation: Strict tool use validates parameters sent to an application tool; it is not a presentation format for sharing a workflow with a team.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A grants officer reads a Claude-written explainer of a funding scheme and notices that it gives one closing date in the opening paragraph and a different closing date three paragraphs later.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude which of the two dates it meant, and use whichever one it settles on when it is asked to resolve the conflict.
options.explanation: Asking the same conversation to arbitrate treats Claude as a singular source of truth on exactly the point where it has already demonstrated it is unreliable, and it will produce a confident answer either way.

options.text: Delete the earlier paragraph so the explainer no longer contradicts itself, and circulate the corrected version today.
options.explanation: Removing one of the two dates makes the internal contradiction disappear without resolving it, which is worse than leaving it visible: the surviving date may well be the wrong one, and the warning sign has been erased.

options.text: Go back to the funder's own published scheme rules and establish which closing date, if either of them, is the real one.
options.explanation: An internal contradiction shows at least one statement is unreliable, and it cannot be settled inside the response. Checking the funder's own published rules resolves it against an authoritative source rather than relying on Claude alone.

options.text: Keep the later of the two dates on the basis that it was written after Claude had processed more of the scheme material.
options.explanation: Position in a response carries no evidential weight; a later sentence is not better sourced than an earlier one. Picking a date by where it appeared leaves the officer publishing a deadline she has never verified.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: During a troubleshooting chat, a user asks Claude, "Is port 443 the default HTTPS port?" Claude's answer is a single confirming sentence.
question: What is the appropriate output treatment for this response?

options.text: Ask a strict tool to validate the port number against a schema before responding, since numeric facts require schema validation
options.explanation: Claude can directly answer common factual questions like default port numbers from its training data without needing external tool validation. Using a tool for such a basic fact would introduce unnecessary overhead and complexity.

options.text: Create a Markdown document artifact titled "HTTPS Port Reference," since any factual networking answer should be saved for later use
options.explanation: Not every factual answer demands an artifact. Artifacts are intended for content that is substantial and reusable, such as comprehensive guides or documents. A single port confirmation is too trivial to warrant an artifact.

options.text: Package the answer as a JSON object with a "confirmed" boolean field, since factual yes/no answers should always use structured data
options.explanation: While structured data can be useful for programmatic interactions, a casual chat does not require packaging every fact into a JSON object. Anthropic’s documentation does not mandate that all yes/no answers be structured; inline natural language is perfectly acceptable.

options.text: Answer inline within the conversation, since a single confirming sentence has no reuse value that would justify an artifact
options.explanation: Inline answers are appropriate for short, simple responses that do not constitute a substantial, reusable piece of content. Artifacts are reserved for content that is more complex and self-contained, such as code, documents, or long-form text. This aligns with Anthropic’s guidance on using artifacts for significant content.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: An analyst has forty Claude-drafted product descriptions. About half will be posted on the public website and half will sit in an internal catalogue, and she has time to check roughly twenty of them properly before the deadline.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Check the longest descriptions first, because a longer description contains more claims to get wrong.
options.explanation: Length is not a proxy for stakes. A short line of public-facing copy can be far more damaging than a long internal entry, so sorting by length would leave the riskiest items unchecked.

options.text: Check the descriptions in the order they were generated, until the time she has set aside runs out.
options.explanation: Working in generation order spends her limited review time at random. The website copy and the internal catalogue do not carry the same consequences, so order of arrival is the wrong basis for choosing.

options.text: Sort the batch by where each description will end up and how hard an error there would be to undo.
options.explanation: With review capacity smaller than the batch, the first step is to triage by exposure and reversibility. Externally published copy that is hard to retract earns the scarce review time; an internal entry anyone can correct does not.

options.text: Ask Claude to mark the descriptions it is least sure of, and check only the ones that it flags.
options.explanation: A model's own stated uncertainty is a weak and unvalidated signal, and it says nothing about consequences. It can be a useful supplement, but it cannot decide which outputs need human eyes.

objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
situation: A learning and development specialist has a Claude-drafted explanation of a new expenses process written for finance staff. She now needs a version for field engineers who never open the finance system.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Cut the draft down to roughly half its present length so that the field engineers will read it.
options.explanation: Halving the length is an arbitrary cut with no principle behind it, and it is as likely to remove the steps the engineers need as the ones they do not.

options.text: Ask Claude to simplify the wording of the existing text until it reads a good deal more easily.
options.explanation: Simplifying the wording keeps the finance staff's version of the process and only changes its surface. The engineers would get an easier read of material that is still organised around someone else's job.

options.text: Ask Claude to add a glossary explaining the finance terms that the draft already uses.
options.explanation: A glossary makes unfamiliar terminology survivable but leaves the engineers reading a finance-system walkthrough that mostly does not apply to them.

options.text: Work out what the field engineers actually have to do differently, and write to that.
options.explanation: Adapting for an audience starts from what that audience needs to do, not from the existing text. Once she knows which parts of the process the engineers actually touch, the register, the length and the level of detail all follow from it.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A grants officer facing a deadline has used Claude to draft eligibility determinations for ninety applicants, and each determination will be sent directly to the applicant. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, which two things must happen before the determinations are issued?
question: Select two.

options.text: Claude is asked to review its own determinations and flag any it is unsure about.
options.explanation: Self-review is not verification. A determination that misread a rule will often be reported as confident, so the cases most in need of attention stay hidden.

options.text: A qualified officer checks each determination against the published eligibility rules.
options.explanation: The Usage Policy requires that a qualified professional review a decision directly affecting individuals before it is finalized. Eligibility for funding is such a decision, so each one needs checking against the actual rules rather than sampling or spot checks.

options.text: Each determination that goes out tells the applicant that Claude helped produce it.
options.explanation: When model outputs are presented directly to individuals, the Usage Policy requires disclosing to them that AI helped produce the decision, so each determination sent to an applicant must say that Claude helped produce it. An internal file note alone would not tell the applicant.

options.text: Only the determinations that look borderline are pulled out for a person to read.
options.explanation: Borderline cases are identified by the same process being verified, so anything wrongly classed as clear-cut is exactly what this approach fails to catch.

options.text: Claude is recorded as the decision-maker, so responsibility for each one rests with the tool.
options.explanation: Responsibility cannot be handed to the tool. The Usage Policy states that the user or their organization is responsible for the accuracy and appropriateness of the information, so recording Claude as the decision-maker leaves no accountable person and does nothing to make the determinations correct.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A sales operations lead asked Claude to summarise two quarters of win-loss notes. Early in the summary it states that deals are lost mainly on price, and two paragraphs later it attributes most losses to slow implementation timelines.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Go back to the win-loss notes themselves and see what they actually say about the losses.
options.explanation: An internal contradiction means at least one of the two statements is unsupported, and the notes she uploaded are the ground truth. Reading what the losses were actually recorded as resolves the inconsistency and shows which half of the summary can be trusted.

options.text: Keep the price explanation, since it appears first and is the more familiar of the two.
options.explanation: Position in the text is not evidence, and preferring the more familiar explanation is exactly the bias the review is supposed to catch. It could entrench a wrong conclusion about why the company is losing deals.

options.text: Ask Claude to produce the summary again and go with whichever explanation comes back next.
options.explanation: Regenerating gives a fresh answer, not a checked one, and picking whichever version arrives next chooses between two unverified claims at random.

options.text: Ask Claude which of the two explanations it considers the more likely to be correct.
options.explanation: Asking the same conversation to arbitrate between its own two claims produces another confident statement with nothing new behind it. The contradiction is evidence that the summary has drifted from the source, and only the source settles it.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A customer support chatbot built on Claude detects that a customer's message expresses distress and references potential legal action.
question: What should the system do with this conversation?

options.text: Let the automated conversation continue but have it apologize more frequently in each generated response
options.explanation: Adding more apologies does not address the substantive risk of mishandling a distressed customer or a legal threat.

options.text: Close the support ticket automatically since the chatbot already provided a complete response
options.explanation: Closing the ticket automatically ignores the escalation risk and could leave a serious concern unresolved.

options.text: Escalate the conversation to a trained human agent instead of letting the automated response continue
options.explanation: Messages signaling distress or potential legal action are high-risk situations where a trained human agent should take over rather than continuing fully automated handling.

options.text: Ask the model to generate a longer response covering more possible resolutions for the customer
options.explanation: A longer automated response does not provide the human judgment needed for a sensitive, potentially legal situation.

objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
situation: An HR team drafts a benefits explanation for employees across countries whose languages and cultural norms around directness differ from the home office.
question: Beyond translation, what should the team check when adapting the content for each region?

options.text: Whether every regional version ends up with the exact same word count once translated
options.explanation: Matching word count across languages is not a meaningful measure of whether content is culturally and tonally appropriate.

options.text: Whether the same idioms from the home office draft are preserved in each translated version
options.explanation: Preserving home-office idioms in translation often produces confusing phrasing rather than adapting content to local readers.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
situation: A chatbot answers a user's question about a niche historical event with a detailed, confident, but entirely fabricated account, since no similar event exists in its training data. The team wants to reduce this kind of failure through prompt design alone, without adding any tools.

options.text: Instruct Claude to always answer within a strict two-sentence limit regardless of how complex the topic is
options.explanation: Limiting response length does not address the underlying cause of fabrication and may even worsen it by forcing an answer without room for caveats.

options.text: Instruct Claude to answer every question using only information gathered during its most recent training run
options.explanation: Claude cannot selectively restrict itself to only the most recent training run, and this instruction does nothing to prevent fabrication on topics with sparse training data.

options.text: Tell Claude it is acceptable, and preferred, to say it cannot verify an answer rather than guessing when unsure
options.explanation: Explicitly permitting Claude to express uncertainty or decline to answer when it lacks grounded information is a well-established prompting technique for reducing confident fabrication, since models often default to producing a plausible-sounding answer when not told otherwise.

options.text: Instruct Claude to always adopt a highly confident, authoritative tone in every reply so users trust the response
options.explanation: Encouraging a confident tone works against fact-checking goals, since it makes fabricated answers sound more credible rather than flagging uncertainty.

situation: A consultant is briefing colleagues on the guidance that Claude should not be relied on as a singular source of truth.

options.text: That she should raise the same question in several fresh conversations and treat consistent answers as adequate confirmation.

options.text: That a claim she is going to act on needs corroboration from an independent source before she treats it as established.
options.explanation: The principle is about where confirmation comes from: anything consequential should be corroborated outside the conversation, so Claude informs the decision rather than being the only thing standing behind it.

options.explanation: Softening the wording does not verify whether the underlying number is correct; it only obscures precision.

options.explanation: A model can consistently reproduce the same fabricated figure on repeated asks, so matching answers do not confirm accuracy.

options.explanation: Detailed, confident writing is not evidence that a specific unsourced statistic is factually accurate.

options.text: Locate an independent, authoritative source that confirms the statistic before including it in the report
options.explanation: An uncited, ungrounded statistic may be a hallucination, so the analyst should confirm it against an independent authoritative source before citing it.

objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
situation: A communications lead inherits a Claude-written fact sheet from a colleague who has left, with no record of what it was based on.

options.explanation: A disclaimer does not make unverified statements safe to publish; it just moves the risk onto the reader.

options.explanation: Claude cannot inspect how an earlier response was produced, and it has no access to the sources that were or were not used.

options.explanation: Context window limits depend on total input size, not on whether the grading model is the same one that generated the text.

options.text: The model's pricing doubles whenever it is reused for both generation and grading tasks
options.explanation: Pricing is based on token usage per request, not on whether the same model is reused across generation and grading steps.

options.text: The model may favor its own outputs, so a separate model or human should grade instead
options.explanation: A recommended best practice is to use a separate model or human reviewers for grading, since a model grading its own generations can be biased toward judging them favorably.

situation: A newsletter editor needs a Claude-drafted piece to quote the organisation's own published figures accurately.

options.text: Gather the published figures; check the draft's numbers against them; give them to Claude as the material; send the piece out to readers.

options.text: Give them to Claude as the material; send the piece out to readers; gather the published figures; check the draft's numbers against them.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

options.text: Shorten the job description so future applicant pools are easier for the model to rank consistently

options.text: An inconsistency, since the citation format breaks from the rest of the response's style

options.explanation: Reading the conclusion first reveals what the brief is asking the client to accept, which identifies the load-bearing claims. Those are checked while time remains, and remaining detail is verified with whatever is left.

options.text: Check those claims; verify the supporting detail; identify the claims the conclusion rests on; read the conclusion.

question: Which issue does the transcript itself clearly show?

options.text: The chatbot gave two answers that contradict each other.
options.explanation: The chatbot first says its support team works only from the London office and later says it works only from the New York office. Both statements cannot be true at once, so the transcript alone shows the chatbot contradicting itself within one conversation, and no outside fact-checking is needed to see it.

options.text: The chatbot favors customers in one city over another.
options.explanation: Both replies describe where the support team works and say nothing that treats one group of customers better than another, so the transcript shows no preferential or prejudiced treatment.

options.text: The chatbot's statements are confirmed to be factually wrong.
options.explanation: Without the company's real office details the reviewer cannot confirm that either statement is wrong, and nothing in the transcript settles it. What the transcript does establish is that at most one of the two statements can be true, which is a contradiction rather than a confirmed factual error.

options.text: The chatbot made up a source for its claim.
options.explanation: Neither reply cites or quotes any source, so there is no invented citation anywhere in the transcript. What is visible is that the two replies disagree with each other, not that supporting evidence was fabricated.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

options.explanation: Fixing only the section where the error was noticed leaves identical errors elsewhere, and the conclusions are re-read before those are found.

options.explanation: One instance of stale data suggests a source problem rather than a typing slip, so the scope of the error is established first, every affected section is then corrected, and the conclusions are re-read against the corrected figures before approval.

options.text: Re-read the conclusions in light of it; correct that section; approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere.
options.explanation: Re-reading conclusions before the figures are corrected judges them against numbers already known to be wrong, and approval precedes the wider search.

options.text: Approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it.
options.explanation: Approval comes before any of the corrective work, so the report is signed off in the state that was already known to be wrong.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A team keeps arguing about whether Claude's drafts of their monthly service report are good enough, and each reviewer reaches a different verdict.

options.text: Agreeing that a draft passes when a clear majority of the reviewers involved consider it good enough to publish.
options.explanation: Voting aggregates opinions formed on different criteria, so it produces a decision without producing a shared standard.

options.explanation: Confidence and detail in a response are not reliable indicators of factual accuracy, especially for events beyond the model's knowledge cutoff.

options.text: Publish the description immediately since Claude is known for broad general knowledge

options.text: Ask Claude the same question again and accept the answer if the second response matches the first

options.text: Regenerate the briefing in a fresh conversation, and publish if the two drafts report the same figures.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A manager has two Claude outputs in front of her: notes from an internal brainstorm, and a statement that will be sent to a regulator.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

situation: An operations analyst asked six specific questions about a supplier's performance and received one flowing summary in reply. She is about to forward it to her manager.

options.text: Ask for the summary again in a shorter form, so her manager can take it in without a long explanation.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: An operations manager is preparing to let her team use Claude-drafted replies across a busy customer queue. She has not yet decided who checks what.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Send the replies out and collect complaints, so the team learns which cases were handled badly.

options.text: Ask Claude to mark the replies it is least certain about so those can be routed for checking.

options.text: Agree what a good reply looks like and which mistakes would actually be costly to the business.
options.explanation: Review only works against a standard. Naming what a correct reply contains and which failures would hurt is what tells the team where scrutiny is needed and where it is not.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A project lead notices that Claude keeps giving the same wrong answer about the travel policy, always matching last year's rules. Both last year's and this year's policy documents sit in the project's knowledge.
question: What best explains this?

options.text: Claude is drawing on the superseded document, so the fault sits in the knowledge, not the model.
options.explanation: A repeatable answer that matches an old document is being read from that document. No amount of reprompting fixes an out-of-date source that is still available to be used.

options.text: Claude has invented the policy, since fabrication is the usual cause of a confident error.
options.explanation: Fabrication produces varied invented detail, not the same answer every time that happens to match a real superseded document.

options.text: Claude is biased towards older material and will always prefer whichever document is oldest.
options.explanation: There is no such preference for age. The problem is that two conflicting versions are both present and nothing marks which is current.

options.text: Claude has contradicted itself within a single answer, which is the definition of an inconsistency.
options.explanation: Nothing here describes two conflicting statements inside one response; the answers are consistent and consistently wrong.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: A project lead has twelve loosely related Claude answers gathered over a month and wants one reference document for her team.
question: What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Decide the structure the reference needs, then have Claude assemble the answers and resolve conflicts.
options.explanation: Curation is more than collection: choosing the structure first and then reconciling what the answers say is what turns scattered material into something a team can rely on.

options.text: Keep the twelve answers as they are and give the team a list of which conversation holds each one.
options.explanation: An index still leaves colleagues reading twelve separate answers and reconciling them individually.

options.text: Paste all twelve of the answers into one document in the order in which they were originally produced.
options.explanation: Chronological order reflects how the questions arose, not how a reader needs the material, and it leaves conflicts in place.

options.text: Ask Claude to shorten each of the twelve answers so that the collection becomes quicker to read.
options.explanation: Shortening reduces reading time but leaves twelve disconnected pieces and can remove the detail that resolves a conflict.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: An events team wants to put a Claude-drafted safety briefing for a public open day on the venue website tomorrow. Nobody has yet been named to check it.
question: What should the team lead do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to review its own briefing and confirm that the safety guidance in it is accurate.
options.explanation: Asking the same conversation to certify its own accuracy provides reassurance rather than assurance, and it does not put a person's name against the content.

options.text: Decide who has to sign the briefing off, given that it is public and safety-related content.
options.explanation: Public, safety-related content sits at the top of the range where a named human must review and own the output before it goes out. Establishing who that person is comes before anything else, because it determines whether tomorrow's deadline is even achievable.

options.text: Publish the briefing and ask staff on the day to correct anything that turns out to be wrong.
options.explanation: Correcting a published safety briefing after members of the public have read it does not undo the harm. High visibility and low reversibility are precisely the conditions that call for review before release, not after.

options.text: Circulate the briefing to the whole team so that anyone who wishes to can comment on it.
options.explanation: General circulation invites comment without assigning responsibility. Everyone may assume someone else has checked the safety guidance, which is how an unreviewed briefing reaches the public.

objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
situation: An analyst appends a reference list that Claude produced to her report without opening any of the items on it.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The list will be longer than the report itself requires, which readers are likely to find distracting.
options.explanation: Length is a presentation issue and says nothing about whether the sources back the claims.

options.text: The references will be formatted in a style that her organisation's template does not permit.
options.explanation: Formatting is easily corrected and does not affect whether the report's claims are supported.

options.text: A reference may not exist at all, or may exist but not support the claim attached to it.
options.explanation: An unopened reference list gives the report the appearance of grounding while providing none, and readers will treat it as though the checking was done.

options.text: Readers will follow the references instead of reading the analysis that she has written herself.
options.explanation: Readers consulting sources is a good outcome; the danger is that the sources will not hold up.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: A user asks Claude.ai to build a working single-page HTML landing page with embedded CSS that they can preview, tweak, and eventually export.
question: Which output format best serves this request?

options.text: Choose an inline HTML code block because code blocks render identically to artifacts and provide the same live preview and export options.
options.explanation: Inline code blocks only display the code as text; they do not offer the live preview or one-click export features that artifacts provide, so they are not equivalent.

options.text: Use a Mermaid diagram because diagrams are the standard way to represent the structure of a web page before writing any code.
options.explanation: Mermaid diagrams are meant for flowcharts and diagrams, not for creating interactive web pages; they cannot fulfill the request for a working, exportable landing page.

options.text: Use a plain-text description of the page layout because writing prose about the design avoids the risk of embedding malformed markup.
options.explanation: A plain-text description of the page layout fails to deliver the functional, previewable HTML page the user explicitly requested, and writing prose does not mitigate markup risks better than actual code.

options.text: Use an artifact because a single-page HTML site is self-contained, substantial, and the user previews and refines it outside the chat.
options.explanation: Artifacts are designed for self-contained, substantial content like a single-page HTML site, allowing the user to preview and refine the work in a dedicated panel and later export it for use outside the chat.

objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
situation: An operations analyst is comparing eight vendors and must decide whether to ask Claude for prose or for a structured table with fixed columns. Which two are sound reasons to choose the structured form?
question: Select two.

options.text: The results will be moved into a tracker where every field has to line up exactly.
options.explanation: When output feeds a downstream system, a predictable field structure removes the manual re-keying that prose would force the analyst to do by hand.

options.text: Tables remove the need to check the content, because the figures are already aligned.
options.explanation: Alignment is presentational. A neat table still needs the same accuracy and completeness checks as any other output before it is relied on.

options.text: Structured output is inherently more accurate than the same content written as prose.
options.explanation: Format does not change correctness. A table can hold exactly the same wrong figure as a paragraph, presented rather more convincingly.

options.text: A fixed set of columns makes it obvious when a vendor has no value for a field.
options.explanation: Visible gaps are a curation benefit distinct from downstream use: prose can pass over a missing vendor detail without the omission ever showing.

options.text: Producing a table takes Claude noticeably less effort than writing flowing paragraphs.
options.explanation: Relative effort is not a reason a knowledge worker should choose a format. The decision should follow from how the information will be used.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A programme manager has a Claude-drafted quarterly performance report and one hour to review it before it goes to her director.
question: In which order should these steps be taken?

options.text: List what the original request asked the report to cover; check the draft against that list for anything missing; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.
options.explanation: Restating what was asked for gives her a standard; comparing the draft against it exposes missing sections cheaply and tells her where the substance actually is; verification effort then goes to the claims that matter most; recording what was checked lets the director see the limits of the review.

options.text: List what the original request asked the report to cover; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director; check the draft against that list for anything missing.
options.explanation: The draft reaches the director before the completeness check, so a missing section is discovered only after the report has already been handed over.

options.text: Verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; check the draft against that list for anything missing; list what the original request asked the report to cover; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.
options.explanation: Verification begins before anyone has established what the report was meant to contain, so the hour is spent on whatever happens to be on the page and the coverage list arrives too late to direct it.

options.text: Check the draft against that list for anything missing; list what the original request asked the report to cover; verify the claims and figures that carry the most weight; note what was checked and pass the draft to the director.
options.explanation: The draft is compared against a list that has not been written yet, so the comparison has no standard behind it and reduces to reading the report and hoping something looks absent.

objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
situation: A coordinator uses Claude to draft an internal wiki page describing how to book a meeting room. Any colleague can edit the page, and a mistake would cost someone a few minutes.
question: What is the most appropriate level of checking?

options.text: A read-through by someone who knows the booking process, then publish it to the wiki.
options.explanation: Verification effort should match consequence. The page is low-stakes and easily corrected, so a quick check by someone who knows the process is proportionate.

options.text: A formal review board should approve the page before it is added to the internal wiki at all.
options.explanation: A standing approval body is disproportionate for a page that is trivially reversible and carries almost no consequence.

options.text: Every step should be performed once by a colleague who then confirms the page in writing.
options.explanation: Physically re-performing each step and documenting it spends far more effort than the risk of a wrong booking instruction justifies.

options.text: No checking is needed, because internal pages are not seen by customers or outside parties.
options.explanation: Some check is still warranted; being internal reduces the stakes but does not remove the value of a quick look.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A bid coordinator has a Claude-assembled tender response built from the company's own past submissions, and has time to review it properly before the deadline.
question: Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Verify the figures against the source submissions, then polish the wording, then check coverage against the tender questions, then check the response for internal contradictions.
options.explanation: Verifying figures before knowing whether every tender question is answered means checking numbers in sections that may still need rewriting, and polishing precedes both remaining content checks.

options.text: Polish the wording, then check the response for internal contradictions, then check coverage against the tender questions, then verify the figures against the source submissions.
options.explanation: Polishing wording first invests effort in sentences that may be deleted, and leaves the coverage check, the most decisive step for a tender, until after two rounds of editing have already been done.

options.text: Check coverage against the tender questions, then verify the figures against the source submissions, then check the response for internal contradictions, then polish the wording.
options.explanation: Coverage comes first because a missing answer is the costliest defect and changes what else needs checking; accuracy of figures and internal consistency come next; wording is polished last, once the content is settled.

options.text: Check the response for internal contradictions, then polish the wording, then verify the figures against the source submissions, then check coverage against the tender questions.
options.explanation: Internal consistency is a useful check but cannot be conclusive while sections are still missing, and coverage, the step that determines whether the bid is even compliant, is left to the very end.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A researcher has checked most of a twenty-claim brief but two claims could not be confirmed against any source before her deadline.
question: What should she do with those two?

options.text: Delete them quietly, on the basis that a brief containing only verified claims is the safest thing to circulate.
options.explanation: Silent deletion hides that a question was raised and not resolved, and a later reader may reintroduce the same claim having no idea it was doubted.

options.text: Keep them but mark them clearly as unconfirmed, so readers know which parts rest on nothing she could check.
options.explanation: Marking them preserves information the reader needs and shows exactly where the evidence stops, which lets anyone relying on the brief decide whether those two points matter to their decision.

options.text: Leave them in the brief unchanged, since they were not shown to be wrong and removing them would weaken it.
options.explanation: Presented alongside verified claims and in the same voice, unconfirmed claims inherit the credibility of the ones that were checked.

options.text: Soften their wording so they read as more tentative, which lowers the risk without drawing attention to them.
options.explanation: Hedged wording signals mild uncertainty rather than absent verification, and it deliberately avoids making the gap visible.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A researcher uploaded a single industry report and asked for a summary of it. Web search was switched off throughout.
question: Which observation is the strongest sign that a detail in the summary was fabricated rather than drawn from the report?

options.text: The summary opens with general background about the industry before it turns to the specific findings the report contains.
options.explanation: General framing before the specifics is a stylistic choice and is easy to remove. It becomes a concern only if the background contains checkable claims, which is not what this observation describes.

options.text: The summary is noticeably longer than the researcher expected for a report of this size, and repeats one point in two places.
options.explanation: Length and repetition point to a shape-and-quality problem rather than an invention problem. A verbose or redundant summary can still be entirely faithful to the document it was built from.

options.text: The summary states a precise figure, with a named source and a year, that appears nowhere in the uploaded report itself.
options.explanation: With no web search and a single uploaded document, everything factual should trace back to that document. A precise, confidently attributed figure that is absent from the source is the classic signature of fabricated detail.

options.text: The summary uses phrasing of its own rather than reusing the exact sentences that appear in the uploaded industry report.
options.explanation: Paraphrasing is normal and often desirable in a summary; different wording says nothing about whether the underlying content came from the report. This would flag almost every competent summary as suspect.

objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
situation: A finance officer pasted eighty rows of expense data into a chat and asked Claude to total them by cost centre. Which two verifications should she perform on the returned figures?
question: Select two.

options.text: Look over the totals to see whether they seem about right for a month of this kind.
options.explanation: A plausibility glance catches only large errors. A total that is wrong by one misfiled row looks entirely normal, which is what makes this check weak on its own.

options.text: Ask Claude to check its own arithmetic and proceed once it reports that all is correct.
options.explanation: Self-checking produces another generated answer, not an independent verification, and it can confidently confirm a figure that was wrong to begin with.

options.text: Confirm that all eighty of the rows are counted in exactly one of the totals.
options.explanation: This is a coverage test rather than an arithmetic one: totals can each be added correctly while several rows were skipped or double-counted.

options.text: Recalculate a sample of the cost centre totals herself and compare them with the output.
options.explanation: An independent recalculation is direct evidence about accuracy, and it catches a total that is internally consistent but simply computed wrongly.

options.text: Check that currency symbols and decimal places are applied consistently across the table.
options.explanation: Consistent formatting says nothing about whether the numbers are right. Tidy presentation is often what makes an incorrect total feel trustworthy.

objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
situation: A city communications team drafts a public road-construction notice, but the first draft uses formal legal phrasing like 'aforementioned thoroughfare' that is likely to confuse residents.
question: What is the best refinement for this audience?

options.text: Keep the legal phrasing exactly as written but enlarge the font of the notice.
options.explanation: Enlarging the font does not make the phrasing any easier to understand; the notice would still contain confusing legal terms. The core issue is word choice, not visibility.

options.text: Translate the phrase 'aforementioned thoroughfare' into another commonly spoken local language.
options.explanation: Translating jargon into another language does not guarantee it becomes plain or accessible; it may remain just as formal and confusing. The goal is to replace complex terms with clear, everyday language, not merely translate them.

options.text: Replace legal jargon with plain language, and ensure all facts remain accurate and complete.
options.explanation: Plain language makes the notice understandable to all residents, not just those familiar with legal jargon. Accuracy must be maintained so the public receives correct and complete information about the road construction.

options.text: Add a formal cover letter from city officials before the notice to provide necessary context.
options.explanation: A formal cover letter would introduce even more official language, failing to simplify the confusing terms in the notice itself. Residents would still encounter the same unclear phrasing.

objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
situation: A Claude draft attributes a sentence to a named industry report as a direct quotation.
question: What is the appropriate validation step?

options.text: Open the report and find that exact sentence, since a close paraphrase may not appear in it.
options.explanation: A quotation asserts that specific words appear in a specific document, so only locating those words in the report validates it.

options.text: Ask Claude for the page number, and accept the quotation once a number has been supplied to her.
options.explanation: A page number can be generated as readily as the quotation, so it adds no independent confirmation.

options.text: Search for the sentence's key phrase and accept it if similar wording appears anywhere.
options.explanation: Similar wording elsewhere does not establish that this report contains this sentence.

options.text: Confirm that the report exists and was published, which establishes the quotation's origin.
options.explanation: The report existing says nothing about whether the quoted sentence is in it.

objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
situation: A communications officer asks Claude for balanced talking points on a contested planning decision. The draft states one side's arguments plainly and introduces the other side's with repeated hedging.
question: How should this be classified?

options.text: A hallucination, because the arguments on one side must therefore have been invented.
options.explanation: Nothing suggests the arguments are fabricated. The issue is how comparable arguments are framed, not whether they exist.

options.text: A bias, because the response treats comparable arguments unevenly through its choice of framing.
options.explanation: Systematically softer language for one side skews the reader's impression even where every individual statement is accurate, which is what bias in an output looks like.

options.text: A formatting problem, because the hedging simply reflects a different paragraph style in use.
options.explanation: Hedging changes how strongly a claim is asserted, which is a matter of substance rather than presentation.

options.text: An inconsistency, because the two halves of the response use rather different sentence constructions.
options.explanation: An inconsistency is a conflict between statements about the same fact, not a difference in phrasing between sections.

objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
situation: A product team compares two Claude-drafted release notes for the same feature, one for a public changelog and one for an internal engineering wiki.
question: What is a key factor to check for each draft's fit?

options.text: Whether the public draft includes internal ticket numbers so support staff can reference them
options.explanation: Internal ticket numbers are meaningful to engineers but are not something a general public audience needs or can act on.

options.text: Whether the internal draft is written with the same marketing tone as the public changelog
options.explanation: A marketing tone suits the public draft but is not a meaningful fit for an internal wiki meant for precise technical reference.

options.text: Whether both drafts are published to the same location so all readers see identical content
options.explanation: Publishing both drafts to the same location defeats the purpose of tailoring one for public users and one for internal engineers.

options.text: Whether the public draft avoids internal codenames and detail that the engineering draft can include
options.explanation: A public changelog should be free of internal codenames and implementation detail, while the internal wiki draft can appropriately retain that detail for engineers.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A team's answers are frequently wrong, and someone proposes moving everything to the deepest-reasoning tier to fix it.
question: What is the greatest risk in doing that?

options.text: The deepest tier will take longer to respond, which will slow the team's daily work down considerably.
options.explanation: Response speed is a real trade-off but a minor one next to continuing to act on wrong answers.

options.text: If the cause is a vague prompt or a stale document, they buy a more confident version of the error.
options.explanation: Reasoning depth cannot supply missing context or override an out-of-date source, so the wrong answers persist while the allowance is consumed faster.

options.text: The team will grow used to the deepest tier and find lighter tiers unsatisfactory afterwards.
options.explanation: Preference drift is speculative and is not the reason this move can fail.

options.text: The deepest tier will refuse tasks it considers too simple, so routine work will stop being done.
options.explanation: No tier refuses work for being simple; that is not a behaviour a user encounters.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A consultant needs Claude to both draft a client proposal referencing the consultant's past proposal templates and also look up the client company's most recent press releases before finalizing the draft.
question: Which approach best fits both needs?

options.text: Work inside a Project with the past templates uploaded to its knowledge base and additionally use research mode within that conversation to gather recent press releases.
options.explanation: A Project's knowledge base is designed to store the consultant's own reusable templates, while research mode can be used within that conversation to gather current external information like recent press releases. This approach combines both features to meet the two distinct needs efficiently.

options.text: Use only research mode to search the web for similar proposal templates and the client's latest press releases, then reference the templates while incorporating the releases into the draft.
options.explanation: Research mode searches the web but does not have access to the consultant's private past proposal templates unless they are uploaded. It would only find publicly available templates, not the specific proprietary ones needed, so it cannot fully substitute for project knowledge.

options.text: Use only a Project with uploaded templates, because its knowledge base will automatically have the client's most recent press releases alongside the consultant's past proposals.
options.explanation: Project knowledge only contains documents that the user has manually uploaded; it does not automatically pull in a company's current press releases. Without an uploaded source or research mode, the client's latest press releases would not be available.

options.text: Avoid both features by manually pasting the templates and press releases into a single long chat message so the model processes everything at once and drafts the proposal.
options.explanation: Manually pasting all templates and press releases into a long message is more effort-intensive and does not provide the persistent reuse benefit of project knowledge. It also lacks the automated, cited gathering that research mode provides, making it less efficient for this task.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A department sets the deepest-reasoning model as the default for all of its work, including short routine replies.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Short replies will be written at greater length than the person asking the question wanted.
options.explanation: Response length is controlled by the request, not by the tier, and it is easy to correct.

options.text: Routine work consumes far more allowance, so it runs out during the work that actually needs it.
options.explanation: The deepest tier uses meaningfully more of the usage allowance per message, so spending it on trivial work leaves less available for the genuinely hard problems.

options.text: Short replies will come back noticeably slower, which colleagues will find frustrating to work with.
options.explanation: Slower replies are an annoyance rather than the substantive cost of this policy.

options.text: The department will be unable to switch to a lighter model once a default has been set for it.
options.explanation: The model can be changed at any time, so nothing about the choice is locked in.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
question: Which of the following best describes the core difference between using Claude's research feature and using a standard chat conversation for a question?

options.text: Research mode conducts multiple agentic, interconnected searches to build a thorough, cited answer, while standard chat usually responds from existing knowledge or a single lookup.
options.explanation: Research mode performs multiple agentic searches that build upon each other to produce a comprehensive, cited answer. In contrast, standard chat typically draws from its pre-trained knowledge or a single lookup, lacking this multi-step investigation.

options.text: Research mode and standard chat use the same underlying model and generation pipeline, differing only in interface color and the inclusion of a search summary, without functional change.
options.explanation: The two differ functionally: research mode’s agentic search process fundamentally changes how information is gathered and used before responding. It is not merely a cosmetic or superficial interface change.

options.text: Research mode operates without generating any citations, producing concise answers solely from search summaries, while standard chat meticulously appends citation markers to verify every assertion.
options.explanation: Research mode does generate citations, producing thorough answers with easy-to-check references. Standard chat does not always include citation markers, contrary to the claim made here.

options.text: Standard chat conversations can access and analyze uploaded project files and attachments, whereas research mode relies solely on the model's pre-existing training data with no access to external documents.
options.explanation: Research mode is specifically designed to perform external searches, not rely solely on pre-existing training data. Standard chat’s ability to analyze project files is a separate capability and not what distinguishes these modes.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A market analyst must produce a competitor briefing drawn from many public sources, and the team will keep editing that briefing for weeks afterwards. Which two Claude features fit this job?
question: Select two.(Select 2)

options.text: Keep the briefing inline in the chat and re-paste the newest version whenever an edit lands.
options.explanation: Re-pasting an inline answer for every edit is precisely the friction artifacts exist to remove, and versions drift apart quickly.

options.text: Turn on a mail connector first so that the competitor facts are drawn from the team inbox.
options.explanation: An internal mailbox is not the source of public competitor information, and connecting one does not answer the sourcing need here.

options.text: Use Research mode, so the briefing is built by multi-step searching and returns citations.
options.explanation: Research mode runs an agentic, multi-step search and returns citations, which is exactly what a sourced competitor briefing needs.

options.text: Ask for the briefing as an artifact, so the team can edit and reuse it outside the chat.
options.explanation: An artifact is the durable, editable deliverable format, so weeks of later editing happen on one object rather than in chat replies.

options.text: Open a separate chat for each competitor so that no single conversation ever grows long.
options.explanation: Splitting by competitor fragments the briefing and does nothing about sourcing or about the editing the team has ahead of it.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user wants Claude to plan a multi-day team offsite by checking the team's shared Google Calendar for open dates, reviewing relevant emails about budget constraints, and cross-referencing venue reviews found on the web.
question: Which combination of feature and prerequisite is needed?

options.text: Enable Research mode with web search and connect Google services as data sources.
options.explanation: Enabling Research mode with web search allows Claude to access and cross-reference venue reviews on the web. Connecting Google services such as Calendar and Gmail as data sources provides live access to open dates and budget emails, meeting all the user's needs.

options.text: A basic chat conversation without web search or external services won't work.
options.explanation: Although a basic chat conversation without web search or external services indeed cannot handle the task, this option does not propose a working combination of feature and prerequisite. The question asks for the combination needed, not a statement of what won't work.

options.text: Using an artifact that shows a static calendar for the offsite avoids web search.
options.explanation: An artifact displaying a static calendar for the offsite avoids web search, but the task explicitly requires web search for venue reviews. Artifacts also do not provide live calendar checks or email review for budget constraints.

options.text: Using a Project containing the team's quarterly calendar PDF can find open dates.
options.explanation: A Project containing a quarterly calendar PDF only captures static snapshots that can quickly become outdated. It lacks the ability to check live calendar availability, review emails about budget constraints, or search the web for venue reviews.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A daily customer-insight digest that used to be quick now takes far longer and uses much more of the team's allowance than it did six months ago, although the tier it runs on has never changed.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Move the digest up to the deepest-reasoning tier, on the basis that stronger answers should need fewer re-runs each morning.
options.explanation: Escalating adds cost to a task that is already consuming too much, and depth does not address inputs that have quietly grown. It is as likely to worsen the allowance problem as to fix the re-runs.

options.text: Spread the digest across several colleagues' accounts, so that the daily allowance draw is shared out rather than falling on just one.
options.explanation: Spreading the draw across accounts hides the consumption rather than reducing it, leaves the underlying growth undiagnosed, and is likely to conflict with how the organisation expects allowances to be used.

options.text: Move the digest down to the fastest and cheapest tier straight away and see whether the daily output is still good enough.
options.explanation: Changing tier is a plausible eventual answer, but doing it first treats a symptom. If the digest is now processing far more material and being re-run repeatedly, a lighter tier will simply do the bloated task less well.

options.text: Look at how the digest itself has grown, in the length of what is fed in and the number of re-runs, before changing tier at all.
options.explanation: Nothing about the tier has changed, so the growth is in the task. Understanding how much longer the inputs are and how often the digest is being re-run identifies the real cause before any tier decision is made.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A researcher's chat approaches its context limit, and Claude begins condensing the earlier messages in that conversation. Which two statements about this are accurate?
question: Select two.
