options.text: Condensing raises the context window of that single chat right up to the next size that is available.
options.explanation: The window is a property of the model in use, and condensing does not enlarge it.

options.text: Condensing permanently erases those earlier messages from the conversation history for good.
options.explanation: Nothing is erased, so treating condensing as deletion misreads what is happening in the conversation.

options.text: Claude condenses the earlier messages so that the conversation is able to carry on past that point.
options.explanation: As a conversation nears the context limit, earlier messages are condensed so the chat can continue rather than stop.

options.text: The full chat history remains accessible to her even after the earlier messages are condensed.
options.explanation: Condensing changes what is held in working memory; the full history of the conversation stays available to read.

options.text: Condensing appears as a signal that her account has run out of usage allowance for the period.
options.explanation: This confuses length limits with usage limits; nearing a context limit says nothing about the period's allowance.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A manager lets each colleague pick a model tier per task according to how important the task feels, with nothing written down.
question: What is the greatest concern?

options.text: Colleagues will always choose the deepest tier, which will exhaust the team's allowance quickly.
options.explanation: Some will over-select and some will under-select, and assuming one direction misses the actual problem.

options.text: The manager will be unable to see which tier each colleague chose for any given piece of work.
options.explanation: Visibility is a reporting question and is not what makes the arrangement unreliable.

options.text: Colleagues will spend a large part of each working day deciding which tier they ought to use.
options.explanation: The decision itself is quick; the cost lies in its inconsistency rather than in the time it takes.

options.text: Similar work gets different treatment, and nobody can tell whether the cheaper choice sufficed.
options.explanation: With no shared standard the same task is handled inconsistently, and because nothing defines adequacy there is no way to learn from any of the choices made.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A colleague suggests running Research for a question with a single settled answer that is already well documented internally.
question: How should this suggestion be assessed?

options.text: It is a good fit, because a multi-step search always produces a more reliable answer overall.
options.explanation: More searching does not automatically mean a better answer when the question is already settled and documented.

options.text: It is a good fit, because Research is the only way to obtain citations for any given factual claim.
options.explanation: Citations are useful, but Research is not the only route to a sourced answer and the value here does not justify the effort.

options.text: It is a poor fit, because Research is built for multi-step investigation and uses limits faster.
options.explanation: Research runs several searches that build on one another, which is valuable for open questions and disproportionate for a settled fact; it also draws on usage limits more quickly.

options.text: It is a poor fit, because Research cannot answer questions that have one settled answer.
options.explanation: It can answer such questions perfectly well. The objection is proportionality, not capability.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A teacher's project instructions have grown to several pages, and she notices less room for the lesson material she pastes into chats.
question: What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Duplicate the instructions into project knowledge as well, so that Claude encounters them twice over.
options.explanation: Duplicating them consumes more space rather than less, and repetition does not make guidance more reliable.

options.text: Leave the instructions exactly as they are, since project instructions never take up any conversation space.
options.explanation: They do take up space in every chat in the project, which is precisely why she is seeing less room.

options.text: Trim the instructions to the essentials, since they occupy window space in every chat inside the project.
options.explanation: Project instructions are carried into each conversation in the project, so keeping them concise leaves more of the window for the material she is actually working on.

options.text: Move the instructions into the first message of every chat so they no longer take up any window space.
options.explanation: The same words consume the same space wherever they sit, and she also loses the durability of project instructions.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user asks Claude to generate a 40-line Python script that parses log files, then five minutes later asks Claude to fix a bug in that same script.
question: Where does the updated script most likely appear so the user can compare it to the earlier version?

options.text: In the artifact panel, updated as a new version accessible through the version selector
options.explanation: A 40-line script is substantial, self-contained content suited to an artifact; when Claude revises it, the update appears in the same artifact panel, and the version selector lets the user switch between the original and fixed versions.

options.text: In a newly created Project, since bug fixes always require project-level knowledge storage
options.explanation: Fixing a bug in an already-generated script does not require creating a new Project; the existing artifact already supports iterative revision without added project structure.

options.text: Nowhere retrievable, since Claude cannot revise previously generated code in the same conversation
options.explanation: Claude can revise previously generated code within the same conversation, and with an artifact, the fixed version remains retrievable through version history.

options.text: In research mode results, since fixing a bug counts as an investigative web search task
options.explanation: Research mode is for gathering external information via web search, not for revising code that Claude already generated in the conversation.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A team is setting up a new recurring weekly task and has to decide how much reasoning depth it needs.
question: Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Pick a tier by how important the task feels, then run it for a month, then write down what good output means, then compare the month's results against that.
options.explanation: Choosing on instinct and defining quality a month later means there is no standard to judge the intervening results against, and a month of work has already been committed to an unexamined choice.

options.text: Run the task on several tiers at once, then write down what good output means, then compare the results against that definition, then keep the tier that did best.
options.explanation: Committing several tiers to the task before any standard exists means the trial is designed without knowing what it is testing for, and it duplicates the work and the allowance draw on every run.

options.text: Compare a sample of results with what colleagues produce by hand, then write down what good output means, then pick a tier on that basis, then run the task each week from then on.
options.explanation: Comparing results before the task has been run is out of order, and benchmarking against manual work is not the same as agreeing what this task's output has to achieve.

options.text: Write down what good output means, then run a real sample on the default tier, then compare that sample against the definition, then change tier only where it falls short.
options.explanation: Define the quality bar, test the default tier on real work, check that sample against the bar, and change tier only where the evidence shows the default falls short or is more than the task needs.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A grants officer on a paid plan needs a one-off overview of the funding landscape, drawn from the published criteria of roughly twenty funders she has not looked at before. Her director will ask where each statement came from.
question: Which approach best fits the job?

options.text: Ask a separate question about each of the twenty funders in ordinary chats, then merge the twenty replies into an overview herself.
options.explanation: Twenty separate questions is slow, and it puts the entire burden of deciding what to investigate and of stitching the findings together back on the officer, which is the work she wanted help with.

options.text: Use Research, which runs the multi-step search across the funders itself and returns an answer with sources she can open and check.
options.explanation: Research is built for exactly this: an agentic multi-step search across many external sources that decides what to look at next and returns an answer with sources attached, which is what her director's question requires.

options.text: Set up a project for the overview, put the twenty funder names into the project instructions and work through them chat by chat.
options.explanation: A project provides durable shared context for recurring work, but this is a one-off task and the funder criteria are external material she has not gathered. The project adds setup without doing any of the searching.

options.text: Ask one broad question in an ordinary chat, then ask for a reference list to be added underneath the overview once it is written.
options.explanation: References requested after the overview is written are assembled to fit text that was produced without them, so they are the weakest form of provenance and still leave every claim to be traced by hand.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A consultant on a paid plan is checking how much material she can work with inside one chat. Which two statements are correct?
question: Select two.

options.text: The context window grows automatically as soon as she upgrades to a higher paid plan.
options.explanation: The window is tied to the model in use, not to how high the plan tier is.

options.text: The largest chat context window is offered on Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 only.
options.explanation: In chat, the largest context window is limited to Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5; other models sit at smaller sizes.

options.text: Every model on a paid plan offers exactly the same context window inside a single chat.
options.explanation: Context window size varies by model, so a paid plan on its own does not give every model the same window.

options.text: A usage limit covers how much she interacts over a period, not what fits in one chat.
options.explanation: A usage limit is a budget for interaction over a time period, while the context window is the working memory of one conversation.

options.text: Her remaining usage allowance is what decides how much one chat can hold at any time.
options.explanation: This is the classic confusion between usage limits and length limits; the allowance does not set a chat's capacity.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user asks Claude to research mode-style investigate an emerging technical standard, but Claude answers immediately from general knowledge without doing multiple searches.
question: What is the most likely reason research mode did not activate?

options.text: Web search was not enabled, or the user did not explicitly prompt Claude for research, so it fell back to a normal response.
options.explanation: Research mode requires web search to be enabled, and if the user does not explicitly prompt Claude to use research capabilities, it may fall back to a normal response. This explains why Claude answered from general knowledge without performing multiple searches.

options.text: Research mode only works when the query is phrased as a single yes-or-no question, so Claude defaults to general knowledge without initiating research.
options.explanation: Research mode is designed for open-ended, multi-faceted investigative queries, not limited to yes-or-no questions. Query phrasing does not determine whether research mode initiates.

options.text: Research mode was permanently removed from Claude.ai and replaced entirely by Projects; all multi-step research now happens within project setups.
options.explanation: Research mode is still available on Claude.ai and has not been replaced by Projects. They are separate features designed for different use cases, so research mode remains a distinct capability.

options.text: The user's account tier does not support any form of web-connected search, regardless of plan, so Claude cannot initiate research mode when requested.
options.explanation: Research mode is supported on certain paid account tiers, so it is not true that no tier supports web-connected search. The scenario does not provide account details, and the feature is not universally unavailable.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user asks Claude to write a two-sentence reply to a coworker's Slack message. Claude responds with the two sentences directly in the conversation rather than opening a side panel.
question: Why did this response not trigger an artifact?

options.text: Artifacts are disabled by default and must be manually enabled for every conversation, preventing side panel opening for any content.
options.explanation: Artifacts are enabled by default and appear based on content length and complexity, not a manual per-conversation setting. Short replies simply do not meet the threshold for triggering an artifact.

options.text: The content is short and conversational, not substantial or self-contained text typically exceeding 15 lines.
options.explanation: Artifacts are designed for substantial, self-contained content, typically over 15 lines, that users may want to modify or reference later. A brief two-sentence reply is short and conversational, so it stays inline rather than opening a side panel.

options.text: Research mode must be active for an artifact to appear, and short conversational replies do not automatically enable this mode.
options.explanation: Research mode and artifacts are separate features; activating research mode is not required for an artifact to appear. Short, conversational replies do not generate artifacts regardless of whether research mode is on.

options.text: Two-sentence replies are only supported when composing within a Project's knowledge base, not in standard chat conversations.
options.explanation: Two-sentence replies are standard in any chat conversation and are not restricted to Projects' knowledge bases. The content's length and self-contained nature—not the conversation type—determine artifact creation.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A support operations lead must classify a large daily backlog of short inbound messages, and separately needs one deep analysis of a tangled contract dispute. Which two choices fit?
question: Select two.

options.text: Use the deepest-reasoning tier for both of the jobs, since the strongest option is never bad.
options.explanation: Using the deepest tier for routine classification spends quota on work that does not need the extra reasoning depth.

options.text: Use the fastest, cheapest tier for both jobs, since the tiers differ mainly in reply speed.
options.explanation: The tiers differ in reasoning depth as well as speed, so the lightest tier is a poor fit for a tangled dispute.

options.text: Use the deepest-reasoning tier for the contract dispute, accepting the larger quota it uses.
options.explanation: A tangled one-off analysis is the case where deeper reasoning is worth the meaningfully larger quota it consumes.

options.text: Use the fastest, cheapest tier for the high-volume classification, where throughput matters.
options.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity classification is exactly where the fastest and cheapest tier earns its place.

options.text: Use whichever tier the team already has open, since the tier rarely changes what comes back.
options.explanation: Tier choice changes depth, speed and quota use, so treating it as incidental is how both of these jobs go wrong.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A marketer says she has 'run out of context', yet she can immediately open a new chat and continue working without waiting.
question: Which statement fits what happened?

options.text: She reached a usage limit for the period; that one chat still had plenty of room left inside it.
options.explanation: A usage limit would block her in every chat, including the new one, until the period reset.

options.text: She reached neither limit, because new chats are only blocked when a plan is downgraded or cancelled.
options.explanation: She clearly hit something; the evidence that a new chat works points specifically to a length limit.

options.text: She reached a length limit inside that one chat; her overall usage allowance was not the constraint.
options.explanation: Length limits are confined to a single conversation's context window, which is why a new chat lets her continue straight away.

options.text: She reached both limits at once, since a chat filling up always exhausts the period's allowance too.
options.explanation: The two limits are independent. Filling one conversation says nothing about the allowance left for the period.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A project lead has let a project's knowledge base grow to hundreds of documents, including several superseded versions of the same policy.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Retrieval will stop working altogether once the knowledge base grows past the model's context window.
options.explanation: It is precisely at that point that retrieval activates automatically, holding far more content than a window alone.

options.text: Retrieval will hold the project to the plan's smallest context window until documents have been removed.
options.explanation: The window is determined by the model in use; retrieval extends reach over the knowledge base rather than shrinking it.

options.text: Retrieval may surface an outdated version, giving confident answers that no amount of reprompting fixes.
options.explanation: When the wrong source is retrieved, the answer is wrong at the root. Rewording the prompt cannot correct a problem that lives in the knowledge base itself.

options.text: Retrieval will require her to configure a search index before the project can answer any questions.
options.explanation: No setup or configuration is required; retrieval turns itself on when the knowledge base grows large enough.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A support team lead wants several colleagues to be able to view and use the same set of onboarding documents and a shared system of custom instructions when chatting with Claude, without each person needing to configure their own settings.
question: Which feature addresses this on a Team or Enterprise plan?

options.text: An artifact exported as a file and emailed to each team member separately
options.explanation: Exporting and emailing an artifact distributes a static file rather than providing an ongoing shared workspace with consistent instructions.

options.text: A single long chat conversation that is copied and sent to each colleague individually
options.explanation: Copying and distributing a single chat transcript does not give colleagues an ongoing shared, editable space with consistent instructions and knowledge.

options.text: A shared Project that team members are added to with view or edit permissions
options.explanation: Team and Enterprise projects can be shared with specific members or the whole organization, with permission levels like 'Can use' and 'Can edit', giving everyone consistent access to the same knowledge base and instructions.

options.text: Research mode configured to fetch the onboarding documents whenever asked
options.explanation: Research mode searches the web and connected sources on demand; it is not a mechanism for sharing a persistent internal knowledge base and instructions among team members.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user is having a quick, one-off conversation with Claude to brainstorm five possible names for a new podcast. The conversation does not need to be revisited later or reference any uploaded files.
question: Which feature is the most appropriate fit for this task?

options.text: A new Project created specifically to store the podcast name brainstorm
options.explanation: Creating a Project adds persistent knowledge-base structure that is unnecessary overhead for a single one-off brainstorm that won't be revisited.

options.text: An artifact, so the list of names appears in a dedicated side panel
options.explanation: A short list of five names is not substantial, standalone content requiring iterative editing, so an artifact is not needed for this simple exchange.

options.text: Research mode, so Claude searches the web for existing podcast names to avoid
options.explanation: Enabling research mode to search the web for existing podcast names is unnecessary for a quick five-name brainstorm and would add latency without meaningful benefit.

options.text: A standard chat conversation, without creating a Project or enabling research mode
options.explanation: A short, self-contained brainstorming task with no need for persistent knowledge or external research fits naturally into a standard chat conversation without the added structure of a Project, research mode, or an artifact.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A project lead is told she cannot send any more messages for several hours, and the block applies even in a brand-new empty chat.
question: Which limit has she reached?

options.text: A length limit, which governs how much information a single chat can work with at one time.
options.explanation: A length limit is confined to one conversation's context window; starting a fresh chat would clear it immediately.

options.text: A knowledge limit, which governs how many documents a single project workspace is able to store.
options.explanation: A cap on stored documents would not stop her sending messages in an unrelated new chat.

options.text: An artifact limit, which governs how many separate documents Claude can produce within one session.
options.explanation: There is no such block on messaging, and artifacts are an output format rather than a messaging quota.

options.text: A usage limit, which governs how much she can interact with Claude over a given period of time.
options.explanation: Usage limits control how much you can interact with Claude across a time period, so they follow you into every chat, including a new one.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A researcher notices that colleagues' very long chats keep running smoothly, while hers stops making room for new content once it fills up.
question: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Automatic context management is unavailable to her because her plan does not include the Artifacts feature.
options.explanation: Artifacts are an output format and are widely available; they have no bearing on context management.

options.text: Automatic context management is unavailable to her because code execution is not switched on in settings.
options.explanation: Code execution must be enabled for automatic context management to work, so without it a conversation simply runs out of room.

options.text: Automatic context management is unavailable to her because web search has not been enabled for the chat.
options.explanation: Web search affects what Claude can look up, not whether earlier messages can be condensed.

options.text: Automatic context management is unavailable to her because she has too many documents inside a Project.
options.explanation: The size of a project's knowledge base does not govern whether a conversation can condense itself.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A project manager drafts talking points live during meetings and wants each suggestion back immediately, knowing she will rewrite them afterwards.
question: Which tier fits best?

options.text: The default middle tier, since anything lighter cannot produce usable talking points at all.
options.explanation: The lightest tier handles short drafting perfectly well, particularly when a person rewrites the result.

options.text: The deepest-reasoning tier, since talking points shape decisions and need the strongest reasoning.
options.explanation: The drafts are rewritten afterwards, so depth she discards is depth she paid for unnecessarily.

options.text: The fastest tier, since immediate response is the binding constraint and the drafts are rough.
options.explanation: Where an immediate reply is what makes the tool usable and the output is a rough first pass, speed is worth more than additional reasoning depth.

options.text: Whichever tier holds the largest context window, since meetings involve a lot of discussion.
options.explanation: Window size governs how much a conversation can hold, not how quickly a short suggestion arrives.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A free-tier user wants to organize their conversations about a personal budgeting spreadsheet into a dedicated space, separate from unrelated chats about recipes and travel planning.
question: Is this possible without upgrading to a paid plan?

options.text: No, because a Pro subscription is required to create a Project, so free accounts cannot have separate spaces.
options.explanation: Anthropic's documentation explicitly states that Projects are available to all users, including free accounts. A Pro subscription is not required; free users can create a maximum of five Projects.

options.text: Yes, but only through research mode, which is available on free accounts and organizes chats into separate threads.
options.explanation: The research does not identify a 'research mode' as the documented way to create separate conversation spaces on free accounts. The supported feature is Projects, which free users can create up to five of.

options.text: Yes, because Projects are available to free accounts, and free users can create a maximum of five Projects.
options.explanation: Yes. According to Anthropic's official documentation, Projects are available to all users, including free Claude accounts, and free users can create up to five Projects. A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history and knowledge base, so the user can isolate budgeting conversations without upgrading.

options.text: No, because free accounts are limited to one continuous chat, preventing users from separating conversations by topic.
options.explanation: Free accounts are not limited to one continuous chat. Users on the free plan can create Projects, each with its own chat history, allowing separation by topic such as budgeting, recipes, or travel.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: An operations team runs one large workload through Claude: several thousand short, repetitive record summaries, plus one difficult reconciliation that decides how the whole set is interpreted. Everything currently runs on the deepest-reasoning tier and the allowance is gone by Wednesday.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Ask for a larger allowance before making any change, since the current work is valuable and the shortfall is only a couple of days.
options.explanation: Asking for more allowance funds the existing pattern rather than examining it, and it leaves thousands of routine summaries consuming the most expensive capacity available for no additional benefit.

options.text: Cut the length of every prompt in the workload, so that each individual request costs less and the allowance stretches further.
options.explanation: Shorter prompts trim the cost of each request but leave the real problem untouched: routine work is still being run on the tier reserved for difficult reasoning, so the same imbalance recurs next week.

options.text: Move the whole workload to the fastest and cheapest tier, then see over the next few weeks whether anyone complains about quality.
options.explanation: Moving everything down applies one answer to two very different tasks, and the reconciliation is exactly the piece that would suffer. Waiting for complaints is a poor detection mechanism for degraded reasoning.

options.text: Separate the bulk repetitive work from the one genuinely difficult piece, so each part can be matched to what it actually needs.
options.explanation: The workload is not one thing. Splitting the high-volume routine part from the small part that genuinely needs deep reasoning is what makes any sensible tier decision possible, and it is where nearly all the waste is.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A student is using Claude to draft a single essay outline and does not plan to reuse any reference material or revisit the conversation after submitting the assignment. A classmate suggests creating a Project first.
question: What is the most reasonable evaluation of that suggestion?

options.text: Required, since Claude cannot generate an essay outline without an active Project, as the outlining process depends on referencing materials, which is only enabled within a Project.
options.explanation: Claude can generate an essay outline directly in a standard chat without needing a Project. While referencing materials can be helpful, it is not required for drafting, and documents can be uploaded in regular conversations if needed.

options.text: Unnecessary, since Projects are exclusively for storing images and cannot contain text-based outlines, as their document handling is limited to visual media like diagrams.
options.explanation: The reasoning here is false: Projects are not exclusively for storing images; they can contain text documents, code, and other file types. Although the conclusion that creating a Project is unnecessary is correct, a reasonable evaluation must be based on accurate information.

options.text: Required, since only Projects allow more than one exchange within a conversation, meaning a student cannot ask follow-up questions or iterate on the outline without a Project.
options.explanation: Standard chat conversations already support unlimited back-and-forth exchanges. A student can ask follow-up questions and iterate without a Project, so this requirement is false.

options.text: Unnecessary, since a Project's main benefit—persistent knowledge and context across multiple conversations—is not needed for a single one-time outline.
options.explanation: A Project’s primary benefit is providing persistent knowledge and context that can be reused across multiple conversations. For a one-time outline task, this persistent structure adds no value and the work can be done in a standard chat.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A strategy lead must reconcile three conflicting demand forecasts and explain the reasoning to an executive committee.
question: Which tier fits this work best?

options.text: Whichever tier her colleagues most recently used, so the team's outputs remain consistent.
options.explanation: Consistency of tier is not a goal in itself, and it ignores what this particular task demands.

options.text: The deepest-reasoning tier, accepting the higher allowance cost, since the value is the reasoning.
options.explanation: When several conflicting inputs must be held together and the argument itself is the deliverable, the extra reasoning depth is what the higher allowance cost buys.

options.text: The default middle tier, because reconciling forecasts is fairly ordinary analytical work for a team.
options.explanation: Reconciling contradictory sources and defending the reasoning is precisely the harder end of the range.

options.text: The fastest tier, because the committee needs the analysis quickly and speed is what matters.
options.explanation: Speed is not the binding constraint when the whole value of the piece lies in the quality of the reasoning.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: An operations manager has kept one chat running for three weeks to plan a vendor migration. Claude's latest answers now contradict constraints the team agreed in the first week.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Send the same question again with stronger wording so that Claude gives the earlier decisions more weight.
options.explanation: Repeating a prompt more forcefully does not restore detail that no longer fits in the conversation's working memory.

options.text: Identify the decisions and constraints that must survive, and record them as durable reference material.
options.explanation: The conversation has outgrown what a single chat can hold, so the working state has to be captured before anything is restarted or moved. Naming what must survive is the step every other option depends on.

options.text: Switch to a model with a smaller window so the conversation is forced to stay short and focused.
options.explanation: A smaller context window reduces how much Claude can hold at once; it makes the loss of earlier detail worse rather than better.

options.text: Ask Claude to repeat the whole conversation back to her in full before she continues working in it.
options.explanation: This spends window space and usage allowance restating material that is already the problem, and a recap produced from a strained conversation is not a reliable record.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: An operations manager is worried that letting a long negotiation chat condense itself will destroy the record of what was said.
question: Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Earlier messages are condensed so the chat can continue, and the full chat history stays readable to her.
options.explanation: Automatic context management compresses what is held in working memory to make room, while the complete history remains accessible in the conversation.

options.text: Earlier messages are moved into project knowledge automatically, where colleagues can then also read them.
options.explanation: Condensed content is not exported into a project, and nothing is shared with colleagues as a side effect.

options.text: Earlier messages are stripped out of the chat entirely, so only the condensed version can be reviewed.
options.explanation: Nothing is removed from the history. Compression affects working memory rather than the stored conversation.

options.text: Earlier messages are exported to a file on her account, which she must download before the chat resumes.
options.explanation: There is no download step; the conversation continues without any manual action from her.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A communications lead simply starts a new chat whenever the current one begins to feel unwieldy, without saving anything out of it.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Her earlier conversations are permanently deleted from her account as soon as a new chat is opened.
options.explanation: Past chats remain in her history; the loss is that the new conversation does not inherit their content.

options.text: Each new chat counts against a monthly cap on conversations, which she will exhaust before month end.
options.explanation: Allowance is measured by how much she interacts over a period, not by a count of conversations opened.

options.text: Decisions and constraints agreed earlier are lost, so she covers the same ground over and over again.
options.explanation: Restarting clears the window but also discards the durable output. Without persisting it, each new chat rebuilds context that was already settled.

options.text: Opening new chats reduces the context window available to her for the rest of that working day.
options.explanation: The window is per conversation and per model; opening a new chat gives her a full one rather than a reduced one.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A marketing team wants to move its weekly performance report from the deepest-reasoning model to a lighter one to save allowance.
question: What should they do first?

options.text: Ask Claude whether a lighter model could produce the same report to the same standard.
options.explanation: That answer is a general claim about models rather than evidence from their own report.

options.text: Switch the report over immediately, and change back if anyone complains about the quality.
options.explanation: Waiting for complaints makes readers the quality check, and subtle thinning of the analysis rarely produces a complaint.

options.text: Shorten the report first, so that a lighter model would have less material to work through each week.
options.explanation: Cutting scope changes the deliverable rather than testing whether the lighter tier can produce it.

options.text: Produce next week's report on both tiers and compare them against what the report must deliver.
options.explanation: A side-by-side run on their own work, judged against an agreed standard, is the only evidence that tells them whether the cheaper tier is adequate here.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A project lead is setting up a new recurring piece of work and is unsure which Claude model to use for it.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Pick the deepest-reasoning model, since starting with the strongest option is always safest.
options.explanation: The deepest tier consumes meaningfully more allowance, and reaching for it by default spends that budget on work that does not need it.

options.text: Judge how much reasoning depth the work really needs, since that is what separates the tiers.
options.explanation: The tiers trade reasoning depth against speed and allowance, so the choice starts with an honest read of how hard the task actually is.

options.text: Pick the fastest and cheapest model, since a lighter model can be upgraded at any later point.
options.explanation: Defaulting to the lightest tier is the same mistake in the other direction, and it can hide a quality gap she never looks for.

options.text: Ask Claude which of the available models it would recommend for the work she has described.
options.explanation: That answer is generated from a general description rather than from her actual quality bar and constraints.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A data analyst asks Claude to generate a single-page HTML dashboard with an embedded chart that visualizes quarterly revenue, and wants to be able to download the finished HTML file.
question: Which feature is designed to produce and export this kind of standalone content?

options.text: The chat history sidebar, which lists previous conversations by date
options.explanation: The chat history sidebar only organizes past conversations; it does not generate or export standalone downloadable content.

options.text: A Project's custom instructions, which define Claude's tone for future chats
options.explanation: Custom instructions shape how Claude responds across a project's conversations; they do not render or export a standalone HTML dashboard file.

options.text: Artifacts, which render self-contained content like HTML pages and support exporting or downloading
options.explanation: Artifacts are built for substantial, self-contained content such as single-page HTML websites, and they support exporting content by copying or downloading the file.

options.text: Research mode, which searches external sites for existing revenue dashboards
options.explanation: Research mode gathers external web information, but generating and exporting a self-contained HTML dashboard is the artifact feature's role, not a search function.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A department shares one pooled allowance. Several colleagues have got into the habit of running everyday drafting and tidying-up work on the deepest-reasoning tier because it is available to them.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The department loses track of which tier produced which document, making it harder to reproduce a particular draft afterwards.
options.explanation: Not recording which tier produced a draft is an untidy practice, but it rarely affects the outcome of everyday drafting and does not explain why the allowance is being exhausted.

options.text: The routine drafts come back more slowly than they need to, so each colleague spends a little longer waiting for everyday work.
options.explanation: Slower turnaround on routine drafting is a real irritation and worth avoiding, but a few extra seconds per draft is minor next to the shared pool running dry before the hard work gets done.

options.text: Colleagues become accustomed to the deeper tier's style of answer and find the default tier's phrasing harder to work with later.
options.explanation: Getting used to one tier's phrasing is a mild adjustment, not a risk to the department's work. Everyday drafting is well within what the default tier handles, and preference is not the issue here.

options.text: The shared allowance is consumed by low-value work, so it is not there when a colleague has genuinely hard analysis to run.
options.explanation: The deepest tier consumes meaningfully more of a shared allowance, so spending it on work the default tier handles well leaves nothing for the small number of tasks that genuinely need that depth.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A colleague new to Claude at work asks why anyone would use the default tier when a deeper-reasoning one is offered alongside it.
question: Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The default tier exists to hold costs down and produces work that is noticeably weaker than the deeper tier on every kind of task attempted.
options.explanation: This understates the default badly. It is a capable tier that handles most everyday work well; the difference in reasoning depth shows on genuinely hard problems, not uniformly across every task.

options.text: The default tier is the quickest and cheapest option available, and it is intended for very high volumes of short, repetitive requests.
options.explanation: This describes the lightest tier rather than the default. Being fastest and cheapest for very high-volume short requests is a different position in the range from the general-purpose default.

options.text: The default tier is fast and capable enough for most everyday work, so the deeper tier's greater allowance cost is worth paying only when depth decides it.
options.explanation: The default is fast and capable and suits the majority of work, while the deepest tier consumes meaningfully more allowance, so it is reserved for tasks where reasoning depth changes the outcome.

options.text: The default tier is intended for people who are still learning to use Claude, and experienced colleagues are generally expected to move up once they feel confident.
options.explanation: Tier choice tracks the demands of the task, not the experience of the user. An expert doing routine drafting is well served by the default, and a beginner facing a hard analysis may need more depth.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A marketing analyst needs Claude to compile a report on a competitor's recent product launches by pulling in current news articles, press releases, and blog posts published in the last month.
question: Which feature should the analyst use?

options.text: Request an artifact so Claude generates a standalone report document with current news and press releases.
options.explanation: Artifacts are a way to display and interact with substantial content generated by Claude, but they do not have web-search capabilities. Requesting an artifact does not enable gathering of current news or press releases.

options.text: Enable the research feature for Claude to run agentic web searches over current sources.
options.explanation: The research feature allows Claude to perform agentic web searches, automatically exploring multiple sources like news articles, press releases, and blogs to gather current information. It synthesizes findings and cites sources, making it ideal for compiling a report on recent competitor launches.

options.text: Lower the model to a smaller size to generate the report from current news and press releases.
options.explanation: Lowering the model to a smaller size affects response speed and cost, not the ability to access external information. Web search functionality is tied to the research feature, not model size.

options.text: Open a Project and rely on its stored knowledge to pull recent articles and press releases for the report.
options.explanation: A Project's stored knowledge consists only of documents manually uploaded by the user; it does not fetch live external content. Therefore, it cannot pull recent articles and press releases from the web.

options.text: Continue in a standard chat conversation to compile the report using recent news and press releases.
options.explanation: Standard chat without research mode typically relies on Claude's internal training data or a single search, which is insufficient for compiling comprehensive, up-to-date information from multiple external sources like news and press releases.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: Five colleagues each keep re-uploading the same three reference documents into their own chats, and they want one shared place for that context.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Check which plan they are on, since sharing one project with colleagues needs Team or Enterprise.
options.explanation: On personal plans a project is private to its creator, so on Free, Pro or Max each colleague would still end up maintaining a separate copy of the same knowledge.

options.text: Nominate one person to hold the documents and forward the answers on to the rest of the team each time.
options.explanation: Routing every question through one colleague creates a bottleneck and does not give anyone else the shared context they need.

options.text: Ask Claude to remember the three documents so that everyone's chats can draw on them later.
options.explanation: Context from one person's conversations does not carry across to colleagues' chats; shared knowledge has to be held somewhere deliberately.

options.text: Create a project each and upload the same three documents into every one of those projects.
options.explanation: Five parallel copies is the duplication they are trying to remove, and the copies will drift apart as documents are updated.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A support team must triage several thousand incoming messages a week, of which a small proportion involve genuinely difficult judgment.
question: What is the most sensible arrangement?

options.text: Run the bulk on the fastest tier and send the cases it flags as difficult to the deepest tier.
options.explanation: A two-stage arrangement matches each message to the depth it needs, so volume is handled cheaply and the small hard tail still gets proper reasoning.

options.text: Run everything on the deepest tier, so that the difficult cases are never handled by a lighter one.
options.explanation: Paying the deepest tier's allowance cost on thousands of routine messages to protect a handful of hard ones is a poor trade.

options.text: Run everything on the fastest tier, since the difficult cases are only a small proportion.
options.explanation: The hard cases are usually where the cost of a mistake sits, so treating them as negligible is the expensive error.

options.text: Alternate between tiers message by message, so that the allowance is spread evenly over time.
options.explanation: Alternating assigns depth at random, which means some hard cases get the lightest treatment.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A market analyst must produce a competitor briefing drawn from many public sources, and the team will keep editing that briefing for weeks afterwards. Which two Claude features fit this job?
question: Select two.

options.text: Open a separate chat for each competitor so that no single conversation ever grows long.
options.explanation: Splitting by competitor fragments the briefing and does nothing about sourcing or about the editing the team has ahead of it.

options.text: Ask for the briefing as an artifact, so the team can edit and reuse it outside the chat.
options.explanation: An artifact is the durable, editable deliverable format, so weeks of later editing happen on one object rather than in chat replies.

options.text: Use Research mode, so the briefing is built by multi-step searching and returns citations.
options.explanation: Research mode runs an agentic, multi-step search and returns citations, which is exactly what a sourced competitor briefing needs.

options.text: Turn on a mail connector first so that the competitor facts are drawn from the team inbox.
options.explanation: An internal mailbox is not the source of public competitor information, and connecting one does not answer the sourcing need here.

options.text: Keep the briefing inline in the chat and re-paste the newest version whenever an edit lands.
options.explanation: Re-pasting an inline answer for every edit is precisely the friction artifacts exist to remove, and versions drift apart quickly.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A logistics company processes a very high volume of straightforward shipment-status classifications per day and has tight per-request latency requirements, but still wants strong reasoning quality for edge cases.
question: Which model tier is the best fit?

options.text: Claude Sonnet, since high-volume straightforward tasks are always better served by a mid-tier model
options.explanation: While Claude Sonnet offers a balance of intelligence and speed, Anthropic specifically designates Claude Haiku for straightforward classifications. There is no universal rule that mid-tier models are always better for such tasks; the choice depends on the specific requirements for latency, cost, and capability.

options.text: A model chosen at random each request, since reasoning quality does not depend on which tier handles the request
options.explanation: Reasoning quality varies significantly across model tiers, and randomly selecting a model would lead to inconsistent performance and unpredictable costs. Best practice is to select the most appropriate model based on the task's requirements.

options.text: Claude Opus, since strong reasoning on edge cases requires the most capable and expensive tier regardless of volume
options.explanation: Claude Opus is the most capable model, but using it for every request in a high-volume scenario would be extremely costly and introduce higher latency, making it unsuitable for straightforward classification tasks. The documentation advises using the appropriate model tier based on task complexity and budget.

options.text: Claude Haiku, since it offers near-frontier performance with the fastest speed at the most economical price point
options.explanation: Anthropic documentation recommends Claude Haiku for straightforward classification tasks like routing and intent detection, emphasizing its speed and cost-efficiency. It provides near-frontier performance at the most economical price, making it ideal for high-volume, low-latency requirements. For edge cases requiring deeper reasoning, a multi-model architecture can escalate requests to more capable models.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A records team reclassifies several thousand short archive descriptions overnight, and an archivist spot-checks a sample of the results each morning before anything is published.
question: Which consideration should carry most weight in the team's tier choice?

options.text: The preference of the archivist who runs the morning check, since she is the person most familiar with how the descriptions read.
options.explanation: The archivist's familiarity makes her a good reviewer, but personal preference is not a basis for a decision about throughput and allowance across thousands of items processed overnight.

options.text: The overall importance of the archive to the organisation, since anything touching the permanent record deserves the best available.
options.explanation: General importance is too blunt to guide the choice. It would justify the deepest tier for every task the team ever runs, including thousands of short, formulaic descriptions that do not need that depth.

options.text: Whichever tier the rest of the organisation has settled on, so that the records team's results stay comparable with everyone else's.
options.explanation: Matching what others use ignores the specifics that actually matter here: this is high-volume, repetitive work with a human check already in place, which is not the shape of most colleagues' tasks.

options.text: The volume and routine nature of the descriptions, together with the fact that a person already reviews a sample before publication.
options.explanation: High volume, short and repetitive items, and an existing human spot-check together point to speed and allowance as the deciding factors rather than the deepest available reasoning.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A team runs two workloads that are alike in volume and subject matter. One is edited line by line by a specialist before use; the other is published automatically with no human reading it.
question: Which consideration should weigh most heavily when choosing a tier for each?

options.text: The subject matter the two workloads share, since comparable material should be handled the same way for consistency of output.
options.explanation: Shared subject matter makes the two workloads look alike, but it is not what determines the risk. Consistency for its own sake ignores the fact that only one of them has anyone checking the result.

options.text: The volume of the two workloads, since equal volumes imply equal throughput needs and therefore the same balance of speed and cost.
options.explanation: Equal volume does mean similar throughput demands, and that matters. It is still secondary to the fact that one workload reaches the outside world without any person having read it.

options.text: How much a downstream human check would catch, since the unchecked workload has to carry its own quality with no safety net.
options.explanation: The strength of the downstream check changes how much the output has to get right on its own, so the unchecked workload justifies more reasoning depth while the edited one can lean towards speed and allowance.

options.text: The seniority of the people who own each workload, since the more senior owner is accountable for the more visible of the two.
options.explanation: Ownership determines who answers for a problem, not how likely a problem is. Seniority is an accountability question and does not tell the team where errors would actually escape unnoticed.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: An operations manager has deliberately kept one chat alive for months, letting Claude condense earlier messages rather than ever starting fresh.
question: What is the biggest concern with this habit?

options.text: A conversation that has been condensed can no longer be exported or shared, so her team is unable to review the thread once it passes the length limit
options.explanation: Condensing does not restrict exporting or sharing a conversation; that is unrelated to how context is managed as a chat grows.

options.text: Condensing earlier messages deletes them from her chat history for good, so nobody on the team is able to go back and reread what was originally agreed
options.explanation: Condensing affects what Claude carries forward as working context; the full chat history remains accessible for her to scroll back and read.

options.text: Automatic condensing is offered only on free accounts, so a paid plan will refuse to shorten the conversation and will simply stop accepting further messages
options.explanation: Automatic context management is not a free-account-only behaviour, and a conversation reaching its length limit does not simply refuse further messages in the way described.

options.text: The decisions her team relies on exist only inside one conversation, and Claude now works from a condensed version rather than what was originally agreed
options.explanation: Two things go wrong at once: the durable decisions are trapped in a single fragile conversation instead of being persisted somewhere reusable, and once earlier messages are condensed Claude is reasoning from a summary rather than the original wording. Moving what must survive into a Project fixes both.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A policy writer expects roughly nine rounds of ordinary wording and structure changes on a report, with one genuinely hard judgement in the middle about how to reconcile two conflicting evidence bases.
question: How should she spread the work across tiers?

options.text: Run every round on the fastest and cheapest tier, and accept whatever it produces for the reconciliation to keep the process simple.
options.explanation: Simplicity is bought at the cost of the one step that matters. The reconciliation of conflicting evidence is precisely the task where shallower reasoning is most likely to produce a weak result.

options.text: Do the wording rounds on the default tier and reserve the deepest-reasoning tier for the one hard reconciliation in the middle.
options.explanation: The default tier is fast, capable and right for routine drafting and wording iterations, while the extra allowance cost of the deepest tier is worth paying only for the single step where reasoning depth genuinely decides the outcome.

options.text: Run every round on the deepest-reasoning tier, so that the hard judgement benefits from all the context built up in earlier rounds.
options.explanation: Running nine wording rounds on the most expensive tier spends heavily on work the default tier handles well, and the accumulated context does not require every earlier round to have used the deeper tier.

options.text: Alternate between the tiers round by round, so that the report gets a mix of perspectives as the drafting work progresses.
options.explanation: Alternating by round bears no relation to what each round demands, so the hard judgement may land on a lighter tier by chance while routine wording changes consume the deeper one.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A recruiting team answers similar candidate questions every week and re-pastes the same rubric and tone rules into every new chat. Which two moves fit the available features?
question: Select two.

options.text: Ask Claude at the end of each chat to remember the rubric for whichever chat opens next.
options.explanation: A request made inside one chat does not durably carry team context into the next one; that is what a Project is for.

options.text: Move the rubric and the tone rules into a Project, so each chat starts from that context.
options.explanation: A Project is the feature for recurring work that needs shared context, so the rubric and tone rules stop being re-pasted every week.

options.text: Run every one of the candidate questions through Research mode so answers arrive with citations.
options.explanation: Research mode is for agentic multi-step investigation of open questions, not for applying a known internal rubric.

options.text: Keep the reusable reply template as an artifact the team can open and edit between chats.
options.explanation: The reply template is self-contained content the team returns to and edits, which is what an artifact is for.

options.text: Keep one very long running chat open so the rubric stays somewhere in the history above.
options.explanation: One ever-growing chat pushes against the context limit and still leaves the rubric buried instead of durably configured.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A teacher pastes a whole term of student feedback into a single chat and keeps asking Claude to summarise themes as the conversation grows very long.
question: What is the greatest risk to the quality of her summaries?

options.text: The chat will refuse to accept any further messages until she upgrades to a higher-priced plan tier.
options.explanation: Reaching a length limit does not force a plan upgrade; she can continue in a new chat or move the material into a Project.

options.text: Every answer will be produced by a weaker model once the conversation has passed the context window limit.
options.explanation: The model in use does not change because a conversation is long. Approaching the limit affects available working memory, not model quality.

options.text: Claude will delete the earlier messages from the chat history, leaving her nothing at all to check.
options.explanation: Condensing earlier messages does not erase them. The full chat history stays readable, so she can still go back and check.

options.text: Detail from early in the chat may be condensed away, so her theme counts can quietly omit some feedback.
options.explanation: As a conversation approaches the context limit, earlier messages are condensed to make room. The summary still reads confidently, but it may no longer rest on every comment she pasted in.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A voice assistant application requires the lowest possible response latency among current Claude models so that spoken exchanges feel natural and immediate.
question: Which model tier has the fastest comparative latency?

options.text: Claude Haiku, since it is described as having the fastest comparative latency of the current model lineup
options.explanation: In Anthropic's model comparison, Haiku is listed with the fastest comparative latency among the current-generation models.

options.text: Claude Opus, since higher intelligence models always respond with lower latency under normal load
options.explanation: Greater intelligence does not translate into lower latency; Opus is listed with moderate comparative latency, slower than both Sonnet and Haiku.

options.text: Claude Sonnet, since its balance of speed and intelligence makes it faster than any other current tier
options.explanation: Sonnet is described as fast, but the comparison table ranks Haiku's comparative latency ahead of Sonnet's.

options.text: All current Claude models share the same comparative latency, differing only in output quality
options.explanation: The models differ noticeably in comparative latency, not just in output quality, which is precisely why latency is one of the criteria for choosing among them.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A team is designing an agent that must autonomously produce very long outputs, such as an extensive generated report or a large batch of generated code, and wants the model tier best associated with handling the most demanding, large-scale generation tasks.
question: Which tier should they choose?

options.text: Any tier works equally well, since maximum output length does not differ meaningfully across current models
options.explanation: Model tiers differ in intelligence, latency, and cost for demanding generation tasks, so the choice of tier is not interchangeable for the most complex, large-scale work described here.

options.text: Claude Sonnet, since it is the only tier that supports generating long-form output at all
options.explanation: Long-form output generation is supported across the current model lineup, not exclusively by Sonnet, so this option misstates the family's capabilities.

options.text: Claude Haiku, since its lower cost per token always outweighs output-length considerations for any task
options.explanation: Lower cost per token is a real advantage of Haiku, but for the most demanding, large-scale generation tasks Anthropic points to the most capable tier rather than defaulting to the cheapest one.

options.text: Claude Opus, since it is positioned for the largest-scale, most complex generation and engineering tasks
options.explanation: Opus is recommended for the largest-scale, most complex engineering and generation work, matching a scenario centered on demanding, large-scale autonomous output generation.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A long strategy chat has drifted off track, and it keeps re-deriving background the team will still need next week. Which two actions are appropriate here?
question: Select two.

options.text: Start a fresh chat that restates the current goal and carries only the material still needed.
options.explanation: Restarting with a tight restatement clears accumulated drift and keeps only the context that is still relevant.

options.text: Switch over to the lightest and fastest tier so that continuing this long conversation costs less.
options.explanation: A cheaper tier does not fix drift, and it does not persist the background the team will need again.

options.text: Move the durable background into a Project, so later chats begin from it without redoing it.
options.explanation: Background needed again next week is durable context, and a Project is where durable context belongs.

options.text: Carry on in the same chat and restate the goal more forcefully every time answers drift off.
options.explanation: Repeating the goal more forcefully in a drifting conversation rarely recovers it and adds to an already crowded context.

options.text: Delete earlier messages from the chat so that older material stops shaping the newer replies.
options.explanation: Pruning messages is not how a drifting chat is repaired, and it does not make the background durable for next week.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A team is deciding between Claude Haiku and Claude Opus for a new internal tool and wants a simple rule of thumb for when accuracy should be prioritized over cost and speed.
question: According to Anthropic's guidance, which situation should push the team toward starting with Opus instead of Haiku?

options.text: When rapid iteration is needed for prototyping new features without real user testing, start with Opus to ensure high accuracy from the start.
options.explanation: Anthropic actually recommends Haiku over Opus for rapid prototyping. Haiku's faster speed and lower cost allow teams to iterate quickly and test ideas without incurring high expenses or latency, making Opus an unnecessarily costly and slow choice at this stage.

options.text: For high-volume repetitive tasks with tight budgets, Opus is preferred over Haiku for its lower cost per task and faster speed.
options.explanation: This statement inaccurately describes Opus. Anthropic guidance states that Haiku is the fastest and most cost-effective model, ideal for high-volume, budget-sensitive tasks. Opus, while more capable, is significantly more expensive and slower, making it unsuitable for such use cases.

options.text: Complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost, such as scientific or advanced coding, calls for Opus.
options.explanation: According to Anthropic's official guidance, Opus models are the most capable and are recommended when accuracy and advanced reasoning are top priorities, even at higher cost. Use cases include complex scientific research, advanced coding, and high-stakes enterprise tasks where output must be reliable on the first pass. This rule of thumb directly aligns with documentation emphasizing Opus for 'complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost.'

options.text: To ensure fast response times for low-latency chatbots during peak traffic, choose Opus over Haiku due to its optimized inference.
options.explanation: Anthropic recommends Haiku for low-latency applications like peak-traffic chatbots because Haiku provides the fastest response times and lowest cost per request. Opus is designed for depth rather than speed, so using it here would lead to higher latency and cost without proportional benefit.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: An operations manager on a Pro plan is working within a single Project whose uploaded reference files are approaching the context limit. The manager wants Claude to keep giving high-quality answers grounded in that large body of documents without manually trimming the file set.
question: What underlying capability does the Project rely on to handle this?

options.text: Research mode replaces the uploaded files with live web search results, automatically expanding project context without manual trimming.
options.explanation: Research mode is a separate web-search capability; it does not tap into the project's uploaded document base or automatically replace files to expand context.

options.text: An artifact compresses all uploaded files into a summarized attachment, expanding project capacity while preserving response quality.
options.explanation: Artifacts are for displaying generated content like code or documents; there is no artifact-based compression or summarization mechanism for uploaded reference files. Capacity expansion is handled by RAG.

options.text: Retrieval Augmented Generation automatically expands project capacity by retrieving relevant chunks, preserving quality.
options.explanation: Projects use Retrieval Augmented Generation to automatically retrieve relevant chunks from uploaded files, expanding effective context capacity while maintaining answer quality without manual trimming.

options.text: A downgrade to a smaller model uses a reduced context window per document, allowing more reference files within the same overall limit.
options.explanation: Downgrading to a smaller model changes generation cost and speed, not the way a project handles its uploaded knowledge base; it does not reduce per-document context usage to fit more files.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A project lead needs Claude to work across a very large set of meeting notes inside one conversation on her paid plan.
question: Which choice best supports that?

options.text: Choose the fastest and cheapest model available, because lighter models are given more room for long inputs.
options.explanation: The fastest, cheapest tier is not the one with the largest window; speed and window size are separate trade-offs.

options.text: Choose whichever model she used last, because the context window is identical across every available model.
options.explanation: Window size varies by model, so the choice of model directly changes how much a single chat can hold.

options.text: Choose a previous-generation model, because older models were given more room before the newer releases.
options.explanation: The newest flagship models offer the largest windows; earlier models are more limited, not less.

options.text: Choose one of the newest flagship models, which offer the largest context window for chatting on paid plans.
options.explanation: The newest flagship models provide a one-million-token window when chatting on any paid plan, which is the most room available for a single conversation.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: Two tasks draw almost identically on a team's allowance: notes from an internal brainstorm that nobody will act on directly, and a figure that will appear in a published statement. A colleague argues the two should therefore be treated the same way.
question: How should the team decide?

options.text: Treat them the same, since equal allowance draw means equal cost to the team and there is no clear financial reason to separate them.
options.explanation: Equal allowance draw only tells the team what each request costs to run. It says nothing about what a mistake costs, which is where the two tasks differ enormously.

options.text: Let what an error would cost drive the decision, so the published figure earns more depth and checking than the internal notes do.
options.explanation: Consequence, not price, should drive the choice: a wrong figure in a published statement is hard to retract, while a weak brainstorm note is discarded, so the published work justifies more depth and scrutiny.

options.text: Treat them the same, since a single rule applied to both tasks is easier for colleagues to remember and to follow consistently.
options.explanation: A single rule is simpler to follow but forces one of two errors: over-spending on throwaway notes, or under-serving a published figure. Simplicity is not worth either outcome.

options.text: Let the person who happens to run each task decide, since they know their own deadline and how much allowance they have left.
options.explanation: Leaving it to whoever runs the task makes an important external output depend on one person's remaining allowance and time pressure, which is exactly when the published figure would be short-changed.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A project lead pastes the same 40-page requirements document into every new chat instead of storing it anywhere.
question: What is the greatest concern with this approach?

options.text: Each re-paste spends both window space and usage allowance that storing the document once would save.
options.explanation: The document consumes a large share of the conversation's working memory every time, and the repeated processing draws on her usage budget for no added benefit.

options.text: The document will be copied into other people's projects across her organisation without her consent.
options.explanation: Pasting into her own chat does not propagate the document to colleagues' workspaces.

options.text: Claude will answer only from the closing pages of the document and silently ignore everything before.
options.explanation: Claude does not restrict itself to the final pages; the real exposure is cost and space, not truncation by position.

options.text: Claude will refuse to accept a document of that size and will ask her to shorten it before continuing.
options.explanation: A document of that size is readable; the cost is in the space and allowance it consumes, not a refusal.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A user needs to generate a report and then make direct edits to its content.
question: Which Claude feature is most appropriate?

options.text: Enable Research mode to refine the report with external sources.
options.explanation: Research mode is designed to gather and incorporate external sources, not to directly edit or refine report text. It does not include a built-in editor for modifying the report's content.

options.text: Generate the report as an Artifact, then edit it in the artifact editor.
options.explanation: Artifacts provide a dedicated editing workspace for longer-form content like reports. Generating the report as an Artifact allows direct, structured modifications in the artifact editor, aligning perfectly with the user's need.

options.text: Use Chat to output the report and then edit the raw text inline.
options.explanation: Chat can generate the report, but editing raw text inline in the chat interface is inefficient and lacks dedicated editing tools. This method is not suited for making structured, direct edits to a report.

options.text: Use Projects to store the report and make edits in a separate file.
options.explanation: Projects are intended for organizing conversations and files, not for direct editing of reports. Storing a report and then editing it in a separate file is a manual workaround that lacks the integrated editing experience needed here.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A team wants to decide whether a lighter tier is good enough for its weekly summary work.
question: What is the most reliable way to make that call?

options.text: Run real examples of their own summaries on both tiers and judge them against an agreed standard.
options.explanation: Adequacy is specific to the task and the bar, so only their own work compared against a stated standard answers the question.

options.text: Read published comparisons of the tiers and adopt whichever one they describe as sufficient.
options.explanation: General descriptions cannot tell the team whether a lighter tier meets their particular standard on their own material.

options.text: Adopt the lighter tier and revisit that decision if the team's allowance stops running out so early.
