options.explanation: Allowance consumption measures cost, not whether the summaries still meet the required standard.

options.text: Ask Claude to compare its own output on both tiers and report which version is the stronger.
options.explanation: A self-assessment is not independent evidence, and it has not been told what this team's summary must achieve.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A team drafts a long monthly report in Claude and keeps exhausting its usage allowance before the month ends. Some sections are routine - recurring summaries and figures pulled from the same sources each time - while other sections carry the analysis the report is read for. The team already signs the report off against an agreed quality checklist, and it wants to cut usage by moving some of the drafting to a lighter Claude model tier without weakening the sections that matter.
question: Which sequence of steps should the team follow?

options.text: Run the routine sections on a lighter tier; decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
options.explanation: The routine sections are moved to the lighter tier before anyone has worked out which sections carry the judgment, so the split is guesswork about the content rather than a decision based on it, and the checklist pass that follows can only repair a division that was arbitrary to start with.

options.text: Decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
options.explanation: Deciding which sections need human judgment comes first because it is the only step that reasons about the content rather than the tooling; the lighter tier is then applied only where quality is not at stake; and the checklist the team already signs the report off against is what tells them which moves to keep and which to send back to the deeper tier. Claude Academy's model-selection tutorial applies the same test - run the work on the lighter model, then judge whether the output met your bar.

options.text: Decide which sections need human judgment; check the drafts against the agreed checklist; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short; run the routine sections on a lighter tier.
options.explanation: The drafts are checked and sections are sent back to the deeper tier before the lighter tier has been used at all, so the move to the lighter tier is the last thing done and nothing verifies its output - the one step the team cannot afford to leave unchecked given that quality is the stated constraint.

options.text: Check the drafts against the agreed checklist; decide which sections need human judgment; run the routine sections on a lighter tier; send back to the deeper tier the sections that fell short.
options.explanation: The checklist pass happens before anything has been moved, so it measures the drafts the team already produces and says nothing about how the lighter tier performs; the final step then sends back sections that were never re-checked after the change.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A support operations lead must classify a large daily backlog of short inbound messages, and separately needs one deep analysis of a tangled contract dispute. Which two choices fit?
question: Select two.(Select 2)

options.text: Use whichever tier the team already has open, since the tier rarely changes what comes back.
options.explanation: Tier choice changes depth, speed and quota use, so treating it as incidental is how both of these jobs go wrong.

options.text: Use the deepest-reasoning tier for the contract dispute, accepting the larger quota it uses.
options.explanation: A tangled one-off analysis is the case where deeper reasoning is worth the meaningfully larger quota it consumes.

options.text: Use the fastest, cheapest tier for the high-volume classification, where throughput matters.
options.explanation: High-volume, low-complexity classification is exactly where the fastest and cheapest tier earns its place.

options.text: Use the fastest, cheapest tier for both jobs, since the tiers differ mainly in reply speed.
options.explanation: The tiers differ in reasoning depth as well as speed, so the lightest tier is a poor fit for a tangled dispute.

options.text: Use the deepest-reasoning tier for both of the jobs, since the strongest option is never bad.
options.explanation: Using the deepest tier for routine classification spends quota on work that does not need the extra reasoning depth.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A marketer's project knowledge has grown far past what a single conversation could hold, and she is unsure whether Claude can still draw on all of it.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Delete older documents until the knowledge base is small enough to fit inside a single conversation window.
options.explanation: Deleting useful material to fit an old constraint throws away knowledge that retrieval could still reach.

options.text: Move the material into individual chats so that each single conversation carries only the documents it needs.
options.explanation: This reintroduces the repeated pasting that a project exists to avoid, and it drains usage allowance.

options.text: Split the material across several smaller projects before she asks any further questions in that workspace.
options.explanation: Splitting fragments the knowledge base and creates maintenance work to solve a problem retrieval already handles.

options.text: Ask questions in the project and check the answers, since retrieval over a large knowledge base is automatic.
options.explanation: When project knowledge approaches or exceeds the context limit, retrieval activates on its own with no setup, holding far more content. Testing it is the cheapest way to find out where she stands.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A marketer's long-running chat has begun producing copy that ignores the campaign brief agreed weeks earlier.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Open a fresh chat; check whether the old chat had grown too long; paste the brief in; capture the decisions afterwards.
options.explanation: Restarting before capturing the decisions risks losing them, and diagnosing after the fact wastes the step.

options.text: Capture the decisions; open a fresh chat; check whether the old chat had grown too long; paste the brief in afterwards.
options.explanation: Working in the new chat before the brief is in place produces exactly the drift she is trying to fix.

options.text: Check whether the chat has simply grown too long; capture the brief and decisions; open a fresh chat; paste them in there.
options.explanation: Diagnosing the cause comes before acting, capturing the durable material protects it, and only then is restarting safe rather than destructive.

options.text: Paste the brief in again; capture the decisions; check whether the chat has grown too long; open a fresh chat right at the end.
options.explanation: Re-pasting into an already overloaded conversation adds pressure to the window before anything has been diagnosed.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A marketer is midway through a one-off brainstorm that will not be revisited, and the conversation is approaching its limit.
question: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Let the conversation continue and condense itself, since nothing in it needs to outlive this session.
options.explanation: When the output is disposable, allowing automatic context management to make room is the lowest-effort choice; there is no durable knowledge worth persisting.

options.text: Build a Project and move the whole brainstorm into project knowledge before writing anything more.
options.explanation: A project is for context that recurs. Setting one up for work that will never be revisited is unnecessary overhead.

options.text: Stop the brainstorm now and restart it in a new chat so the ideas come from a completely clean window.
options.explanation: Restarting discards the ideas generated so far and forces her to regenerate them at further cost.

options.text: Split the brainstorm across four separate chats so that no single conversation ever nears its limit.
options.explanation: Fragmenting the session means no chat holds the full set of ideas, which undermines the brainstorm itself.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A company is scaling a content-creation and data-analysis product used by thousands of business customers. They need strong general capability across code generation, analysis, and visual understanding, without committing to the most expensive tier.
question: Which model tier matches this description in Anthropic's model selection matrix?

options.text: Use a mix of unrelated third-party models because Claude tiers fail to include data analysis and visual understanding.
options.explanation: Claude models, especially Sonnet, include robust data analysis and visual understanding features, so the described product's needs are well covered without resorting to external models.

options.text: Choose Claude Sonnet, as it offers frontier intelligence for coding, analysis, and visual understanding at scale.
options.explanation: Claude Sonnet offers frontier intelligence for coding, analysis, and visual understanding at scale, making it the right tier for a product that needs strong, general capabilities without the highest cost.

options.text: Select Claude Haiku because code generation and analysis tasks should default to the cheapest model tier available.
options.explanation: Defaulting to the cheapest tier ignores that this product requires robust performance across demanding tasks; Haiku is optimized for cost-efficient, simpler workloads, not the breadth of capabilities needed here.

options.text: Opt for Claude Opus because content platforms need peak reasoning and visual analysis, requiring the top tier.
options.explanation: Opus is designed for the most complex, high-autonomy, or accuracy-critical tasks; a scaling content and analysis product fits Sonnet's balanced profile better than the top, most expensive tier.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: An operations lead has two hundred short, standard customer replies to prepare today and is worried about her weekly allowance.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to estimate how much of her allowance the batch is likely to consume in total.
options.explanation: An estimate of consumption does not change what the batch costs or tell her which parts need care.

options.text: Run the whole batch on the deepest-reasoning model, so no reply needs to be redone afterwards.
options.explanation: Applying the most expensive tier to two hundred routine items is the fastest way to exhaust the allowance she is worried about.

options.text: Separate the replies that genuinely need judgment from the routine bulk of the batch.
options.explanation: Once the small number of awkward cases is identified, the routine bulk can go to the fastest and cheapest tier and the allowance is reserved for the cases that need it.

options.text: Split the batch across several days, so that no single day uses too much of her allowance.
options.explanation: Spreading the work delays the replies without reducing the total allowance the batch consumes.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A teacher wants Claude to answer student questions from a large and steadily growing set of course materials, across many separate chats.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Add the course materials to each chat; create a Project; ask questions in that project; keep the instructions brief.
options.explanation: Pasting the materials into individual chats is the very repetition a project is meant to remove.

options.text: Ask questions in a plain chat; keep the instructions brief; create a Project; add the course materials as project knowledge.
options.explanation: The questions are asked before any of the course materials exist as project knowledge, so those first answers have nothing to draw on.

options.text: Keep the instructions brief; create a Project; ask questions in that project; add the course materials as project knowledge.
options.explanation: Asking before the materials are uploaded means the early answers have nothing to draw on.

options.text: Create a Project; add the course materials as project knowledge; keep the instructions brief; ask questions in that project.
options.explanation: The project has to exist before materials can be attached, brief instructions leave more room for the materials themselves, and only chats started inside the project can draw on them.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A facilitator wants Claude to produce short prompts and summaries live during workshops, with participants waiting in the room. She standardises on the deepest-reasoning tier so that the material is always as good as it can be.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The facilitator becomes reliant on having Claude available, so a session held somewhere without connectivity is harder to run.
options.explanation: Dependence on connectivity is a sensible contingency to plan for, but it applies equally whichever tier she picks, so it is not the risk created by standardising on the deepest one.

options.text: The material becomes more detailed than a live workshop can absorb, so participants receive more text than they can read aloud.
options.explanation: Over-long output is a genuine annoyance, but it is fixed by asking for something shorter. It is not caused by the tier choice, and the facilitator can control length in the request itself.

options.text: The workshop material varies in tone between sessions, so participants attending more than one workshop notice the difference.
options.explanation: Some variation between sessions is expected with any tier and matters little for workshop prompts. It is a consistency preference rather than something that stops the session working.

options.text: The answers take longer to come back than a room of waiting participants can tolerate, so the help is unusable in the moment.
options.explanation: Depth is bought with time, and in a live setting responsiveness is the binding constraint. Choosing the deepest tier here sacrifices the very quality, immediacy, that made Claude useful in the room.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A developer asks Claude to build a small interactive React component that visualizes sales data with adjustable filters, and expects to iterate on the code across several follow-up messages.
question: Which feature will display this output in a way that supports iterative editing and version history?

options.text: A Project's knowledge base, which stores the component as reference material for future chats
options.explanation: Project knowledge is meant for background reference documents the user uploads, not for displaying and iteratively editing generated code with version tracking.

options.text: Research mode, which searches the web for similar existing React components
options.explanation: Research mode is for gathering external information through web searches, not for rendering or iterating on generated code.

options.text: The main chat transcript, where the code is printed inline with each response
options.explanation: Printing code inline in the main transcript does not provide the dedicated side-panel view or version history that iterative component development benefits from.

options.text: The artifact panel, which shows the component separately and tracks versions as it is revised
options.explanation: Artifacts open substantial, self-contained content like a React component in a dedicated side panel and provide a version selector, letting the developer iterate and switch between revisions.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A marketer runs a new campaign chat each week and re-pastes the same brand guidelines and tone-of-voice document into every one. She wants to stop repeating herself.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Add project instructions; run each campaign chat inside it; create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge.
options.explanation: Instructions and chats are both scoped to a project, so neither can come before the project is created.

options.text: Upload the guidelines as project knowledge; run each campaign chat inside it; create a Project; add project instructions.
options.explanation: Knowledge is uploaded into a project, so the upload cannot precede creating one, and the chats would run without the instructions.

options.text: Create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge; add project instructions; run each campaign chat inside it.
options.explanation: The workspace has to exist before knowledge and instructions can be attached to it, and the chats only inherit that context once they are started inside the finished project.

options.text: Run each campaign chat first; add project instructions; create a Project; upload the guidelines as project knowledge.
options.explanation: The campaign chats would run before the guidelines and instructions are in place, so the early work gets none of the benefit, and instructions cannot be added before the project exists.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: After a cost review, a team switches every Claude task to the fastest and cheapest tier.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Every task will now be completed rather faster than the team is able to review the output properly.
options.explanation: Faster turnaround is not the danger, and review capacity is a separate scheduling matter.

options.text: Responses will be much shorter, so colleagues will have to ask more follow-up questions.
options.explanation: Length is set by what is asked for rather than by the tier, and it is not the substantive exposure.

options.text: The small number of genuinely hard analyses will thin out with no agreed standard to catch it.
options.explanation: A blanket switch removes reasoning depth from the work that needed it, and without a defined quality bar the degradation shows up as slightly weaker answers nobody flags.

options.text: The team will be unable to move any of the tasks back to a deeper tier at a later stage.
options.explanation: Nothing prevents moving back; the tier can be changed whenever the team decides to.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A project lead notices that three colleagues each re-explain the same programme background to Claude every week in their own chats.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask each colleague to summarise their chats weekly and circulate those summaries by email.
options.explanation: Circulating summaries adds manual work each week without giving Claude the background in any of the chats.

options.text: Ask each colleague to keep one very long chat open so their own context accumulates over time.
options.explanation: Very long personal chats condense their own history and draw more heavily on usage allowance, and the context stays siloed.

options.text: Ask Claude to remember the programme background so nobody has to supply it again in future.
options.explanation: A chat does not carry context to colleagues' conversations; shared background has to be persisted deliberately.

options.text: Gather the background the team keeps repeating into one agreed set of reference documents.
options.explanation: Before choosing where to put shared context, the team needs to agree what that context actually is. A single reference set is what any later Project or hand-off will be built from.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A new team member asks how the Claude model tiers actually differ from one another in everyday use. Which two statements are accurate?
question: Select two.(Select 2)

options.text: The deepest tier suits genuinely hard problems, and it consumes meaningfully more allowance.
options.explanation: The deepest tier buys reasoning depth for harder problems and costs meaningfully more of the usage allowance.

options.text: The tiers differ only in writing style, so any of them may be used for any task at any time.
options.explanation: The difference is reasoning depth, speed and cost, not writing style, and the tiers are not interchangeable.

options.text: The lightest tier gives answers of the very same depth, only more slowly than the other two.
options.explanation: The lightest tier is the fastest of the three, and it trades some reasoning depth for that speed and low cost.

options.text: The mid tier is the fast, capable default, and it is the right pick for most everyday work.
options.explanation: The middle tier is positioned as the fast, capable default that handles most knowledge work well.

options.text: Moving up one tier is the standard fix whenever a prompt comes back with a vague or shallow answer.
options.explanation: A vague answer usually signals an under-specified prompt, and a deeper tier cannot supply context that was never given.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: An operations team must summarise several thousand short product blurbs every night, and the summaries get only a light human check. Which two factors should drive the tier choice?
question: Select two.

options.text: How long each finished summary turns out to be, because length is what separates the tiers.
options.explanation: Output length is set by the request, not by the tier, so it tells you nothing about which tier to pick.

options.text: The reasoning depth the hardest problem anywhere in the company would need, as a safety margin.
options.explanation: Sizing for an unrelated hardest-case task overspends depth and quota on work that is simple and lightly reviewed.

options.text: The allowance the run consumes, because this same job repeats every single night of the week.
options.explanation: A nightly repeat multiplies the allowance the job consumes, so recurring cost is a legitimate driver of the decision.

options.text: Whether the deepest tier appears on their plan at all, since availability settles the whole matter.
options.explanation: Availability is not the question; suitability for the task on cost, speed and quality is.

options.text: The throughput needed each night, because the volume makes speed per item a real constraint.
options.explanation: Thousands of items a night makes speed per item a genuine constraint, which is a core input to tier choice.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: An analyst must deliver a carefully reasoned briefing by the end of the day and has limited allowance left.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Check it against the brief; cut the scope to what the briefing needs; run that scope on the deepest tier; expand it if time allows.
options.explanation: Checking comes before anything has been produced, which makes the first step impossible.

options.text: Cut the scope to what the briefing actually needs; run that scope on the deepest tier; check it against the brief; expand it if time allows.
options.explanation: Narrowing scope is what makes the deeper tier affordable within the remaining allowance, and the check confirms the reduced briefing still meets the requirement.

options.text: Run the full scope on the deepest tier; cut the scope to what the briefing needs; check it against the brief; expand it if time allows.
options.explanation: Running the full scope on the most expensive tier first spends the constrained allowance before any trimming happens.

options.text: Cut the scope to what the briefing actually needs; expand it if time allows; run that scope on the deepest tier; check it against the brief.
options.explanation: Expanding the scope before it has been produced undoes the trimming that made the deeper tier affordable.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A colleague proposes running every request on two different tiers and comparing the two answers each time.
question: What is the most reasonable assessment?

options.text: It is wasteful, because the two tiers will always return answers that are effectively identical.
options.explanation: They genuinely differ on demanding work, so the objection is cost rather than a lack of difference.

options.text: It is sensible, because using two tiers spreads consumption across two separate allowances.
options.explanation: Usage is measured across all of a person's activity, so nothing is spread by using two tiers.

options.text: It is wasteful, since it doubles the allowance spent on a comparison worth doing only once.
options.explanation: Comparing tiers is worth doing on a representative sample to settle the choice; repeating it on every request pays twice for a decision already made.

options.text: It is sensible, since comparing two answers each time is the surest way to catch any error.
options.explanation: Two answers that agree can both be wrong, so this buys far less assurance than it costs.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A newsletter team produces about thirty short social posts each week and a person edits every one before it goes out.
question: Which tier fits this work best?

options.text: A different tier for each post, chosen according to which social platform it is destined for.
options.explanation: The platform does not change the reasoning the task requires, so varying tier by channel is arbitrary.

options.text: The fastest and cheapest tier, since the posts are short, routine and edited by a person after.
options.explanation: High volume, low complexity and a human editing step is exactly the profile the fastest tier is for; reasoning depth would add little to a two-line post.

options.text: The deepest-reasoning tier, because published content should always use the very strongest option.
options.explanation: The posts are short and human-edited, so the extra depth changes little while consuming much more allowance.

options.text: The default middle tier, because short marketing copy is too nuanced for any lighter option.
options.explanation: It would work, but it spends more allowance than thirty short, edited posts a week justify.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A team moves its live pricing sheet into a project's knowledge so every chat in the project can use it, and then changes its prices two months later.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The pricing sheet will be counted twice, once as knowledge and once in each conversation.
options.explanation: Nothing is double-counted in that way, and this does not describe a real failure mode.

options.text: Every chat in that project will keep quoting the superseded prices with complete confidence.
options.explanation: Making knowledge durable also makes staleness durable. Until the sheet is replaced, the project answers confidently from a document that no longer reflects reality.

options.text: Colleagues outside the project will be unable to see the pricing sheet in their own chats.
options.explanation: That is the expected scope of a project rather than a risk created by the price change.

options.text: The project will refuse any further uploads until the outdated pricing sheet has been removed.
options.explanation: There is no such block, and framing this as an upload problem misses where the damage actually occurs.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: An operations manager has finished a long planning chat and expects the team to revisit the same topic every month.
question: What is the best way to keep that context available?

options.text: Rely on Claude recalling the earlier planning chat automatically whenever she opens a new conversation.
options.explanation: Automatic recall is not a dependable store for decisions the team must rely on months later; durable context should be persisted into project knowledge deliberately.

options.text: Keep reopening the same long chat every month so that all of the history stays inside one conversation.
options.explanation: A conversation that grows for a year will keep condensing its own earlier content and will draw heavily on usage allowance.

options.text: Copy the whole transcript into the first message of every monthly chat so that nothing at all is ever left out.
options.explanation: The transcript is mostly working discussion rather than durable fact, and re-pasting it each month wastes window space and allowance.

options.text: Save the agreed decisions into a Project as knowledge, then start each monthly review as a fresh chat there.
options.explanation: Persisting the durable output into project knowledge keeps the context available to every future chat without carrying months of transcript inside one conversation.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A teacher reaches the length limit in a chat while working through a stack of graded feedback.
question: What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Start a new chat and carry forward only the material and decisions the remaining work actually needs.
options.explanation: The length limit applies to one conversation, so a fresh chat clears it. Bringing only what is still needed keeps the new conversation lean.

options.text: Buy additional usage credits, which will raise the context window available inside that conversation.
options.explanation: Credits extend how much she can interact with Claude. The context window is fixed by the model and is not enlarged by buying allowance.

options.text: Wait several hours for the length limit to reset, then carry on in the same conversation thread.
options.explanation: Length limits do not reset on a timer; that is how usage limits behave, and the two are easily confused.

options.text: Switch to a shorter reply style, which will free up the window space the earlier messages took.
options.explanation: Shorter future replies slow the fill rate slightly but cannot recover space already occupied by earlier messages.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: An analyst's first draft from Claude is vague, and she wonders whether she should move up to a deeper-reasoning tier to fix it. Which two responses are sound?
question: Select two.

options.text: Escalate to the deepest tier right away, since depth is the usual cause of a weak first draft.
options.explanation: Reaching for the deepest tier as a reflex spends quota without fixing the under-specified request underneath.

options.text: Stay on the lightest tier no matter what, because the tier has little effect on answer quality.
options.explanation: The tiers do differ in reasoning depth, so refusing to escalate is as unexamined as escalating by default.

options.text: Check first whether the request was under-specified, since a deeper tier supplies no context.
options.explanation: Vagueness most often comes from a thin prompt, and no tier can invent the audience, format or source material you left out.

options.text: Escalate the tier only when the work truly needs more reasoning depth than it is now getting.
options.explanation: Escalating is the right move when reasoning depth is genuinely the binding constraint, and only then.

options.text: Split the same request across three chats on three tiers and merge whichever parts look best.
options.explanation: Running the same weak prompt three times multiplies the cost and still leaves the original specification problem in place.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A marketing manager's answers keep coming back shallow, and a colleague suggests moving straight to the deepest-reasoning model.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Check whether the prompt states the depth needed; improve the prompt and retry; move to the deepest-reasoning model; keep the lighter model for routine parts.
options.explanation: A shallow answer is often an under-specified request, so the prompt is checked first, and reasoning depth is escalated only once that has been ruled out.

options.text: Move to the deepest-reasoning model; check whether the prompt states the depth needed; improve the prompt; keep the lighter model for routine parts.
options.explanation: Changing tier before looking at the prompt spends more allowance on what may be an instruction problem rather than a capability one.

options.text: Improve the prompt and retry; move to the deepest-reasoning model; check whether the prompt states the depth needed; keep the lighter model for routine parts.
options.explanation: The prompt is revised before anyone has looked at what it actually says, and the diagnosis arrives after the tier has already been changed.

options.text: Keep the lighter model for routine parts; move to the deepest-reasoning model; improve the prompt and retry; check whether the prompt states the depth needed.
options.explanation: Every diagnostic step happens after both model changes, so the tier decisions are taken with no evidence behind them.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: An operations manager finds she hits her usage limit before lunch nearly every working day and is frustrated by the interruption.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Upgrade immediately to the highest plan tier available so the daily interruptions simply stop happening.
options.explanation: An upgrade may be justified later, but buying more allowance before understanding what consumes it is guesswork.

options.text: Review the usage view in her settings to see what recent sessions actually consumed, before changing anything.
options.explanation: The fix depends on the cause, and the usage view shows how much of her session and weekly allowance has gone. Diagnosing first avoids paying for a change that would not help.

options.text: Switch every task to the deepest-reasoning model so that fewer follow-up messages are needed to finish.
options.explanation: The deepest-reasoning tier consumes meaningfully more allowance per message, so this is likely to make matters worse.

options.text: Move all of her work into brand-new chats each morning so that every conversation starts with an empty window.
options.explanation: A fresh window addresses a length limit, not a usage limit, which follows her across all conversations.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: A finance team runs an overnight batch of several thousand transaction narratives that must be finished before the six o'clock reporting cut-off. They move the batch to the deepest-reasoning tier because they want the best possible quality.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The team grows used to a higher standard of narrative and finds the earlier output unacceptable if they ever have to revert.
options.explanation: Raised expectations are a soft consequence and only matter if the team later reverts. They have no bearing on whether tonight's batch clears the six o'clock deadline.

options.text: The narratives come back written in a more elaborate style than the reporting template was originally designed to accommodate.
options.explanation: An elaborate style is a formatting mismatch that can be corrected by asking for a tighter format. It does not threaten the report itself in the way a missed cut-off does.

options.text: The batch does not finish inside the overnight window, so the morning report goes out incomplete or does not go out at all.
options.explanation: At this volume the binding constraint is throughput against a fixed deadline. Depth that cannot complete in the window fails the task outright, which is worse than slightly plainer narratives delivered on time.

options.text: The batch produces more detail per transaction than the finance team has time to read through before the reporting cut-off.
options.explanation: Excess detail costs reading time, but the narratives are generated per transaction and are not all read individually. The scheduling failure is the far more serious outcome here.

objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
situation: An education lead is choosing a model tier to help draft feedback that will contribute to students' marks.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Choose the deepest tier, since anything involving students should use the strongest option.
options.explanation: It may well be right, but choosing it before the quality bar is stated is a guess rather than a judgment.

options.text: Establish how the feedback will be used and what an error in it would cost a student.
options.explanation: The quality bar comes from the consequence of the output. Once she knows an error affects a mark, the tier decision follows from that bar rather than from cost alone.

options.text: Compare the tiers on a sample and pick whichever produces the longest and most detailed drafts.
options.explanation: Length is not the standard, and choosing on it rewards verbosity rather than accuracy.

options.text: Choose the fastest tier, since drafting feedback for a class is a high-volume repetitive task.
options.explanation: Volume is only half the picture, and choosing on throughput ignores what an error here would cost.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A startup has a new application idea and wants to minimize development cost and iteration time before deciding whether a more capable model is truly needed.
question: Following Anthropic's recommended approach for this situation, which model should they implement first?

options.text: Claude Sonnet, since it should always be the first model tried regardless of budget concerns
options.explanation: Anthropic frames two valid starting approaches based on the use case; Sonnet being the universal first choice regardless of budget priorities is not part of that guidance.

options.text: Whichever model the startup's investors specify in the term sheet
options.explanation: Model selection should follow the technical criteria of capability, speed, and cost fit for the application, not external non-technical instructions unrelated to those criteria.

options.text: Claude Opus, then downgrade later once prompts have been optimized for cost
options.explanation: Starting with Opus and optimizing down over time is the recommended path for complex reasoning tasks where accuracy outweighs cost, not for a startup explicitly prioritizing low initial cost and fast iteration.

options.text: Claude Haiku, then upgrade only if testing reveals a specific capability gap
options.explanation: Anthropic recommends starting with a fast, cost-effective model like Haiku, testing thoroughly, and upgrading only if performance reveals a specific capability gap, which fits a startup minimizing cost and iteration time.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A new team member asks how the Claude model tiers actually differ from one another in everyday use. Which two statements are accurate?
question: Select two.

options.text: The tiers differ only in writing style, so any of them may be used for any task at any time.
options.explanation: The difference is reasoning depth, speed and cost, not writing style, and the tiers are not interchangeable.

options.text: The deepest tier suits genuinely hard problems, and it consumes meaningfully more allowance.
options.explanation: The deepest tier buys reasoning depth for harder problems and costs meaningfully more of the usage allowance.

options.text: Moving up one tier is the standard fix whenever a prompt comes back with a vague or shallow answer.
options.explanation: A vague answer usually signals an under-specified prompt, and a deeper tier cannot supply context that was never given.

options.text: The mid tier is the fast, capable default, and it is the right pick for most everyday work.
options.explanation: The middle tier is positioned as the fast, capable default that handles most knowledge work well.

options.text: The lightest tier gives answers of the very same depth, only more slowly than the other two.
options.explanation: The lightest tier is the fastest of the three, and it trades some reasoning depth for that speed and low cost.

objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
situation: A communications lead is drafting an announcement in a chat that is close to its length limit, and the announcement is due in an hour.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Upgrade to a higher plan tier straight away so that the conversation gains a larger context window.
options.explanation: The context window is fixed by the model in use, so buying more allowance does not enlarge the window inside that chat.

options.text: Delete the earliest messages in the conversation so that the newer content has more room to work with.
options.explanation: Removing earlier messages by hand is slow, destroys the record, and is not how room is reclaimed in a chat.

options.text: Switch the conversation to a faster, cheaper model so the remaining exchanges take up less of the window.
options.explanation: Lighter models generally come with smaller context windows, so this shrinks the room she has left rather than extending it.

options.text: Capture the current draft and the outstanding decisions outside the chat before she does anything else.
options.explanation: With a deadline close, the priority is making the work durable. Once the draft and open points are safely out of the conversation, restarting or continuing becomes a low-risk choice.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A new joiner asks how the Claude model tiers differ from the point of view of someone using the Claude app.
question: Which description is accurate?

options.text: Sonnet reasons most deeply, Opus is the everyday default option, and Haiku handles only images.
options.explanation: Sonnet is the capable default rather than the deepest tier, and Haiku is a general fast model, not an image-only one.

options.text: Haiku gives the deepest reasoning, Sonnet is the fastest option, and Opus suits routine bulk work.
options.explanation: This inverts the tiers. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest rather than the deepest-reasoning option.

options.text: Opus reasons most deeply and uses more allowance, Sonnet is the capable default, Haiku is fastest.
options.explanation: As an end user experiences them, the tiers trade reasoning depth against speed and how much of the usage allowance each message consumes.

options.text: The tiers produce identical answers and differ only in how quickly those answers come back to you.
options.explanation: Speed is one axis, but reasoning depth genuinely differs, which is why the choice matters on hard work.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A research lab needs help with a scientific analysis task involving nuanced multi-step reasoning, where correctness matters far more than response time or token cost.
question: Which model tier does Anthropic's guidance point to?

options.text: Select Claude Opus, because scientific and mathematical tasks where accuracy outweighs cost are core use cases.
options.explanation: Anthropic explicitly recommends Claude Opus for complex reasoning, scientific, and mathematical tasks where accuracy outweighs cost and speed, exactly matching this scenario.

options.text: Select Claude Sonnet, because it is the best general-purpose choice regardless of how much accuracy is prioritized.
options.explanation: Sonnet is a strong general-purpose model, but when nuanced, multi-step reasoning and accuracy are paramount, Anthropic points to the most capable tier (Opus) rather than a general-purpose default.

options.text: Select Claude Haiku, because near-frontier reasoning at the lowest cost is adequate for standard research tasks.
options.explanation: Haiku is optimized for cost and latency sensitivity; Anthropic's guidance reserves it for tasks where speed or economy is the priority, not nuanced scientific work demanding maximum correctness.

options.text: Select Claude Opus with effort set to its lowest level, because minimizing effort improves reasoning accuracy.
options.explanation: Lowering the effort parameter limits reasoning depth to reduce latency and cost; it does not improve accuracy and would undermine performance on a task requiring nuanced reasoning.

objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
situation: A software team wants a coding assistant for daily feature development: reviewing pull requests, generating unit tests, and answering questions about the codebase. They want strong code quality and agentic tool use without paying premium enterprise pricing.
question: Which model tier fits best?

options.text: Claude Opus delivers the highest accuracy for pull request reviews and test generation, essential for daily feature development.
options.explanation: While Claude Opus may offer the highest accuracy, it is designed for the most complex, large-scale agentic coding challenges and comes with premium pricing. For routine daily development work, Sonnet provides sufficient accuracy at a more appropriate cost, making Opus unnecessary for this scenario.

options.text: Claude Haiku is the only model with extended thinking, enabling step-by-step code review and test generation at the lowest cost.
options.explanation: While Claude Haiku offers extended thinking that can facilitate step-by-step reasoning, the team requires strong general code quality and agentic tool use for daily development. Haiku's primary strength is speed and cost efficiency, not the frontier-level coding capability needed for thorough pull request reviews and test generation.

options.text: Claude Sonnet delivers frontier-level coding and agentic tool use at a mid-range price, ideal for daily dev tasks.
options.explanation: Claude Sonnet provides frontier-level coding performance and agentic tool use at a price point that balances cost and capability, making it ideal for daily development tasks like code review and test generation. This matches the team's need for strong code quality without enterprise premium pricing.

options.text: Claude Opus in fast mode matches Sonnet's pricing while delivering the highest accuracy for pull request reviews and test generation.
options.explanation: Fast mode on Claude Opus improves output speed but does not reduce pricing to Sonnet's level. Opus fast mode still operates at a premium price point, so it does not meet the team's requirement to avoid premium enterprise pricing.

objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
situation: A game designer asks Claude to build a playable HTML5 prototype of a simple puzzle game with score tracking, and wants to keep tweaking the mechanics over the next hour based on playtesting.
question: Which feature keeps the running prototype visible and editable throughout that session?

options.text: A shared team workspace is necessary because individual accounts cannot render and tweak HTML5 prototypes.
options.explanation: Individual accounts can render artifacts including HTML5 prototypes without a shared team workspace. The artifact panel works within a single user’s session to display and iteratively edit the prototype.

options.text: Research mode is required because its engine renders and updates interactive content during iterative tweaks.
options.explanation: Research mode performs web searches and has no engine for rendering or updating interactive HTML5 content. That rendering and iterative edit capability comes from artifacts, not research mode.

options.text: A Project is needed since project knowledge alone renders the HTML5 prototype and supports iterative tweaks.
options.explanation: Project knowledge bases store reference documents and do not render live interactive content. Artifacts—not a Project—are required to render the HTML5 prototype and support iterative tweaks within the conversation.

options.text: The artifact panel keeps the prototype rendered separately while accepting live iterative edits.
options.explanation: The artifact panel is designed to render self-contained content like an HTML5 game prototype separately from the chat, allowing the designer to see a live view while requesting iterative edits to the mechanics. It explicitly supports this interactive, visible feedback loop.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: While designing a Claude-assisted tender-summary arrangement, an analyst finds that every draft needs the same three corrections.
question: Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep making the three corrections by hand, since they take only a minute
options.explanation: Hand-correcting works while one person runs it, but the fix vanishes the moment anyone else uses the arrangement.

options.text: Move to a more capable model, which should stop the corrections recurring
options.explanation: A stronger model cannot infer three unstated requirements, so the same three corrections will keep appearing.

options.text: Fold those three corrections into the written instructions and try again
options.explanation: A repeated correction is a specification the instruction is missing. Writing it in makes the fix part of the design instead of something the analyst re-applies every time.

options.text: Ask for three separate drafts each time and pick whichever needs least work
options.explanation: Generating extra drafts increases the work of choosing without addressing why every draft has the same gap.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
question: A product manager tells the team, "Once we roll out Claude for contract drafting, we won't need any legal review at all." How should a solutions architect best respond to this claim?

options.text: Confirm that Claude has passed legal certification for autonomous contracts, so review is unnecessary after the pilot.
options.explanation: Claude is not legally certified to autonomously produce binding contracts, and no vendor certification eliminates the need for professional legal review.

options.text: Suggest that legal review can be replaced by running the draft through a second Claude session with a different prompt.
options.explanation: Running a second Claude session does not substitute for qualified human legal judgment and does not eliminate the underlying risk of errors.

options.text: Explain that Claude can speed up drafting, but a qualified legal reviewer should still check every clause before it is used.
options.explanation: Claude can accelerate drafting, but it can still produce plausible-sounding but inaccurate or non-compliant clauses, so human legal review remains essential before contracts are finalized.

options.text: Recommend dropping contract drafting entirely, since Claude cannot produce usable legal language in any context.
options.explanation: Claude is genuinely useful for accelerating contract drafting; the correct guidance is to pair it with review, not abandon the use case.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A back-office team plans to remove three handoffs between reviewers by having Claude carry each case straight through. Those handoffs are also where colleagues currently catch one another's mistakes.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Reviewers may resist a change that removes part of what they currently do each day.
options.explanation: Resistance to change is common and is addressed by involving the reviewers in the redesign. It affects how smoothly the change lands rather than whether the resulting process is safe.

options.text: The informal checks that lived in those handoffs disappear with nothing put in their place.
options.explanation: The handoffs were doing two jobs, and only the visible one is being replaced. Removing them takes out the peer review that was catching errors, so the redesigned process is not just faster but materially less accurate unless a deliberate check is designed back in.

options.text: The redesigned process may be considerably harder to explain to auditors than the version it replaces.
options.explanation: Explaining a new process to auditors takes documentation effort and is a normal part of any change. It becomes a serious problem only because of the missing checks, which is the underlying issue.

options.text: The time saved may be less than expected once the new process is running at full volume.
options.explanation: A smaller saving than hoped would make the change less worthwhile, which is disappointing but recoverable. The team would still be able to see the shortfall and adjust.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: An analyst is presenting a Claude-assisted workflow to sceptical senior stakeholders next week. Which two things should the presentation include?
question: Select two.

options.text: A comparison of technical benchmark scores across each of the underlying model tiers.
options.explanation: Benchmark scores are not what a business audience needs, and they say nothing about this workflow's value.

options.text: A claim that Claude will not make any factual errors once all its instructions are written well.
options.explanation: Good instructions reduce error but do not eliminate it, so this claim is false and will damage trust later.

options.text: A specific, measured example of what the workflow improved during the pilot it ran on.
options.explanation: A measured pilot result is concrete evidence of value rather than an assertion stakeholders are asked to take on trust.

options.text: Where a human still reviews the output, and why that review step has been kept in place.
options.explanation: Naming where human review remains, and why, is honest limitation-setting and is what makes the value claim credible.

options.text: A promise that the workflow removes any need to check the output from this point onward.
options.explanation: Promising that checking is no longer needed oversells the tool and sets the expectation that will break first.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: An HR analyst plans to use Claude to analyse requirements for a new grievance-handling process. The best source material is a folder of named employee case files.
question: What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Check the organisation's policy for this category of data and mask identifiers before anything is uploaded.
options.explanation: Requirements analysis is still legitimate here, but grievance case files are sensitive personal data. Confirming what policy allows and removing or masking identifiers first lets the analysis proceed on the patterns that matter while keeping the material within the rules.

options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the case files, then delete the conversation once the analysis has been finished.
options.explanation: Deleting afterwards does not undo the upload, and it treats a data-handling decision as something to clean up later. The judgment about whether identifiable case files may be shared has to be made before, not after.

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm whether the case files contain any personal data before any of them are uploaded to it.
options.explanation: Claude cannot assess files it has not been given, so this either does nothing or requires the very upload that is in question. The analyst already knows the files name employees, so the answer is not the missing piece.

options.text: Upload the case files into a private project workspace so only the analyst can open the resulting chats.
options.explanation: Restricting who can see the resulting chats does not address whether the material should have been uploaded in the first place. Access control inside the tool is not a substitute for the organisation's rule about this class of data.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A project manager asks Claude for a delivery plan and receives a confident schedule that quietly assumes full-time availability the team does not have.
question: What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask Claude to compress the proposed schedule so that it still lands on the original date promised to the sponsor.
options.explanation: Compressing a schedule that was already built on an impossible assumption makes it less achievable, not more. The date is preserved on paper while the plan moves further from what the team can deliver.

options.text: Ask Claude to add a contingency buffer to each phase so the plan can absorb the availability problem.
options.explanation: Buffers absorb ordinary variation, not a structural error in the availability the plan assumes. Padding phases spreads the same wrong assumption across the whole schedule and makes it harder to see.

options.text: Give Claude the real constraints and ask for a plan that states its assumptions where facts are missing.
options.explanation: The schedule is wrong because the planning inputs were missing, so the fix is to supply them. Asking Claude to state its assumptions explicitly also makes the next gap visible immediately instead of leaving it buried inside confident dates.

options.text: Ask Claude to explain how it built the schedule so the manager can judge whether to trust the dates.
options.explanation: Understanding the reasoning is a reasonable check and may reveal the flawed assumption, but it stops short of fixing anything. The manager already knows the availability is wrong; what is missing is the correct input.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A team is setting up a Claude-assisted way of producing meeting notes. Nothing has been agreed or written down, people on the team hold different views about what the notes should contain, and the notes will be circulated to everyone who attended, so the team needs something it can depend on before this goes into regular use.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Run it over one week of real work; collect specific examples of where it fell short; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; revise the written instructions and run it again.
options.explanation: Starting with a week of live use puts notes in front of every attendee while the team still disagrees about what those notes should contain, so the shortcomings it turns up describe several people's private habits rather than one shared way of working, and there is nothing agreed for the evidence to be measured against.

options.text: Collect specific examples of where it fell short; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; revise the written instructions and run it again; run it over one week of real work.
options.explanation: There is no agreed practice yet whose shortcomings could be collected, so the sequence opens with evidence it cannot have, and the week of real use lands at the very end, after the written instructions have already been revised, where the evidence it produces feeds nothing.

options.text: Revise the written instructions and run it again; run it over one week of real work; draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; collect specific examples of where it fell short.
options.explanation: Nothing has been written down, so there are no instructions to revise first, and the specific failure examples are gathered last, at the point where there is no remaining step to act on them.

options.text: Draft the new way of working with the people who do the job; run it over one week of real work; collect specific examples of where it fell short; revise the written instructions and run it again.
options.explanation: Drafting with the people who do the job settles the goal and how the work is split between them and Claude before anything is delegated, a week of real use then produces honest evidence against that agreed intent, specific failure examples say what to change, and revising the written instructions and running it again closes the evaluate-and-refine loop for another pass.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: Over three weeks a team refined the instructions for a Claude-drafted internal newsletter until the editor was consistently happy with every draft. Nobody asked the readers.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The three weeks of refinement consumed effort that could have gone into writing newsletters.
options.explanation: The refinement effort is a sunk cost that will be repaid if the arrangement works. Time spent iterating is expected; the problem is what the iteration was aimed at.

options.text: The instructions have grown long enough that new team members will find them hard to follow at first.
options.explanation: Long instructions are an onboarding inconvenience that can be tidied up. They make the arrangement harder to hand over, but they do not make the newsletter less effective for the people reading it.

options.text: The drafts are now tuned to one editor's taste, and no one has checked that they serve the readers.
options.explanation: Iteration improves whatever it is measured against, and here the only measure was one editor's approval. Three weeks of refinement have optimised for a proxy, so the drafts could satisfy the editor completely while serving readers worse than before.

options.text: The editor may become the only person able to judge whether a draft is ready to be published.
options.explanation: Concentrating judgment in one person is a genuine weakness in the design, and it follows from the same root cause. It is a consequence of tuning to one taste rather than the primary danger, which is that readers were never consulted.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: With no internal documents to hand, an analyst asks Claude to list the standard requirements for a customer complaints process and pastes the reply straight into the project brief.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The analyst will have to repeat the request if the conversation is closed before the reply is saved.
options.explanation: Losing the reply costs a few minutes to regenerate. It is an inconvenience rather than a risk to the correctness of the requirements the project will be run against.

options.text: The brief will be rather longer than the sponsor expects and may need trimming before the next review meeting.
options.explanation: Length is easy to fix and easy to notice. A brief that is too long gets edited, whereas plausible requirements nobody sourced tend to survive review precisely because they read like standard practice.

options.text: The brief will carry generic requirements that sound authoritative but reflect no source and no context.
options.explanation: Asked for standard requirements with no material to work from, Claude produces a confident generic list. Pasted straight into the brief it becomes the team's stated scope, even though it reflects no regulator, no system and no customer this organisation actually has.

options.text: The reply may be phrased for a general audience rather than in the complaints team's own vocabulary.
options.explanation: Vocabulary mismatch is a readability problem that a rewrite fixes. It may slow the team down slightly, but the brief would still be built on requirements that were never traced to anything real.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: An operations director wants Claude added to a customer onboarding process that the team agrees is slow, full of rework, and poorly understood.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to redesign the whole onboarding process from scratch and compare it with what happens now.
options.explanation: A redesign proposed before the current problems are diagnosed rests on assumptions about why the process fails. It also asks the team to compare today's process against a proposal, when what they lack is an understanding of today's process.

options.text: Give every member of the onboarding team access and let each of them find their own uses for it.
options.explanation: Open access encourages useful experimentation but leaves the process itself untouched. Individuals will speed up their own steps in different ways, which can make an already inconsistent process harder to follow.

options.text: Establish why the current process produces rework, before deciding where Claude would fit into it.
options.explanation: Integrating Claude into a process nobody understands simply performs the existing mistakes faster. Finding out where the rework originates tells the team whether the answer is to augment a step, redesign a sequence, or fix something that has nothing to do with Claude at all.

options.text: Add Claude at the step that generates the most documents, since that is where the volume sits.
options.explanation: Document volume marks where effort is spent, not where the process breaks. If the rework is caused by incomplete information arriving at step one, accelerating the busiest step produces more flawed documents rather than fewer.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A trade association's events team submits a use-case request stating that Claude should "take over the speaker selection" for next year's conference. The business analyst who reviews intake requests must assess it.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Check whether the events team's plan fits inside the association's current allowance
options.explanation: Cost is a real consideration, but it is a downstream question. A use case that should not be delegated at all does not become sound because it is affordable.

options.text: Establish what the selection actually decides and who is accountable for the outcome
options.explanation: Requirements analysis starts with understanding the decision itself: what it determines, for whom, and who must answer for it. Only then can you say which parts are delegable and which must stay with the panel.

options.text: Ask Claude to draft selection criteria from the previous three years of speaker lists
options.explanation: Drafting criteria assumes the use case is sound and that past selections are a fair model; that assumption is exactly what has not been tested yet.

options.text: Run a trial in which Claude ranks this year's applicants and compare with the panel
options.explanation: A comparison trial is a reasonable later step, but running it before anyone has defined what the selection is for gives no basis for judging the result.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: An analyst asks Claude to redesign a claims workflow using a process map stored in the team's project, unaware that the map has not been updated for two years.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The redesign may optimise a process the team no longer follows, and nothing in the output flags it.
options.explanation: Claude works from the project knowledge it is given, so a map that is two years stale can yield a polished redesign of a process the team has already changed. The help centre warns that Claude can sound convincing while not being grounded in fact, so nothing in the redesign marks its starting point as obsolete, and no amount of reprompting repairs a stale source - only refreshing the map does.

options.text: The project may hold several versions of the map, making it unclear which one Claude actually used.
options.explanation: Ambiguity about which version was used is a housekeeping weakness worth fixing. In this scenario the problem is not which map was chosen but that the only map available may be out of date.

options.text: The analyst may need to rerun the request once an updated version of the process map is available.
options.explanation: Rerunning the request once the map is refreshed is the remedy, not the risk. The cost of a repeated request is trivial next to acting on a redesign nobody realised was obsolete.

options.text: The redesign may use terms for the workflow stages that the current claims team no longer recognises.
options.explanation: Outdated terminology is a visible symptom that would prompt someone to question the output. It is a useful warning sign rather than the underlying danger.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A team designed its Claude-assisted case-note arrangement around one unusually clean example case, and it worked perfectly. They now plan to put all case types through it.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Claude will produce case notes that are noticeably longer than the previous ones
options.explanation: Note length is a formatting matter that a reviewer would spot immediately and can be specified away.

options.text: The arrangement was tuned to a case that does not represent the messy real ones
options.explanation: A design validated on one tidy case has been fitted to the easiest conditions it will ever face. The awkward, incomplete and contested cases are where it will fail, and none of them was tested.

options.text: Colleagues will find the written instructions too long to read before using it
options.explanation: Instruction length is a usability nuisance that is easy to notice and easy to shorten.

options.text: The team will exceed its weekly usage allowance within the first fortnight of use
options.explanation: Allowance pressure is a manageable operational cost, and it would show up plainly rather than producing quietly wrong case notes.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: In a pilot of a new Claude-assisted briefing arrangement, three of eight testers report that the output is "not quite right" but say nothing more specific.
question: What should the pilot's owner do first?

options.text: Rewrite the instructions to cover the areas the owner believes are most likely to be causing the trouble.
options.explanation: Rewriting on a hunch changes the arrangement without knowing what is wrong. If the guess misses, the pilot now has two versions and still no diagnosis, and the testers' original complaint remains unexplained.

options.text: Ask the three testers for specific examples, with what the output said and what it should have said.
options.explanation: "Not quite right" is not actionable, and the cheapest way to make it actionable is to ask for cases. A concrete pair of what was produced and what was wanted turns vague dissatisfaction into a specific gap the instructions can address.

options.text: Ask the five satisfied testers what they did differently and circulate that as guidance to everyone.
options.explanation: Learning from the satisfied testers may eventually help, but it assumes the difference lies in how the tool was used rather than in the briefings themselves. It also leaves the three unresolved complaints uninvestigated.

options.text: Pause the pilot until the owner can sit with each tester and watch a full briefing being produced.
options.explanation: Direct observation is thorough but slow, and pausing the pilot stops the flow of evidence just when it is needed. Asking for examples costs an email and usually locates the problem immediately.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: An operations team wants to evaluate whether invoice-query triage, currently done by two people, is a sound use case to hand to Claude.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Compare and fix the guidance; run the small sample; agree what a correct decision looks like; extend to the full queue.
options.explanation: Fixing the guidance before anything has been run means correcting problems nobody has observed, and the standard for a correct decision arrives after the sample has already been judged against it.

options.text: Agree what a correct decision looks like; run the small sample; compare and fix the guidance; extend to the full queue.
options.explanation: The standard comes first so results can be graded, the pilot stays small so mistakes are cheap, the comparison against the current handlers shows where the guidance falls short, and only a corrected approach is extended to the full queue with continued spot checks.

options.text: Extend to the full queue; agree what a correct decision looks like; run the small sample; compare and fix the guidance.
options.explanation: Going to the full queue first is the opposite of piloting. Every later step then happens under live load, so mistakes reach real invoice queries before anyone has agreed what a good triage decision even is.

options.text: Run the small sample; agree what a correct decision looks like; extend to the full queue; compare and fix the guidance.
options.explanation: Running the sample before agreeing what a correct decision looks like leaves the team with output they cannot grade, and extending to the full queue before the comparison means any weakness is discovered at full volume.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A claims team is deciding whether to augment its current process with Claude or to redesign the process around what Claude makes possible.
question: Which condition most justifies a redesign rather than augmentation?

options.text: Several steps exist only to work around a limitation that no longer applies to this work.
options.explanation: Redesign is warranted when the structure of the process encodes a constraint that has gone away, because no amount of speeding up those steps removes work that no longer needs doing. Augmenting them would preserve the workaround permanently.

options.text: Leadership has asked for a visible improvement that staff and customers will both notice soon.
options.explanation: A demand for visible improvement sets an expectation about impact, not about which approach is appropriate. Augmenting a well-chosen step can be highly visible, and redesigning for visibility invites disruption without a structural reason.

options.text: The team finds the current process tedious and would welcome a change to how the work is done.
options.explanation: Tedium is a good reason to look for delegation candidates within the process, which is augmentation. It does not indicate that the shape of the process itself is wrong.

options.text: The current process has more steps than the equivalent process at a comparable organisation.
options.explanation: A step count comparison ignores why the extra steps exist. Another organisation may face different regulation, volumes or systems, so the difference is a prompt to investigate rather than evidence for a redesign.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A stakeholder is confused that Claude gave two slightly different summaries of the same document on two separate runs, and asks whether the model is broken.
question: What is the best explanation to give?

options.text: Explain that document summaries always fail after the first request, so each summary attempt requires a new conversation.
options.explanation: Document summaries do not systematically fail after the first request; this explanation wrongly portrays expected variability as a failure. Each summary attempt can produce slightly different wording without needing a new conversation.

options.text: Explain that Claude's responses are not perfectly deterministic, so minor wording variation between runs is normal and expected.
options.explanation: Claude's responses are not perfectly deterministic because text generation involves random sampling, which can lead to minor wording differences between runs. This variability is normal and expected, not a malfunction.

options.text: Explain that the second summary is correct and the first one should be treated as a bug that support must investigate right away.
options.explanation: Treating the second summary as correct and the first as a bug misrepresents normal output variability. Slight variations between runs are common and do not indicate a defect requiring investigation.

options.text: Explain that variation only occurs when a document exceeds the context window, so shortening the document resolves the issue.
options.explanation: Output variation is not caused by document length or exceeding the context window; it stems from Claude's probabilistic generation process. Shortening the document will not eliminate normal, minor wording differences between runs.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A conference organiser wants Claude to help plan the run-up to a 400-delegate event.
question: Which input will make the resulting plan most useful?

options.text: The actual dates, the team's availability and the tasks that went wrong last year
options.explanation: Real dates, real capacity and the known failure points from last year are the material that makes a plan specific to this event rather than a template anyone could have written.

options.text: The delegate list and the venue's promotional brochure for this year's conference
options.explanation: A delegate list and a brochure describe who attends and how the venue markets itself, neither of which shapes the run-up schedule.

options.text: A request to produce the most thorough conference plan that Claude is able to write
options.explanation: Asking for thoroughness without supplying facts produces length, not fit; the plan still has to guess the constraints.
