options.text: A note that the event is important and that the plan must not miss anything at all
options.explanation: Emphasis is not information. Telling Claude the event matters gives it nothing new to plan around.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
question: What is an effective way to use Claude to analyze requirements and use cases early in the development process?

options.text: Ask Claude to simulate a developer reviewing requirements and ask clarifying questions for ambiguity.
options.explanation: Simulating a developer reviewing requirements and asking clarifying questions allows Claude to proactively identify ambiguities, gaps, and inconsistencies, improving clarity and reducing downstream issues.

options.text: Ask Claude to ignore the current requirements draft and generate a completely new set of use cases from scratch.
options.explanation: Ignoring the current requirements draft to generate new use cases from scratch risks losing valuable context, stakeholder input, and business alignment; instead, Claude should refine and analyze the provided requirements.

options.text: Ask Claude to examine the completed code for missing logic and infer requirements that were not documented.
options.explanation: Examining completed code for missing logic is a reactive approach that addresses issues only after development, missing the chance to catch ambiguities early and leading to costly rework.

options.text: Ask Claude to independently review requirements, resolve ambiguities, and finalize them with no human check.
options.explanation: Having Claude independently review and finalize requirements without human check eliminates necessary oversight; human validation is critical for context, ethics, and domain nuances, so Claude should augment, not replace, human reviewers.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: An operations planner asks Claude to compress a six-week onboarding schedule into four weeks. The returned plan is detailed and internally consistent, and the planner circulates it as the new schedule.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The plan will be written for a reader who is far more senior than the planner is
options.explanation: Register is easy to adjust and easy to notice. It does not determine whether the compressed schedule is workable.

options.text: The plan will take longer to read than the six-week schedule it is meant to replace
options.explanation: A long plan is an inconvenience. An unexamined assumption inside it is what breaks the onboarding.

options.text: Claude will decline to shorten a schedule without seeing the original planning file
options.explanation: Claude will attempt the compression with whatever it is given; refusing for want of a file is not the failure mode here.

options.text: Steps were dropped or overlapped on assumptions the planner never stated or checked
options.explanation: To fit six weeks into four, something had to give. Because the plan reads as coherent, the compromises it made are invisible, and nobody has confirmed that they are acceptable.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A team has spent three weeks refining a Claude-assisted weekly digest. The last two rounds of changes produced no difference anyone could notice.
question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to grade its own digests and continue until the grades stop rising
options.explanation: Self-grading tells the team how the digest scores itself, which is not the same as whether readers can use it.

options.text: Keep refining until the digest needs no editing at all before it is circulated
options.explanation: Requiring zero editing sets a standard the arrangement was never designed to meet and delays any benefit indefinitely.

options.text: Start again with a fresh set of instructions written by a different team member
options.explanation: Discarding three weeks of refinement resets the work without any evidence that a fresh start would do better.

options.text: Put the current version into use and review it after a period of real work
options.explanation: Iteration has stopped yielding gains, so the remaining information will come from real use. Adopting it with a review date set keeps the loop open without spending more effort on a plateau.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: An operations team is embedding Claude into a high-volume workflow that must remain low cost while still handling reasoning tasks such as classifying incoming requests with strong accuracy.
question: Which model tier best matches this integration's requirements?

options.text: The most capable, highest-priced model tier, since only it can perform any classification reasoning
options.explanation: Reasoning capability is not exclusive to the most expensive tier; using it here would add unnecessary cost for a workflow prioritizing low cost at high volume.

options.text: A model tier selected purely for its support of computer use screenshots and clicks
options.explanation: Computer use support is unrelated to classifying incoming text requests and is not the deciding factor for this workflow.

options.text: A model tier chosen only because it supports the longest possible context window available
options.explanation: Context window length is not the stated constraint in this scenario, so choosing a tier for that reason alone ignores the cost and volume requirements described.

options.text: The fastest, most economical model tier, since it offers strong reasoning at high volume for low cost
options.explanation: The fastest, most economical model tier is positioned for high-volume intelligent processing and cost-sensitive deployments that still need strong reasoning, matching this workflow's requirements.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A stakeholder asks what a model's "reliable knowledge cutoff" means when the solutions architect recommends verifying any recent-event claims Claude makes.
question: What is the most accurate explanation?

options.text: It is the date up to which the model was trained, so its awareness may be limited after this date.
options.explanation: The reliable knowledge cutoff is the date through which the model's training data extends, making its knowledge most dependable up to that point. Events occurring after this date may be unknown to the model without external tools, so verification is recommended for recent claims.

options.text: It is the exact date the model will stop being available for use through the API going forward.
options.explanation: This describes a model deprecation or end-of-life date, which is unrelated to the knowledge cutoff. The knowledge cutoff refers to the timeframe of the training data, not the availability of the model via the API.

options.text: It is a setting that administrators can change at any time to extend how current the model's knowledge is.
options.explanation: The knowledge cutoff is fixed by the data used during training and is not a configurable setting. Administrators cannot modify it to extend the model's knowledge after deployment.

options.text: It is the date after which every response becomes randomly generated instead of based on training data.
options.explanation: Responses after the knowledge cutoff are not randomly generated; the model continues to reason based on its training. Its awareness of recent events may be limited, but it does not suddenly produce random output.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A school's exams officer has been asked to plan a new revision-support programme for the summer term and intends to use Claude to help build the plan.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Have three colleagues each request their own plan and compare the four versions later
options.explanation: Comparing four unconstrained plans multiplies the work without adding information, because none of them was told what has to be true.

options.text: Request the plan and next year's examination timetable in one long single message
options.explanation: Combining two unrelated planning problems in one request makes both weaker and makes it harder to see which answer belongs to which.

options.text: Ask Claude for a general revision-programme plan and adapt whatever it produces
options.explanation: A generic plan built on unstated constraints has to be unpicked afterwards, and the assumptions it made stay invisible while she adapts it.

options.text: Set out the real constraints — dates, staffing, rooms, budget — then ask for a plan
options.explanation: A plan is only useful if it respects the constraints it has to live inside. Stating dates, staffing, rooms and budget up front is what turns a generic outline into something the school can actually run.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A shared services team receives a request to use Claude for summarising supplier contracts.
question: Which sequence best analyses the use case before any commitment is made?

options.text: Confirm the decision the summaries support; check the upload policy; try a handful of contracts; compare with trusted summaries.
options.explanation: Knowing which decision the summaries feed defines what they must contain, the policy check establishes whether the contracts may be uploaded at all, a small trial gives real evidence cheaply, and comparing against summaries the team already trusts shows whether the quality is good enough to commit to.

options.text: Try a handful of contracts; confirm the decision the summaries support; check the upload policy; compare with trusted summaries.
options.explanation: Trying contracts first means uploading material before anyone has checked whether that is permitted, and the trial is run without knowing what the summaries are for, so there is no basis for judging the results.

options.text: Check the upload policy; compare with trusted summaries; confirm the decision the summaries support; try a handful of contracts.
options.explanation: Comparing with trusted summaries before any have been produced is impossible, and confirming the purpose after that comparison leaves the trial run at the very end with nothing left to inform.

options.text: Compare with trusted summaries; try a handful of contracts; confirm the decision the summaries support; check the upload policy.
options.explanation: Starting with a comparison there is nothing to compare against, and leaving the policy check until last means the contracts have already been uploaded by the time anyone asks whether they should have been.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: An operations director presents the results of a two-week Claude pilot to the executive team, showing only the three best outputs the team produced.
question: What is the greatest risk in communicating the results this way?

options.text: The pilot's outputs cannot be reused afterwards, because examples shown to executives must be regenerated.
options.explanation: There is no such constraint on reusing output that has been presented.

options.text: Executives will conclude the pilot used the wrong tool and will ask for a different vendor to be evaluated instead.
options.explanation: Strong examples do not prompt a vendor challenge; the problem is that they are not representative.

options.text: The team will be required to repeat the whole pilot from the start before any rollout decision is taken.
options.explanation: A repeat pilot is not the inherent risk; misplaced expectations are.

options.text: Executives set expectations from unrepresentative examples and are surprised when routine output needs editing.
options.explanation: Cherry-picked results overstate the typical case, and the gap surfaces later as disappointment or lost trust.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A project manager has two hundred pages of stakeholder interview notes and needs to turn them into a requirements draft. Which two uses of Claude fit this task?
question: Select two.

options.text: Have Claude list where the notes contradict one another so a person resolves each conflict.
options.explanation: Surfacing contradictions is analysis that helps humans decide; the resolution itself stays with the people accountable for scope.

options.text: Have Claude supply the missing answers for the stakeholders who were never interviewed.
options.explanation: Inventing answers nobody gave is fabrication presented as research, and it corrupts the requirements it feeds.

options.text: Have Claude group the interview notes into themes that the team then reviews and challenges.
options.explanation: Grouping a large volume of text into reviewable themes is well-specified, text-heavy work that a person still checks afterwards.

options.text: Have Claude settle which of the requirements make the final scope, so that the debate is skipped.
options.explanation: Scope is a decision the team owns, and delegating it removes the accountability that has to sit with a person.

options.text: Have Claude sign the requirements off on behalf of the stakeholders who were interviewed.
options.explanation: Sign-off on behalf of stakeholders is not a task to delegate; it misrepresents people who never agreed to it.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: Claude has produced two credible candidate plans for a departmental restructure, and the sponsor asks the planning lead which one is better.
question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite both plans in the same structure so the sponsor can read them side by side more easily.
options.explanation: A common structure makes the plans easier to read and is worth doing, but presentation is not evaluation. The sponsor would still face two neatly formatted options with no agreed basis for choosing between them.

options.text: Ask Claude which plan it prefers and take that as the department's recommendation to the sponsor.
options.explanation: A stated preference gives an answer without an argument the sponsor can examine. The choice between restructure plans depends on what the department values, which is a judgment the department owns rather than one the tool can settle.

options.text: Combine the strongest parts of both plans into a third plan and present that to the sponsor instead.
options.explanation: Merging attractive pieces of two plans often breaks the internal logic that made each coherent, and it produces a third option nobody has evaluated. It also avoids the comparison the sponsor actually asked for.

options.text: Agree the criteria that matter here, then compare both plans against them and record the reasoning.
options.explanation: Naming the criteria first turns "which is better" into a question that can be answered and defended, and recording the reasoning gives the sponsor something to challenge. Claude can then do the comparison work against a standard the humans set.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: Two rounds into designing a Claude-assisted induction pack, an education team finds the drafts are accurate but pitched at the wrong level for new teaching assistants.
question: What should they do first?

options.text: Ask the teaching assistants to edit each draft themselves as part of their induction
options.explanation: Pushing the rewrite onto the readers hides the design fault rather than fixing it, and the pack stays mispitched for everyone.

options.text: State who the reader is and what they already know, then try the same case again
options.explanation: The fault is a missing specification, not a reasoning limit. Naming the audience and their starting knowledge addresses the actual cause, and re-running the same case shows whether it worked.

options.text: Move the work to the most capable model available and re-run the same instruction
options.explanation: A stronger model still has no idea who the reader is; escalating tier does not supply information the instruction never contained.

options.text: Rewrite every part of the arrangement at once so the next round is a clean start
options.explanation: Changing everything at once means that if the next draft is better, nobody will know which change was responsible.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A customer support director wants to justify a Claude-based ticket triage pilot to executives and asks how to frame its value.
question: What is the best way to present this business case?

options.text: Present only the model's technical architecture details, since executives mainly evaluate proposals on implementation specifics.
options.explanation: Executives generally care about business outcomes and ROI more than low-level technical architecture, so this framing misses the audience's priorities.

options.text: Present concrete metrics such as reduced average handling time and ticket deflection rate compared against the current process.
options.explanation: Framing value in terms of measurable business outcomes, such as handling time or deflection rate, gives executives a concrete basis for evaluating the pilot against the current process.

options.text: Present a claim that the pilot requires no evaluation period, since Claude's output quality never needs to be measured.
options.explanation: Skipping evaluation removes the evidence needed to demonstrate value and identify quality issues before wider rollout.

options.text: Present the pilot as guaranteed to eliminate the entire support team's workload within the first month of deployment.
options.explanation: Promising complete elimination of the team's workload overstates the technology's impact and sets an unrealistic expectation.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A shared services director says the invoice-processing team should be "more efficient" and asks an analyst to use Claude to work out how.
question: What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to list the common inefficiencies in invoice processing and check which of them apply here.
options.explanation: A generic list of inefficiencies gives the analyst somewhere to look but no way to prioritise. Whether a given inefficiency is worth removing depends on which measure the director cares about, which has not been settled.

options.text: Ask the invoice team which parts of their work they would most like to stop doing altogether now.
options.explanation: The team's least favourite tasks are worth hearing and may be a good source of hypotheses, but they indicate irritation rather than cost. The analyst would still not know which measure of efficiency the director wants moved.

options.text: Agree with the director which measure of efficiency matters: cycle time, cost per invoice, or errors.
options.explanation: Efficiency pulls in different directions: faster processing can raise error rates, and cutting cost per invoice can lengthen cycle time. Fixing which measure matters turns a vague instruction into a target the analysis can aim at and later be judged against.

options.text: Ask Claude to redesign the invoice process end to end so the director can see what is possible.
options.explanation: A full redesign produced before the goal is agreed optimises for whatever the tool assumes efficiency means. It also invites the director to react to a finished proposal rather than to state the outcome being sought.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A workflow owner wants feedback from a four-week pilot that will genuinely help her improve the arrangement.
question: Which feedback format is most useful for that purpose?

options.text: Logged cases pairing the input given, the output produced, and what the user needed instead.
options.explanation: Improvement needs cases, not impressions. A logged triple of input, output and the required result shows exactly where the arrangement diverged from what was needed, which is the only feedback that can be turned directly into a change.

options.text: A weekly satisfaction score from each participant, tracked to show the trend across the four weeks.
options.explanation: A satisfaction trend tells the owner whether things are getting better or worse but never why. A falling score gives her no defect to fix, and a rising one may simply reflect participants lowering their expectations.

options.text: A count of how often each participant used the arrangement during each week of the pilot period.
options.explanation: Usage counts show adoption rather than quality. Heavy use can mean the arrangement is valuable or that people are repeatedly retrying it because the first result was unusable.

options.text: A free-text comment box at the end of the pilot for any observations participants wish to record.
options.explanation: An end-of-pilot comment box collects thoughts long after the events that prompted them, so the detail has faded. It also mixes design feedback with unrelated grumbles and offers no link to specific outputs.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: An insurer's manual claims process involves five separate teams handing a claim off through email at each stage. Leadership decides to rebuild the process so a single Claude-driven agent triages, requests documents, and routes each claim end to end.
question: Which term best describes this change?

options.text: Caching the workflow, since previous claim decisions are being reused for new claims
options.explanation: The scenario does not describe reusing prior claim decisions as cached context; it describes restructuring who performs each step.

options.text: Batching the workflow, since claims will now be processed together instead of individually
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario describes grouping claims for batch processing; the change is about who owns each step of the process.

options.text: Redesigning the workflow, since the multi-team handoff process is being replaced by an agent-driven process
options.explanation: Replacing the multi-team, email-driven handoff structure with a single agent that owns triage, document requests, and routing end to end is a redesign of the workflow rather than a small addition to it.

options.text: Augmenting the workflow, since the existing five-team handoff structure is being kept in place unchanged
options.explanation: The five-team handoff structure is being removed, not preserved, so this is not augmentation of the existing process.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A research team spends much of each week manually copying findings between four separate documents. Which two responses fit this situation best?
question: Select two.

options.text: Treat the copying itself as the thing to redesign, rather than speeding it up as it stands.
options.explanation: Duplicated copying is a symptom of process design, so this is the case where redesign beats augmentation.

options.text: Have Claude consolidate the four documents into one source the team then maintains together.
options.explanation: Consolidating to a single maintained source removes the duplication instead of automating it.

options.text: Add a fifth document in which Claude records what it copied into each of the other four weekly.
options.explanation: A fifth document adds another artefact to maintain and makes the duplication problem worse than before.

options.text: Have Claude do the copying between all four documents on the team's behalf every week.
options.explanation: Automating the copying preserves four diverging documents and simply performs the waste faster.

options.text: Keep all four documents and ask Claude to double the speed at which each one is updated.
options.explanation: Speeding up a redundant step leaves the structural problem, and four sources still drift apart from each other.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A stakeholder wants to send an entire year of raw customer support transcripts, well beyond the model's context window, in a single request and asks why this fails.
question: How should this limitation be explained?

options.text: Explain that Claude rejects large inputs purely as a cost-control step, and the limit lifts once the account tier is upgraded.
options.explanation: The context window is a technical limit on how much input the model can process at once, not simply a billing lever tied to account tier.

options.text: Explain that the failure means the account is rate-limited and will refuse further requests for the next 24 hours.
options.explanation: Exceeding the context window is a distinct failure from rate limiting and does not imply a 24-hour account block.

options.text: Explain that transcripts must always be converted into images before Claude will process any amount of text content.
options.explanation: Text does not need to be converted to images to be processed; this misrepresents how context limits work.

options.text: Explain that each model has a maximum context window, so transcripts must be chunked, summarized, or retrieved selectively.
options.explanation: Every model has a fixed context window, so inputs that exceed it must be broken into chunks, summarized, or narrowed via retrieval rather than sent in one request.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A pilot of a Claude-assisted proposal workflow has produced mixed results across its first month. Which two iteration steps are appropriate now?
question: Select two.

options.text: Compare the weak outputs against the strong ones to find what the weak requests were missing.
options.explanation: Comparing weak and strong cases diagnoses the cause instead of guessing, which is what iteration on a pilot is for.

options.text: Roll the workflow out to every team at once so that far more data arrives much faster.
options.explanation: Scaling an unresolved pilot spreads the failure mode rather than diagnosing it, and it makes rollback harder.

options.text: Abandon the pilot right away, because a mixed opening month shows the workflow cannot ever work.
options.explanation: Mixed results in month one are the normal input to iteration, not proof that the workflow is unworkable.

options.text: Fold what worked into the shared instructions so the whole team gets the same improvement.
options.explanation: Making the fix persistent in shared instructions stops the team re-solving the same problem one person at a time.

options.text: Ask each person to keep a private list of tricks rather than changing the shared set-up.
options.explanation: Private tricks leave the shared configuration untouched, so the improvement never reaches anyone else.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A team is designing a Claude-assisted arrangement for handling supplier complaints.
question: Which step should most clearly stay with a person?

options.text: Pulling the supplier's complaint history together into a single summary
options.explanation: Assembling history into a summary is repetitive, text-heavy work whose output is reviewed before anyone relies on it.

options.text: Grouping the month's complaints by the type of issue that they describe
options.explanation: Grouping complaints by issue type is classification work that is easy to check and carries no external commitment.

options.text: Deciding whether a goodwill credit is offered and how large it should be
options.explanation: Committing the organisation's money to a supplier is a decision with external consequences that someone must be accountable for, so it stays with a person even when everything around it is delegated.

options.text: Drafting the acknowledgement telling the supplier that work has now begun
options.explanation: An acknowledgement is a routine, low-stakes draft that a person can check quickly before it goes out.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: An events manager is about to hand an end-to-end campaign setup task to Claude in Cowork for the first time, working across her own files and connected tools.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Choose the largest campaign of the quarter, so the value of the new arrangement is obvious to all.
options.explanation: Making the first run the biggest campaign maximises the consequences of an untested arrangement. A first outing should be chosen so that mistakes are cheap, not so that success would be impressive.

options.text: Turn off the automatic checks so that the task can complete without interruption on its first run.
options.explanation: Removing the checks on a first run is the opposite of prudent. Uninterrupted completion is worth little if the manager cannot see what was done to her files and messages along the way.

options.text: Decide which actions in the task a person must approve before they happen, and set that up.
options.explanation: A task that spans files and connected tools will take actions with real consequences, so the first decision is which of those a person must approve. Setting the approval points up front is what keeps the manager in control of the steps that cannot be undone.

options.text: Ask Claude to describe how it would approach the task and keep that as the record of the plan.
options.explanation: A stated plan is a useful reference and worth having, but it is a description rather than a control. The task can still take an action she would not have sanctioned, because nothing stops it to ask.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
question: Which approach best leverages Claude for prioritizing customer feedback?

options.text: Feed all feedback items to Claude with a broad instruction to prioritize them, such as 'Rank these by urgency,' without providing a scoring rubric, impact categories, or customer segments to guide the prioritization.
options.explanation: Providing only a broad instruction without a scoring rubric, impact categories, or customer segments leaves the prioritization arbitrary and inconsistent. Claude requires clear guidelines to produce reliable, repeatable outputs aligned with business goals.

options.text: Categorize and cluster feedback manually into broad themes such as bugs, usability, and feature requests, then use Claude to summarize each category and extract insights that guide prioritization.
options.explanation: While manual categorization into broad themes is a useful first step, delegating only the summarization to Claude misses the opportunity to scale and standardize the prioritization process. Without defined prioritization criteria, the resulting insights may still lack consistent, actionable guidance.

options.text: Directly ask Claude to evaluate feedback and decide next quarter's features, requesting a prioritized roadmap and engineering estimates, fully automating the decision without human review.
options.explanation: Fully automating strategic decision-making by having Claude directly decide next quarter's features and provide engineering estimates without human review introduces significant risk of unrealistic or misaligned outcomes. Such decisions require product context and human validation, as LLMs cannot replace the nuanced judgment needed for roadmap planning.

options.text: Define clear prioritization criteria (e.g., impact, effort, customer segment), then ask Claude to categorize each feedback item and assign a priority score or rank based on that rubric.
options.explanation: Defining clear prioritization criteria (impact, effort, customer segment) and using Claude to categorize each feedback item against that rubric ensures a structured, objective, and repeatable prioritization. This approach produces reliable, scalable outputs that directly inform planning.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
question: In a redesigned client-reporting workflow where Claude pulls the analysis together and produces the draft, which step should most clearly remain with a person?

options.text: Deciding which chart style is used for the recurring performance section of each report.
options.explanation: Chart style is a house-style decision with no consequence for accuracy. It is exactly the kind of well-specified, repeatable choice that suits delegation.

options.text: Confirming that the figures and commitments in the report going to the client are correct.
options.explanation: The report is an external commitment the firm will be held to, and once it is sent the claim cannot be withdrawn quietly. Verification of the figures and promises is the accountable, low-reversibility step, so it stays with the person who can answer for it.

options.text: Choosing the order in which the report's sections are arranged for the client's convenience.
options.explanation: Section ordering is a presentation preference that can be specified once and applied consistently. A wrong choice is noticed easily and corrected in the next edition.

options.text: Setting the day of the month on which the report is produced and issued to the client.
options.explanation: The issue date is a scheduling rule that someone sets once. It needs to be agreed, but it carries no judgment that a person must exercise each cycle.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A communications team's approval chain is slow, but each of its steps is required by regulation. Which two integration choices fit this situation?
question: Select two.

options.text: Replace the reviewers with a checklist prompt that Claude runs at the end of every draft.
options.explanation: A prompt cannot stand in for an accountable human approval that regulation requires a person to give.

options.text: Route the approvals through Claude, so reviewers only see the items that Claude was unsure of.
options.explanation: Filtering what reviewers see means required approvals are no longer genuinely being performed on every item.

options.text: Augment the chain as it stands by having Claude prepare each reviewer's material in advance.
options.explanation: When the steps must stay, augmenting them is the available gain: reviewers arrive prepared and each step takes less time.

options.text: Keep every required approval step in place, since this constraint is legal, not procedural.
options.explanation: A legally required step is not a candidate for removal, so the design has to work within it rather than around it.

options.text: Redesign the chain to drop the approval steps that Claude's drafting quality now makes needless.
options.explanation: Better drafts do not remove a regulatory requirement, and dropping required approvals creates a compliance failure.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A support manager is designing a new way of working in which Claude drafts replies to routine tickets. Which two design decisions are sound?
question: Select two.

options.text: Define up front what a good draft looks like, so that drafts can be judged against that bar.
options.explanation: Defining what good looks like before delegating is what makes the output reviewable rather than merely plentiful.

options.text: Measure the pilot only by how many tickets were drafted, since the volume is the whole point.
options.explanation: Volume with no quality measure rewards output the process was never meant to optimise for.

options.text: Let drafts go out unreviewed once the first week of the pilot has produced no complaints.
options.explanation: One quiet week is not evidence of reliability, and removing review is the change most likely to surface publicly.

options.text: Design the process so that Claude also closes each of the tickets it has drafted a reply to.
options.explanation: Closing tickets is an accountable outcome, and bundling it into drafting removes the checkpoint the design needs.

options.text: Keep a human approval step before any drafted reply is sent to the customer who asked.
options.explanation: A customer-facing reply is externally published, so keeping a human approval step in the design is the right call.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A trading desk stakeholder wants Claude to report the current live stock price directly from its own knowledge, without connecting any external data source.
question: How should this limitation be explained?

options.text: Explain that real-time data requests always trigger a permission error and there is no supported way, such as a webhook, to add live data access.
options.explanation: Real-time data requests do not always trigger a permission error; Claude supports tool integrations like web search or webhooks to access live data. There are supported methods to add live data access.

options.text: Explain that stock prices are static values set at the daily close, so any past training data would reflect the official price and remain accurate today.
options.explanation: Stock prices are not static values set at the daily close; they change constantly during trading hours. Past training data reflects historical prices and would be outdated, not accurate today.

options.text: Explain that Claude has no access to live, real-time data on its own, so a tool like web search must be connected to fetch current prices.
options.explanation: Claude has no built-in ability to access live, real-time data on its own; its knowledge is static, drawn from training data. To retrieve current stock prices, an external tool such as web search must be connected and invoked.

options.text: Explain that Claude continuously streams live market data through a direct internal feed from major exchanges, so no external tool integration is ever required.
options.explanation: Claude does not continuously stream live market data internally; it has no direct feed from major exchanges. Real-time information requires integration with an external data source or tool.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A finance team frequently asks Claude to build the same type of formatted spreadsheet report from raw data, and wants this repeated task folded into its existing reporting workflow without re-explaining the steps every time.
question: Which capability best supports this?

options.text: Computer use lets Claude click through a spreadsheet application's interface for every report.
options.explanation: Computer Use could interact with a spreadsheet application, but it would require manually clicking through the interface each time, making it inefficient for a repeated task; it lacks the reusability of a packaged skill.

options.text: Agent Skills packages reusable spreadsheet-building instructions and scripts for reuse.
options.explanation: Agent Skills allow you to encapsulate reusable instructions and scripts, enabling the finance team to define the report-building process once and invoke it repeatedly without re-explaining.

options.text: The citations feature makes every cell in the spreadsheet link back to a source sentence.
options.explanation: Citations ground responses in source documents for verifiability, but they do not create links in spreadsheet cells; this feature is unrelated to packaging reusable report-building steps.

options.text: Prompt caching caches the raw data itself instead of storing the report-building instructions.
options.explanation: Prompt caching is meant to reuse prompt prefixes to reduce latency and cost, not to cache raw data; it does not provide a mechanism to store and reuse report-building instructions.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
question: Which prompt would best leverage Claude's research, planning, and process optimization capabilities to create a comprehensive biology lesson plan?

options.text: Write a biology syllabus that includes a week-by-week topic outline, grading policies with percentages, lab safety rules, and a detailed list of required materials for the semester.
options.explanation: This prompt focuses on syllabus logistics such as grading policies, lab safety, and materials, but omits state standards, learning objectives, activities, and differentiation. It does not fully leverage Claude's research, planning, and process optimization abilities for generating a comprehensive lesson plan as described in the documentation.

options.text: Given state standards for high school biology, generate a week-by-week lesson plan for a 15-week semester with learning objectives, activities, assessments, and differentiation suggestions.
options.explanation: This prompt explicitly includes the subject (high school biology), references state standards, and requests a week-by-week 15-week plan with learning objectives, activities, assessments, and differentiation suggestions. Per Anthropic's Claude for Education documentation, Claude can generate standards-aligned lesson plans and support differentiation; standard backward design also prioritizes clear objectives, varied activities, and formative/summative assessments. By naming biology and incorporating all these elements, this prompt best leverages Claude's research, planning, and optimization capabilities for creating a comprehensive biology lesson plan.

options.text: Create a detailed lesson plan for high school biology covering major topics with unit-by-unit learning objectives, lab activities, and formative assessments for a full year.
options.explanation: This prompt includes the subject (biology) and many components, but it omits alignment to state standards and differentiation suggestions. Anthropic's Claude for Education guidance emphasizes starting with state standards and including differentiation to meet diverse learners, so this prompt does not fully leverage Claude's capabilities for comprehensive curriculum planning.

options.text: List all required high school biology topics as per state standards, organized by unit with major concepts, subtopics, hands-on activities, and formative assessments for a full-year curriculum.
options.explanation: This prompt aligns with state standards and covers biology content, but it does not request week-by-week planning, explicit learning objectives, or differentiation suggestions. Comprehensive lesson planning guidance from Anthropic and standard pedagogy includes week-by-week objectives and differentiation, so this prompt is incomplete for fully leveraging Claude's planning capabilities.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A housing association wants to use Claude to help shorten the time it takes to allocate a repair appointment.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Describe the current steps; agree what better looks like; ask Claude where time is lost; trial one change on one patch
options.explanation: You cannot optimise a process you have not described, or judge a suggestion without an agreed target. Describe, agree the target, then ask for suggestions, then test one change on a small scope.

options.text: Trial one change on one patch; ask Claude where time is lost; describe the current steps; agree what better looks like
options.explanation: Beginning with a trial commits the association to a change chosen at random, and leaves the target it is aiming at undefined until the end.

options.text: Ask Claude where time is lost; describe the current steps; trial one change on one patch; agree what better looks like
options.explanation: Asking where time is lost before describing the process means Claude answers from generic assumptions rather than from how this association actually works.

options.text: Agree what better looks like; trial one change on one patch; ask Claude where time is lost; describe the current steps
options.explanation: Trialling a change before any analysis means the change is arbitrary, and describing the current steps last makes the description pointless.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A charity is designing a way of working in which Claude drafts its monthly supporter update.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Draft one past month with Claude; agree what a good update contains; have the editor mark what is wrong; change one thing and try again
options.explanation: Drafting before agreeing the standard means the editor's marks are personal preference, and the design converges on one person's taste.

options.text: Draft one past month with Claude; have the editor mark what is wrong; change one thing and try again; agree what a good update contains
options.explanation: Leaving the definition of a good update until last means the first three steps were judged against nobody's stated standard.

options.text: Agree what a good update contains; draft one past month with Claude; have the editor mark what is wrong; change one thing and try again
options.explanation: Agree the standard, produce a draft on a known month, have it marked against that standard, then change one thing at a time. Each round then tells you something you can act on.

options.text: Agree what a good update contains; have the editor mark what is wrong; draft one past month with Claude; change one thing and try again
options.explanation: Marking what is wrong before anything has been drafted is impossible; there is no draft to mark.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A director tells a service manager to "roll Claude out across the department next quarter." The department runs eleven distinct workflows of varying sensitivity.
question: What should the service manager do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to review all eleven workflows and recommend which of them to change first.
options.explanation: Claude can help compare the workflows once someone describes them, but it cannot know which of them the department most needs to fix or which carry unacceptable risk. Handing the prioritisation over skips the manager's own judgment.

options.text: Draft a departmental policy covering how Claude may be used in each of the eleven workflows.
options.explanation: A usage policy will be needed eventually, particularly for the sensitive workflows. Writing it for all eleven before anything has been attempted means guessing at the practices it should govern.

options.text: Give every team access at the start of the quarter so that people can begin finding uses for it.
options.explanation: Broad access with no chosen target produces scattered experiments across eleven workflows, including the sensitive ones. At the end of the quarter the manager will have activity to report but no evidence of improvement.

options.text: Choose one workflow and one outcome to improve, and agree how that will be measured.
options.explanation: A vague rollout instruction becomes deliverable by narrowing it to one workflow and one measurable outcome. That gives a bounded first integration, a clear basis for judging whether it worked, and evidence to take back to the director before spreading further.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A hospital wants to integrate Claude into its clinical documentation workflow to help physicians summarize patient charts, where accuracy is far more important than response speed or cost.
question: Which starting approach best fits this integration?

options.text: Start with a model selected only for its support of the newest client-side tools
options.explanation: Client-side tool support is unrelated to the summarization accuracy this clinical documentation workflow needs.

options.text: Start with the most capable model, since accuracy outweighing cost considerations favors this choice
options.explanation: Applications where accuracy outweighs cost considerations, such as clinical documentation, are a case for starting with the most capable model rather than a faster, cheaper one.

options.text: Start with the fastest, cheapest model, since most patient charts are short and simple to summarize
options.explanation: Prioritizing speed and low cost does not match a scenario where the stated priority is accuracy over speed or cost.

options.text: Start with a model chosen for its low output token pricing, since pricing is the deciding factor here
options.explanation: Optimizing for output token pricing contradicts the scenario's explicit priority of accuracy over cost.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A transformation office asks Claude to score two hundred candidate use cases on effort and value from their one-paragraph descriptions, and plans to fund the top twenty exactly as ranked.
question: What is the greatest concern?

options.text: The scored list will need reformatting before it can be presented to the executive funding committee.
options.explanation: Reformatting for a committee is routine presentation work. It changes nothing about the reliability of the ranking that the committee would be asked to approve.

options.text: Scoring two hundred use cases in one conversation may exceed what a single chat can comfortably hold.
options.explanation: Volume is a practical constraint that can be handled by working through the list in batches. It affects how the scoring is run, not whether a funding decision should be handed to the scores that come out of it.

options.text: A ranking drawn from short summaries can look authoritative while resting on assumptions nobody checked.
options.explanation: A one-paragraph description does not contain the effort and value evidence the scores imply, so Claude must infer it. The numbers then carry an air of objectivity that a spreadsheet reinforces, and funding follows the ranking without anyone testing the assumptions underneath it.

options.text: Some of the two hundred descriptions were written by staff who are quite unfamiliar with what Claude can do.
options.explanation: Uneven familiarity with the tool affects how well individual submissions are phrased, and it is worth correcting, but it is a quality-of-input issue that sits well below the danger of treating an inferred ranking as a funding decision.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A bank wants Claude to prepare a recommendation for each loan application, but a compliance officer must still approve or reject every decision before it takes effect.
question: Which integration pattern does this describe?

options.text: A human-in-the-loop pattern where Claude assists with a recommendation and a person retains final decision authority
options.explanation: Requiring a compliance officer to approve or reject every Claude-generated recommendation before it takes effect is a human-in-the-loop integration, where Claude augments the decision process but a person retains authority.

options.text: A tool-use pattern where Claude directly updates the core banking ledger as soon as it drafts a recommendation
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario has Claude writing directly to the ledger; the compliance officer's approval step sits between the recommendation and any action.

options.text: A fully autonomous pattern where Claude both generates and finalizes the loan decision without further review
options.explanation: The scenario explicitly keeps a human approval step, so the decision is not finalized autonomously by Claude.

options.text: A batch-only pattern where loan applications are processed in bulk once per week with no live interaction
options.explanation: The scenario does not describe a weekly bulk process; it describes ongoing review of individual recommendations.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A team is deciding which steps of its onboarding process to hand to Claude and which to keep. Which two steps should stay with a person?
question: Select two.

options.text: The final decision on whether a new hire has passed the probation review for this quarter.
options.explanation: A probation outcome affects someone's employment, so the decision needs the accountability only a person can carry.

options.text: The conversation with a new joiner about a personal difficulty raised in their first week.
options.explanation: A personal difficulty raised by a colleague calls for human judgment and duty of care, not a delegated reply.

options.text: Drafting the standard welcome message that each of the new joiners receives on their first day.
options.explanation: A standard welcome message is a low-stakes, repetitive draft, which is a good candidate for delegation.

options.text: Turning the existing onboarding handbook into a shorter checklist for the new joiners.
options.explanation: Condensing an existing handbook is well-specified text work that a person can review before it is published.

options.text: Summarising last year's onboarding survey feedback into a set of recurring themes.
options.explanation: Theming survey feedback is high-volume analysis whose output the team can check against the underlying responses.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: To win support for a new Claude-assisted proposal-drafting arrangement, a team demonstrates the best output from about twenty attempts and does not mention the other nineteen.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The demonstration may run longer than the slot the sponsors set aside in the meeting agenda.
options.explanation: Overrunning the agenda is an inconvenience for the meeting chair. It is unrelated to the honesty of what the demonstration implies about everyday performance.

options.text: The twenty attempts consumed usage that the team had allocated to its ordinary client work.
options.explanation: Usage spent preparing a demonstration is a minor and one-off cost. It affects the team's own budget rather than the decision the sponsors are about to make.

options.text: The team will have to repeat the demonstration for other departments that were not present.
options.explanation: Repeating a demonstration costs a little time and is entirely normal when several departments are interested. It has no bearing on whether the expectations being set are accurate.

options.text: Sponsors will fund the arrangement expecting a standard the everyday output does not reach.
options.explanation: Showing the best of twenty sets the expected quality at a level the arrangement reaches roughly one time in twenty. Funding, staffing and review effort are then planned against a standard that will not materialise, and the credibility loss lands on the team.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A stakeholder wants Claude to answer questions about their company's internal product catalog, which was updated last week and was never part of Claude's training data.
question: How should this limitation and solution be communicated?

options.text: Explain that the catalog only needs to be emailed to Anthropic once so it joins the base model going forward.
options.explanation: Sending data to Anthropic does not add it to the base model’s training; to keep answers current with recent changes, retrieval-based or tool-based approaches must be used.

options.text: Explain that Claude cannot process proprietary data, so supplying the catalog via retrieval or a connected tool will not help.
options.explanation: Claude can effectively process proprietary data when it is supplied in the prompt or via retrieval; the limitation is a lack of prior knowledge, not an inability to use supplied information.

options.text: Explain that Claude automatically indexes any company website within days, so no integration work is ever required.
options.explanation: Claude does not automatically crawl, index, or learn from any company website; integration work is always required to supply it with proprietary or recently updated data.

options.text: Explain that Claude lacks internal data knowledge, so the catalog must be supplied via retrieval or a connected tool.
options.explanation: Claude lacks built-in knowledge of internal company data, so the updated product catalog must be provided through retrieval mechanisms like RAG or a connected tool for accurate answers.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A sponsor wants to deploy a new Claude-powered feature to all users in every region simultaneously on day one.
question: What rollout approach should be recommended instead, and why?

options.text: Recommend delaying the launch indefinitely, since no rollout strategy can reduce risk for AI-powered features.
options.explanation: Indefinite delay is unnecessary; a phased approach allows launch to proceed while managing risk.

options.text: Recommend the simultaneous global launch as proposed, since phased rollouts add no measurable risk-reduction benefit.
options.explanation: Phased rollouts are a standard risk-reduction practice; claiming no benefit contradicts common deployment guidance.

options.text: Recommend a phased rollout to a small user segment first, so issues can be caught and addressed before scaling to everyone.
options.explanation: A phased or pilot rollout to a limited audience lets the team observe real-world performance and fix issues before exposing the full user base to them, reducing overall risk.

options.text: Recommend launching only in the region with the least usage data, since regional differences do not affect quality.
options.explanation: Regional usage patterns and data characteristics can affect performance, so ignoring them is not sound rollout planning.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A team lead must brief a sceptical director on a new Claude-assisted reporting arrangement.
question: Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: Say that results will improve automatically as newer models become available
options.explanation: Promising automatic future improvement asks the director to accept an outcome nobody can commit to.

options.text: Say that the pilot's best output shows what every report will look like now
options.explanation: Presenting the best single output as typical sets an expectation the arrangement will not meet in ordinary use.

options.text: Say that the arrangement removes the need for the team's current review step
options.explanation: Claiming the review step is unnecessary oversells the arrangement and removes the safeguard the director is most likely to ask about.

options.text: Say what it does reliably, what needs checking, and who does the checking
options.explanation: Honest communication pairs capability with limitation and names where human review stays in the loop. That is what lets a sceptical stakeholder judge the arrangement rather than the pitch.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: An events team has redesigned its exhibitor-liaison workflow so that Claude carries a request from first enquiry through to a confirmed booking slot.
question: Where does an approval checkpoint most clearly belong?

options.text: Only if an exhibitor complains about the slot they were allocated
options.explanation: Waiting for a complaint makes the exhibitor the quality control, which is precisely what a checkpoint is meant to avoid.

options.text: After the exhibitor has replied to the confirmation that was sent
options.explanation: A check after the exhibitor has replied comes after the commitment, so it can only manage the consequences.

options.text: At the end of each month, when all bookings are reviewed together
options.explanation: A monthly review catches patterns but arrives long after individual bookings have gone out.

options.text: Before anything is sent to the exhibitor on the team's behalf
options.explanation: The checkpoint belongs at the last moment where a person can still prevent an external, hard-to-retract action. Once the exhibitor has been contacted, the commitment has been made.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A stakeholder wants Claude to read scanned engineering drawings and return exact millimeter measurements for manufacturing tolerances.
question: How should the solutions architect set expectations about this vision use case?

options.text: Confirm that Claude's vision accuracy is unaffected by image resolution or scan quality, ensuring consistent measurements across all scenarios.
options.explanation: Image resolution and scan quality can affect how accurately Claude interprets visual details, so its vision accuracy is not independent of these factors.

options.text: Confirm that Claude can read pixel-level measurements directly from any scanned drawing, ensuring guaranteed manufacturing-grade precision.
options.explanation: Claude does not guarantee pixel-level measurements with manufacturing-grade precision, which overstates its vision capabilities for this use case.

options.text: Explain that Claude lacks image processing capabilities, so drawings must be manually transcribed into text by staff before analysis.
options.explanation: Claude does support image input and can reason about visual content, so manual transcription into text is not required; this understates its actual capabilities.

options.text: Explain that Claude can describe and reason about visual content, but exact measurements should be verified with dedicated tools.
options.explanation: Claude can describe and reason about visual content, but it is not a calibrated measurement tool; precise tolerance values should be verified with dedicated measurement instruments before use in manufacturing.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A consultancy team on an Enterprise plan wants Claude's research on a client sector to draw on the firm's own past engagement reports, not only on public material.
question: What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Paste the single most relevant engagement report into each new chat whenever it seems likely to be needed.
options.explanation: Relying on someone to notice the right report and paste it in means the internal evidence is used inconsistently. It also limits each piece of research to one report when the value lies in the pattern across many.

options.text: Put the past engagement reports into the project so every research chat in it works from that material.
options.explanation: Project knowledge is durable background for every chat in that project, so the firm's own engagement history informs each piece of research without anyone re-pasting it. That makes the internal evidence a standing input rather than something remembered on a good day.

options.text: Ask Claude to describe what a firm like this one would probably have learned in past engagements.
options.explanation: Asking Claude what such a firm would probably have learned invites it to invent the firm's experience. The reports exist and can be supplied, so guessing at their contents is the one option that produces confident fiction.

options.text: Summarise the past engagement reports into a single page and rely on that page from then onwards.
options.explanation: A single summary page discards the detail that makes past engagements useful, and it becomes stale the moment new work is completed. The team would be researching against a snapshot rather than the record.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A legal team wants to fold Claude into its existing contract-review workflow so that an entire multi-hundred-page merger agreement can be analyzed in a single request instead of being split into many smaller calls.
question: Which capability makes this integration possible?

options.text: Batch processing, which lets many small requests run overnight instead of one large request
options.explanation: Batch processing helps with running many separate requests asynchronously; it does not let a single request hold more content than the context window allows.

options.text: The effort parameter, which reduces the number of tokens needed to represent the agreement
options.explanation: The effort parameter trades off response thoroughness for token efficiency in Claude's output; it does not change how much input content a single request can hold.

options.text: Adaptive thinking, which shortens a long agreement before any of it is read by Claude
options.explanation: Adaptive thinking controls how Claude reasons about a request; it does not shrink or summarize the agreement before Claude reads it.

options.text: A large context window, which lets a single request hold the entire lengthy agreement at once
options.explanation: A large context window allows a single request to hold large documents, extensive code bases, or long conversations, which is what lets the entire lengthy merger agreement be analyzed in one request.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: Four analysts on an Enterprise plan are running separate chats to analyse requirements for the same programme, and each keeps re-pasting the same brief, glossary and stakeholder map.
question: What is the most appropriate improvement?

options.text: Ask each analyst to paste a shortened summary of the documents rather than the full versions each time.
options.explanation: Shortened summaries mean each analyst works from a different reduction of the same material, which is how definitions quietly diverge. Requirements analysis depends on everyone reading the same glossary, not four paraphrases of it.

options.text: Agree that a single analyst holds the source documents and answers the other three analysts on request each time.
options.explanation: Funnelling the documents through one person creates a bottleneck and leaves the other three analysts analysing from second-hand descriptions. It solves the duplication by removing access rather than by sharing context.

options.text: Merge the four conversations into one long chat so the shared material has to be pasted only once.
options.explanation: One very long shared conversation mixes four unrelated lines of analysis, becomes hard to follow, and pushes against the limits of a single chat. It also gives no way to start a fresh piece of analysis from the same background.

options.text: Put the brief, glossary and stakeholder map into a shared project so every analysis chat starts from them.
options.explanation: Recurring work over a stable set of source material is exactly what a project is for: the brief, glossary and stakeholder map become durable background for every chat in that project, so all four analysts work from the same current version instead of from whatever each last pasted.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A grants team is designing a new way of working in which Claude prepares the first draft of each funding decision summary. Nothing has been built yet.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Agree what an acceptable summary contains, so drafts can be judged against it
options.explanation: Defining what "good" looks like before delegating is what makes every later round of iteration meaningful; without it, nobody can say whether a draft is acceptable or whether a change helped.

options.text: Announce the new arrangement so that people begin sending their cases through
options.explanation: Announcing an arrangement that has not been designed pushes unfinished work onto colleagues and makes problems harder to withdraw from.

options.text: Write the longest and most detailed instruction the team can manage in one go
options.explanation: Instruction length is not the design. A long instruction written before the team knows what it wants encodes guesses at scale.

options.text: Ask every member of the team to try their own approach and compare next month
options.explanation: Four private approaches produce four private standards, and a month later there is still no agreed standard to compare them against.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A manager asks whether the new Claude-assisted process means the team can cut its review budget. Which two responses are honest and useful?
question: Select two.

options.text: Share what the pilot actually changed in the cycle time, and what it did not change at all.
options.explanation: Reporting both what improved and what did not is what sets an expectation the rollout can actually meet.

options.text: Confirm that the review budget can be cut right now, since the pilot produced no visible errors.
options.explanation: Absence of visible errors in a short pilot is weak evidence, and cutting review on it removes the safeguard.

options.text: Say that the process is fully reliable, so the manager's confidence in it is not undermined.
options.explanation: Claiming full reliability is an overstatement, and confidence built on it collapses at the first real error.

options.text: Explain that review is still needed, because outputs continue to need checking before release.
options.explanation: Review remains part of the design, and saying so plainly is the honest answer to a budget question.

options.text: Avoid the question, since discussing limitations now would weaken support for the rollout.
options.explanation: Withholding limitations to protect support is exactly the communication failure this competency warns against.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: An operations team wants Claude to help find where a twelve-step expense reimbursement process loses time.
question: Which input will produce the most useful analysis?

options.text: The actual step list with who does each step, the handoffs between them, and typical waiting times.
options.explanation: Delay in a multi-step process almost always sits in the handoffs and the waiting between steps, so the analysis is only as good as the map it is given. Supplying the real steps, owners and typical waits lets Claude point at specific queues instead of generalising.

options.text: A summary of the process written for new starters, which explains its purpose and the policy behind it.
options.explanation: A new-starter summary explains why the process exists and what policy governs it. That is the wrong level of detail for finding delay, because it deliberately omits the handoffs and waiting that create it.

options.text: A description of how the team feels the process performs, written by the team's most experienced approver.
options.explanation: An experienced approver's impression is a useful hypothesis but not evidence. Perceived slowness usually clusters around visible effort rather than around the queues where time is genuinely lost.

options.text: A list of the complaints employees have raised about reimbursement over the past two reporting quarters.
options.explanation: Complaints record where employees felt the pain, which is often the last step before an outcome rather than the step that caused the wait. They are a helpful cross-check but a poor primary input for locating a bottleneck.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A finance team is designing a way of working in which Claude prepares the monthly variance commentary.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Write the instruction for the rest; try it on last month's figures; decide which parts a person must own; adjust one thing and try again
options.explanation: Writing instructions before deciding what stays human means the instruction may quietly cover work that should never have been handed over.

options.text: Try it on last month's figures; decide which parts a person must own; write the instruction for the rest; adjust one thing and try again
options.explanation: Testing before the boundary or the instruction exists gives a result nobody can interpret, and the design decisions come too late to shape it.

options.text: Decide which parts a person must own; write the instruction for the rest; try it on last month's figures; adjust one thing and try again
options.explanation: Delegation boundaries come first: decide what a person must own, write instructions for the remainder, test on real past figures, then adjust one thing at a time.

options.text: Write the instruction for the rest; decide which parts a person must own; adjust one thing and try again; try it on last month's figures
options.explanation: Adjusting before the arrangement has been tried at all means the first adjustment is made blind, and the test arrives after the changes.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A shared services group wants to take a Claude-assisted purchase-request triage from an idea to everyday use across eight teams.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed.
options.explanation: Extending to every team first is a full rollout before any evidence exists, which makes the later pilot and comparison pointless because the risk has already been taken.

options.text: Run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary.
options.explanation: Running alongside the existing process before choosing a team and a slice means the trial has no defined scope, and the scoping decision arrives after the comparison it was supposed to make possible.

options.text: Pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; run it alongside the existing process for a month; compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary.
options.explanation: A bounded slice on one team keeps early mistakes cheap, running alongside the existing process gives a fair comparison rather than an impression, fixing what failed happens while the scope is still small, and the wider rollout then carries the human checks the comparison showed were needed.

options.text: Compare the two sets of results and fix what failed; pick one team and a bounded slice of requests; extend to the other teams with the checks that proved necessary; run it alongside the existing process for a month.
options.explanation: There are no results to compare at the start, and the parallel run that would have produced them is left until after the arrangement has already been extended to all eight teams.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A charity is scoping a use case in which Claude would decide which grant applications are rejected at first screening, removing the review panel's initial pass entirely.
question: What is the greatest concern with this use case?

options.text: The screening criteria may be worded differently across the charity's several grant programmes.
options.explanation: Inconsistent criteria across programmes is a real quality problem, and it is worth fixing, but it can be corrected by harmonising the wording. It does not touch the question of who is answerable for a rejection.

options.text: The number of applications in each round may be larger than one conversation can work through.
options.explanation: Volume is a workload constraint that can be handled by processing applications in batches. It affects how the screening would be run rather than whether the decision should be delegated at all.

options.text: Panel members may need extra training before they can interpret the reasoning given for each decision.
options.explanation: Training panel members to read the reasoning would help, but it assumes the panel still reviews the decisions. In the use case as described the panel's initial pass has been removed, so there is nothing left for them to interpret.

options.text: Rejection at first screening is not seen or appealed by anyone, so no person owns the decision made.
options.explanation: A first-pass rejection is effectively final for the applicant and no human sees it, so an error is neither visible nor recoverable and nobody is accountable for it. Work carrying that kind of consequence should keep a person in the decision, with Claude preparing the assessment instead.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A charity's operations analyst asks Claude to produce a requirements list for a new volunteer scheduling process, giving it only the notes from the two coordinators who happened to be available that week. The list reads as thorough and is circulated as the agreed requirements.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Claude will refuse to produce a requirements list from notes covering part of the service
options.explanation: Claude will work with whatever it is given; it does not withhold an answer because the input covers only part of the service.

options.text: The two coordinators will be named in the list, exposing internal comments to everyone
options.explanation: Attribution is a housekeeping matter and easily corrected; it does not affect whether the requirements themselves are real.

options.text: The list will present gaps in the source notes as settled requirements nobody stated
options.explanation: Claude will fill an incomplete picture with plausible, well-written material. Circulated as "the agreed requirements", inferred content becomes indistinguishable from what stakeholders actually asked for.

options.text: The list will be too long for the sponsor to read before the decision has to be made
options.explanation: Length is a presentation problem. A concise list built on the same partial input would carry exactly the same defect.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
question: What is the most effective way to use Claude to analyze and categorize a list of requirements?

options.text: Ask Claude to design a new spreadsheet layout for organizing the requirements, including columns for type and priority.
options.explanation: Designing a spreadsheet layout focuses on formatting rather than analyzing or categorizing requirements. It does not leverage Claude's ability to classify requirements but instead adds a workflow artifact that doesn't directly address the need for analysis.

options.text: Ask Claude to review each requirement for completeness, clarity, and testability without performing classification.
