options.explanation: File format is an administrative convention with no bearing on the quality of the conclusions. It is exactly the kind of low-stakes, easily specified choice that does not need senior attention.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A market researcher needs Claude to incorporate current, real-world information published this week into a competitive-landscape summary, since this data postdates the model's training.
question: Which capability should the researcher enable?

options.text: Structured outputs, which guarantees the response conforms to a defined JSON schema
options.explanation: Structured outputs controls response formatting, not access to current external information.

options.text: The web search tool, which augments Claude's knowledge with current data from across the web
options.explanation: The web search tool augments Claude's comprehensive knowledge with current, real-world data from across the web, which is needed for this week's information.

options.text: Prompt caching, which reduces cost by reusing previously cached background context
options.explanation: Prompt caching lowers cost and latency for repeated context; it does not fetch new external information.

options.text: The memory tool, which stores and retrieves information across separate conversations
options.explanation: The memory tool persists information across sessions but does not retrieve fresh external web content.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A project lead has a single sentence from a director: "We need faster case handling." She wants to use Claude to turn this into a requirement set that goes to stakeholders for sign-off with no open questions left once it is drafted.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: List the open gaps; draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected; take the gaps to stakeholders.
options.explanation: This option drafts the requirement set in step two, before the outcome is even stated in step three and before the gaps are ever taken to stakeholders in step four -- the draft goes out carrying the same open questions the project lead wanted resolved first, and the closing stakeholder step happens too late to change a draft that already exists.

options.text: State the outcome and who is affected; list the open gaps; take the gaps to stakeholders; draft the requirement set.
options.explanation: Naming the outcome and who is affected turns the director's one sentence into a target the gaps can be measured against; listing what is still unknown surfaces the open questions; taking those to stakeholders closes them before anything is written down; only then does the draft go out with no open questions left, which is exactly what the project lead needs.

options.text: Take the gaps to stakeholders; list the open gaps; draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected.
options.explanation: This option takes gaps to stakeholders in step one, before any gap has been listed in step two, so there is nothing yet to ask stakeholders about; it also drafts the requirement set before the outcome and audience are named, so the draft is written without knowing what it is meant to achieve or for whom.

options.text: Draft the requirement set; state the outcome and who is affected; list the open gaps; take the gaps to stakeholders.
options.explanation: The project lead wants a requirement set with no open questions left once it is drafted, so drafting cannot be the first step: nothing is known yet about the outcome, who is affected, or what is missing when this option's draft is written, and that draft is never revisited after the outcome is stated or the gaps are surfaced.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A finance shared-service team already has a working month-end checklist and wants to bring Claude into it without disrupting the close.
question: What should they do first?

options.text: Pick one checklist step that is text-heavy and repetitive and try Claude there
options.explanation: Augmenting a process that already works means starting with the smallest, most suitable slice, where a failure is contained and the rest of the close carries on unchanged.

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the whole checklist before the next month-end close runs
options.explanation: Rewriting the checklist before anyone has tried a single step changes the whole close on an untested assumption.

options.text: Replace the checklist with an arrangement built around what Claude can do now
options.explanation: Redesigning around the tool is the wrong move when the existing process works; it puts a hard deadline at risk for no demonstrated gain.

options.text: Have every preparer use Claude however they prefer during the next close cycle
options.explanation: Uncoordinated individual use during a deadline-driven close produces inconsistent output and no learning the team can reuse.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
situation: A manufacturing engineer has a detailed transcript of a production process and wants to convert it into a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) using Claude.
question: Which approach best leverages Claude's capabilities to create an accurate, complete, and company-standard SOP?

options.text: Ask Claude to generate a generic manufacturing SOP, then insert specific details from the transcript into the template, relying on manual review to align steps with the process.
options.explanation: Starting with a generic SOP template and inserting details from the transcript can lead to misalignment between the template's structure and the actual process, requiring extensive manual review to correct. This approach fails to capitalize on Claude's capacity to directly generate a tailored, accurate SOP from the source material.

options.text: Provide the transcript to Claude and request a complete SOP without specifying details, letting the model infer all necessary steps and formatting.
options.explanation: Providing the transcript without specifying details relies entirely on Claude's inference, which may overlook critical safety notes, tools, or quality checks necessary for a complete SOP. This approach also lacks iterative refinement to ensure the output matches company-specific formatting and content requirements, increasing the risk of omissions or inaccuracies.

options.text: Ask Claude to extract steps from the transcript, then iteratively add safety notes, tools, and quality checks, and format as a company SOP template.
options.explanation: This method leverages Claude's capabilities by breaking the task into logical steps: extracting process steps, then iteratively adding safety notes, tools, and quality checks, and finally formatting into a company SOP template. This iterative process ensures the SOP is accurate, complete, and aligned with company standards.

options.text: Manually rewrite the transcript into bullet points, then structure them into an SOP draft, and use Claude only to check grammar and style, not to suggest or organize content.
options.explanation: Limiting Claude to only grammar and style checks underutilizes its ability to analyze the transcript, suggest organizational improvements, and ensure procedural completeness. Manual rewriting and structuring risk introducing errors or missing details that Claude could otherwise catch and enhance.

objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
question: What is the best approach for using Claude to create a detailed timeline from a marketing campaign brief?

options.text: Provide the brief, specify the exact launch date, ask for a backward-scheduled timeline with dependencies and responsible teams, and request that Claude flag any unrealistic constraints.
options.explanation: This approach anchors the timeline to the exact launch date, uses backward scheduling, and includes dependencies and responsible teams. Flagging unrealistic constraints allows for proactive adjustments, and grounding the plan in the provided brief ensures it is comprehensive and actionable. It fully leverages Claude for structured planning.

options.text: Tell Claude to create a timeline based on typical marketing best practices, specify a generic campaign structure, ask for a forward-scheduled plan with standard phases, and ignore any specific dates from the brief.
options.explanation: Ignoring specific dates from the brief prevents the timeline from reflecting actual project constraints. A generic forward-scheduled plan based only on best practices lacks the necessary context to be actionable. Claude should incorporate the brief’s details to create a relevant and accurate timeline.

options.text: Use Claude to rewrite the brief as a press release, specify the dateline and boilerplate, ask for a narrative flow, and then extract a timeline from the generated release for the campaign's key phases.
options.explanation: Rewriting the brief as a press release is an unnecessary transformation that doesn’t directly support timeline creation. Extracting a timeline from narrative prose risks losing key details and is less accurate than having Claude produce a structured schedule from the outset.

options.text: Instruct Claude to list all possible marketing activities, categorize them by phase, and output a sequential plan without specific dates, relying on the team to schedule execution using their own project management tools.
options.explanation: Listing activities by phase without specific dates does not produce a workable timeline. Relying on the team to schedule execution later shifts critical planning decisions away from Claude, missing the opportunity to integrate temporal dependencies directly into the output.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A department switches all fifty of its staff to a redesigned, Claude-assisted case-handling process on the same Monday morning, with no trial group kept back.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The department's usage may rise sharply in the first week as fifty people start using Claude.
options.explanation: A jump in usage is a predictable consequence of fifty people starting at once and can be planned for. It affects cost and capacity, not the soundness of the redesigned process.

options.text: Some staff will need considerably longer than others to become comfortable with the new way of working.
options.explanation: Uneven adoption is expected in any change and is managed with support and coaching. It slows the benefit rather than exposing the department to a failure it cannot see.

options.text: Any flaw hits every case at once, and there is no unchanged group to compare results against.
options.explanation: A full switch removes both safeguards at once: every case is exposed to a design that has never run live, and with no group still on the old process there is nothing to compare against, so the team cannot even tell whether results have got worse.

options.text: Training all fifty staff in one week will strain the two people who designed the new process.
options.explanation: Straining the two designers is a real resourcing problem during the first week. It is a delivery pressure rather than the reason a simultaneous switch is dangerous.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A council's improvement team has four candidate use cases and can take only one forward this quarter.
question: Which is the soundest first candidate for Claude?

options.text: Setting the annual budget allocation across all six of the council's neighbourhood teams
options.explanation: A budget allocation is a sole-source judgement with accountability attached, and the reasoning behind it must be owned by named people.

options.text: Deciding which of the housing repair requests are downgraded to a lower priority band
options.explanation: Downgrading a repair affects a resident's service directly and needs judgement someone must answer for; Claude may inform that decision but should not make it.

options.text: Summarising the free-text comments on the monthly residents' survey for service leads
options.explanation: It is repetitive, text-heavy and well specified, the output is reviewable before anyone acts on it, and a mistake is recoverable. That is the profile of a good delegation candidate.

options.text: Issuing the final refusal letters for licence applications directly to the applicants
options.explanation: Sending a refusal to an applicant is an outward-facing, effectively irreversible act, which is precisely what should not be handed over unreviewed.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A Claude-assisted case-summary way of working produces good results for the analyst who designed it, but two colleagues get noticeably worse results from the same written instructions.
question: What should the designer do first?

options.text: Add examples of good summaries to the instructions so the expected standard is unmistakable.
options.explanation: Worked examples usually improve an arrangement and may well be part of the eventual fix. Adding them before the divergence has been observed is still a guess at the cause.

options.text: Rewrite the instructions in much more detail so that less is left to the individual using them.
options.explanation: More detail is a plausible fix but an untargeted one. Without knowing which part of the colleagues' use diverges, the designer may add paragraphs about something that was never the problem.

options.text: Ask the two colleagues to use the designer's own saved wording word for word every time.
options.explanation: Copying the designer's wording exactly hides the difference rather than explaining it, and it will not transfer to the next case. It also suggests the arrangement only works when one person operates it.

options.text: Watch each colleague run the work once and see where their inputs differ from the designer's.
options.explanation: The same instructions producing different results means the difference is in what people actually do with them. Watching one run each is the quickest way to find the unstated step the designer performs without noticing, and it is what makes any later rewrite land in the right place.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A team is choosing which slice of work to use for a two-week trial of a new Claude-assisted contract summarising arrangement.
question: Which slice is the best choice for the trial?

options.text: The contracts causing the most delay right now, so the trial also clears the urgent backlog.
options.explanation: Using the trial to clear a backlog mixes two goals and puts urgent work in the hands of an untested arrangement. The most delayed contracts are also often the least typical, so they are a poor sample.

options.text: A random sample drawn from the whole archive, including contracts that are no longer in force.
options.explanation: A random archive sample sounds rigorous but includes expired contracts the team no longer handles. Effort goes into cases that will never recur, and the awkward live cases may not appear at all.

options.text: A representative mix, including the awkward cases the team knows the arrangement must survive.
options.explanation: A pilot is only useful if it is a fair rehearsal of the real work, which means deliberately including the hard cases. Two weeks on a representative mix shows both what the arrangement handles well and where it must keep a person involved.

options.text: The simplest contracts, so the trial is not derailed by problems that affect only unusual cases.
options.explanation: An easy slice produces a flattering result that does not predict live performance. The arrangement would then meet its first difficult contract after the team has already committed to it.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A communications team has decided that Claude will draft its recurring stakeholder update, but the team cannot yet say how they will judge whether the arrangement is working.
question: Which action best prepares them to delegate the task?

options.text: Write down what an acceptable draft must contain and avoid, and agree it before any drafting is handed over.
options.explanation: Defining what good looks like before delegating is what makes the delegation reviewable: the team gains a shared standard to check drafts against, a basis for correcting the instructions, and evidence for whether the arrangement is working rather than an argument about taste.

options.text: Agree a rota naming who will paste the source material into Claude for each reporting cycle in turn.
options.explanation: A rota settles who performs the task, which is useful operationally, but it does not give anyone a way to judge the output. The team would still have no agreed answer to whether a given draft is acceptable.

options.text: Draw up a shortlist of other tools to fall back on if the drafts disappoint during the first month.
options.explanation: Planning a fallback before defining success means the team cannot tell whether the fallback is ever needed. Without a quality standard, disappointment is a matter of opinion and switching tools would not fix it.

options.text: Set a target for how long each draft should take compared with the time the current manual version takes today.
options.explanation: A time target measures effort saved but says nothing about whether the drafts are fit to send. A fast draft that misses required content is worse than the slower manual version it replaced.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A programme team asks Claude to condense forty stakeholder interview transcripts into a single requirements list, then plans to send that list to a supplier as the final agreed scope without further review.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The supplier may raise follow-up questions that the programme team cannot answer without rereading material.
options.explanation: Follow-up questions from a supplier are normal in any scoping exercise and are answerable by returning to the material. This is an inconvenience rather than the central danger of treating an unverified summary as agreed scope.

options.text: Working through forty long transcripts may take several minutes and consume a large share of the team's usage.
options.explanation: Processing time and usage consumption are real but recoverable costs. They do not affect the correctness of the scope being sent out, and they would not survive a comparison with a defect that only surfaces after the supplier has started building.

options.text: Needs raised in only one interview may be lost, and nobody has checked the list against the transcripts.
options.explanation: Summarising forty transcripts naturally favours what was said repeatedly, so a genuine but rarely voiced requirement can quietly disappear. Because the list becomes contractual scope with no verification pass against the sources, an omission is both likely and expensive to discover later.

options.text: The list may be written as flowing prose when the supplier's template expects a numbered table of items.
options.explanation: Formatting is a presentation issue that is trivially fixed by asking for a different layout. It has no bearing on whether the scope the supplier is being asked to build is actually the scope the stakeholders described.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A manager is about to tell her team that Claude will now produce the first draft of every incident report.
question: What should the announcement make clear above all?

options.text: How much time the change is expected to save the team over the course of a full year.
options.explanation: A projected annual saving is the business case rather than the operating instruction. It tells the team why the change is happening but leaves them unsure what they are now responsible for.

options.text: What changes, what stays with each person, and where their review is still required.
options.explanation: People need to know exactly where the boundary now sits: which part Claude drafts, which judgments remain theirs, and that their review is still a required step. Without that, reports are either double-handled or sent out with nobody checking them.

options.text: Which other departments have already adopted the same approach to their own reports.
options.explanation: Naming other departments builds confidence in the decision but says nothing about how this team should work. It is reassurance, not direction.

options.text: How the manager tested the new arrangement before deciding to introduce it to the team.
options.explanation: Describing the testing is good practice and supports trust in the change. It still leaves the team without a clear statement of their own remaining responsibilities.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: An operations manager has collected about sixty requirement statements from five departments for a new supplier onboarding process. Many overlap, several contradict each other, and some are one-line wishes. She wants Claude to help her make sense of the list.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to rank all sixty statements by business value so the team can start on the top ten items.
options.explanation: Ranking is premature while duplicates and contradictions are still in the list. A value ranking built over sixty unclean statements will rank the same need twice and score wishes that nobody can define, so the ordering would have to be redone once the list is tidied.

options.text: Paste the full list into Claude and ask it to group related items and flag statements too vague to act on.
options.explanation: Analysis has to start with understanding what is actually in the list. Grouping related statements and surfacing the ones that are too vague to act on gives the manager a clean picture of overlaps, conflicts and gaps, which is exactly the work Claude accelerates well and which every later step depends on.

options.text: Ask Claude to estimate how long each of the sixty requirements would take to deliver before reviewing.
options.explanation: Effort estimates depend on requirements being unambiguous. Estimating vague one-line wishes produces numbers with no basis, and the manager would be attaching delivery figures to items that may turn out to be duplicates of one another.

options.text: Ask Claude to draft the finished onboarding process document so the departments can react to something real.
options.explanation: Drafting the finished process before the requirements are understood invites departments to react to Claude's assumptions rather than to their own stated needs, and it makes the analysis harder because disagreements now attach to a document instead of to the underlying requirement.

objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
situation: A department head asks for a one-page summary of what Claude will and will not do in a redesigned review workflow.
question: What is the most important thing for that summary to include?

options.text: A technical comparison of the model options so the department can judge the quality of the choice.
options.explanation: A model comparison is not what a department head needs to understand value and limits.

options.text: A ranked list of every Claude feature the department could adopt over the next financial year.
options.explanation: A feature roadmap does not tell the department what the workflow will and will not do.

options.text: A statement that the outputs are reliable enough for review to be dropped once staff are trained.
options.explanation: Promising that review disappears oversells the tool and removes the accountability step.

options.text: Where Claude drafts and where a named person reviews, with the checks that stay in human hands.
options.explanation: Stakeholders need the boundary between assisted work and human accountability stated plainly.

objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
situation: A department head tells an analyst, "I want Claude to handle our client onboarding." The analyst has been given no other detail.
question: What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Draw up a list of onboarding steps that Claude could not perform, and send that list to the department head.
options.explanation: Cataloguing limitations before the goal is known produces an answer to an unasked question. Some of those steps may be irrelevant to the department head's actual concern, and the list reads as resistance rather than analysis.

options.text: Set up a shared project workspace and upload the current onboarding documents so Claude has background.
options.explanation: Loading the current documents is useful eventually, but doing it first assumes the existing process is the thing worth automating. If the real problem is that onboarding starts too late or asks clients for the wrong information, the documents encode the problem rather than the solution.

options.text: Ask the department head which onboarding outcome is failing today, and for whom, before naming any tool.
options.explanation: The request names a tool, not a problem. Establishing which onboarding outcome is failing and who feels it defines the problem to be solved, and that definition determines which steps are worth delegating at all and how success would later be judged.

options.text: Run a series of trial prompts to see how well Claude drafts onboarding emails, then share the results.
options.explanation: Trial prompts show what Claude can produce, not what the department needs. Demonstrating a capability before the problem is defined tends to anchor everyone on whichever step happens to demo well rather than on the step that is actually hurting.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A charity's donation-thank-you process works well overall but is slow only at the drafting step.
question: Which integration approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Augment the process by having Claude draft, with the same person signing off
options.explanation: When one step is the constraint and the rest of the process is sound, augment that step and leave the controls in place. The sign-off is not what was slow.

options.text: Redesign the process so donors receive whatever Claude drafts straight away
options.explanation: Sending unreviewed drafts to donors is an outward-facing, effectively irreversible step and should not be delegated unchecked.

options.text: Keep the process as it is and offer Claude as a tool people may use or ignore
options.explanation: Optional, unstructured use leaves the bottleneck exactly where it was and produces inconsistent letters to donors.

options.text: Redesign the process around Claude and drop the sign-off step that slows it
options.explanation: Removing the sign-off removes the check that makes the process safe, in exchange for time that was not being lost there.

objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
situation: A pilot has worked well, and the team wants the new way of working to survive the departure of the person who created it.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; capture the working instructions in one shared place; write down what a good result looks like.
options.explanation: This begins by correcting instructions that do not yet exist in a shared place and ends by defining the standard, so every earlier step was taken without knowing what success meant.

options.text: Write down what a good result looks like; capture the working instructions in one shared place; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck.
options.explanation: The quality standard has to exist before anyone can tell whether a handover succeeded, the instructions must be captured somewhere shared to be handed over at all, a second person running from them alone is the real test, and their sticking points show precisely what to correct.

options.text: Capture the working instructions in one shared place; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; write down what a good result looks like; have a second person run the work from those instructions alone.
options.explanation: Correcting the instructions before anyone has tried to follow them means correcting imagined problems, and the standard for a good result is written after the corrections it should have guided.

options.text: Have a second person run the work from those instructions alone; write down what a good result looks like; correct the instructions wherever they got stuck; capture the working instructions in one shared place.
options.explanation: The second person cannot run the work from instructions that have not yet been captured, and writing down what good looks like after the test leaves them no way to judge their own output.

objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
situation: A team plans to bring Claude into a workflow that three other departments feed into.
question: Which step is most important before the change goes live?

options.text: Wait until the other departments adopt the same arrangement themselves
options.explanation: Making the change conditional on three other departments adopting it first blocks a workflow improvement that is entirely within this team's control.

options.text: Tell the feeding departments what changes for them and what does not
options.explanation: Integration touches everyone who feeds the workflow. Being explicit about what changes for them, and what stays the same, is what stops the redesign breaking at its handovers.

options.text: Give each department its own version of the new written instructions
options.explanation: Separate instruction versions per department guarantee that the workflow behaves differently depending on who fed it.

options.text: Ask the departments to stop sending work until the change is settled
options.explanation: Halting incoming work to make an internal change imposes the cost on other departments unnecessarily.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A training manager is setting up a project so that every chat produces course outlines in the department's standard format.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Write the project instructions; refine the wording; define the audience and format; test with a real request.
options.explanation: Refining before the standard is defined means editing wording with no agreed target to edit towards.

options.text: Define the audience and format; write the project instructions; test with a real request; refine the wording.
options.explanation: Agree the standard, encode it as durable direction, try it on real work, then tighten what missed.

options.text: Refine the wording; test with a real request; write the project instructions; define the audience and format.
options.explanation: Nothing exists to refine at the start, and the format is agreed only after everything is already built.

options.text: Test with a real request; define the audience and format; refine the wording; write the project instructions.
options.explanation: Testing before any instructions exist tells you nothing about whether the instructions work.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project shared across a department has no named owner. Several people hold edit access and each has added documents over the past year.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Edit access is revoked automatically after a long period of inactivity, so the project becomes read-only.
options.explanation: Access is not withdrawn on its own because a project has been quiet.

options.text: Shared projects reset their instructions whenever a second person saves a change to the knowledge.
options.explanation: Editing knowledge does not clear the project's instructions.

options.text: Each new document replaces the previous one, so the project only ever holds the most recent upload.
options.explanation: Uploads accumulate; they do not overwrite one another.

options.text: Nobody is accountable for removing outdated material, so contradictory documents accumulate unchecked.
options.explanation: Shared editing without ownership is precisely how a knowledge base fills with conflicting versions.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: An analyst has a specific quarterly business review deck outline that they need occasionally, in several different projects and sometimes in plain chats.
question: Where does this routine best belong?

options.text: Put it into every project's instructions, so the deck outline is imposed on all of the chats in each one.
options.explanation: This forces an occasional format onto every conversation in those projects and must be maintained in each.

options.text: Keep it in a document inside one project's knowledge base and copy that file across into the other projects as needed.
options.explanation: Copying a file around leaves several versions to maintain and does not make the routine act on demand.

options.text: Store it in the account-wide instructions, so the deck outline shapes every conversation the analyst has.
options.explanation: An occasional deck format would then influence unrelated work in every conversation.

options.text: Package it as a skill, so the routine is available across projects and applies when the task calls for it.
options.explanation: Skills are reusable procedures that load when relevant, rather than always-on direction tied to one workspace.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: An operations lead runs a project whose instructions describe the team's standard weekly status report. This week only, a board member has asked for a one-page version.
question: What is the best way to handle the request?

options.text: Create a second project duplicating the same knowledge base but with one-page reports as its house rule.
options.explanation: A whole parallel workspace is heavy maintenance for a single request, and the two projects will drift apart.

options.text: Add a permanent line to the project instructions saying every status report must be exactly one page long.
options.explanation: Baking a one-off requirement into durable direction changes every future report for a single exception.

options.text: Ask for the one-page version in that chat, leaving the project instructions describing the normal report.
options.explanation: A one-off need belongs in the individual request; durable instructions should keep describing the standing format.

options.text: Upload the board member's request into project knowledge so Claude applies the shorter format from now on.
options.explanation: Knowledge is background material, not direction, and this still makes a temporary need permanent.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A shared project supports a process that changes every quarter.
question: Which practice best keeps the project trustworthy over time?

options.text: Name an owner and a review date so the instructions and the documents are checked each quarter.
options.explanation: Accountability plus a scheduled review is what keeps configuration aligned with a changing process.

options.text: Re-upload every document once a week so that the knowledge base is refreshed whether or not it changed.
options.explanation: Re-uploading unchanged files costs effort without detecting anything that actually changed.

options.text: Ask anyone who spots an error to correct the knowledge base themselves whenever they happen to notice.
options.explanation: Ad hoc fixes by whoever notices leave gaps and produce inconsistent, unrecorded changes.

options.text: Rely on members to say in their prompts which parts of the documents are now out of date.
options.explanation: This assumes every member already knows what changed, which is rarely true.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A logistics coordinator depends on a carrier rate sheet that the finance team edits every week.
question: Which maintenance approach is better?

options.text: Upload one copy of the rate sheet, since an uploaded copy follows the original whenever it changes.
options.explanation: An uploaded document is a snapshot; it does not update when the original is edited.

options.text: Keep the rate sheet reachable through the connected drive so Claude works from the current version.
options.explanation: A connected source reflects the file as it stands, which removes a weekly manual refresh.

options.text: Ask Claude to remember the rates in one chat and to reuse those figures in all later chats.
options.explanation: Detail mentioned in one conversation is not carried into other chats as project context.

options.text: Paste the rate figures into the project instructions, where they are least likely to be edited by others.
options.explanation: Figures that change weekly are the worst possible content for durable instructions.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project owner has been sent the replacement version of a document that is already in the project's knowledge base.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Test a question whose answer changed; remove the superseded file; upload the replacement; identify the outdated document.
options.explanation: Verification happens before anything has been fixed, and identification comes last of all.

options.text: Upload the replacement; test a question whose answer changed; identify the outdated document; remove the superseded file.
options.explanation: Testing while both versions are loaded produces an unreliable result.

options.text: Identify the outdated document; upload the replacement; remove the superseded file; test a question whose answer changed.
options.explanation: Find it, replace it, remove the old copy so both cannot be cited, then verify with a question that changed.

options.text: Remove the superseded file; identify the outdated document; test a question whose answer changed; upload the replacement.
options.explanation: The file is deleted before it has been identified, and the project has no current source during the test.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A manager wants Claude to help draft a weekly customer newsletter, always drawing on the brand guide, the past issues and a fixed tone.
question: What should the manager do first?

options.text: Paste the brand guide into a single long chat and keep returning to that same conversation each week.
options.explanation: One growing conversation is fragile and does not carry the direction into any new chat.

options.text: Ask Claude for a first newsletter and add the brand guide only if the draft misses the intended tone.
options.explanation: This defers the setup and produces a first draft with none of the context that matters.

options.text: Put the brand guide into the account-wide instructions so that it shapes every conversation they ever have.
options.explanation: Newsletter-specific material would then influence unrelated work across the whole account.

options.text: Create a project for the newsletter work so the guide, the past issues and the tone rules sit together.
options.explanation: Recurring work with shared context and standing rules is exactly what a project is for.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A support team lead creates a Claude Project and wants Claude to always answer in a formal tone and respond as a senior support engineer for every conversation in that workspace, without repeating those directions in each chat.
question: What should the lead configure?

options.text: Upload a text file describing the tone to the knowledge base and name the file 'instructions.txt'
options.explanation: A file named like instructions is still treated as knowledge base content, not as project-level behavioral instructions.

options.text: Create a separate project for every tone and role combination the support team might ever need
options.explanation: Creating a project per tone combination is unnecessary overhead when a single project's instructions field already covers this need.

options.text: Paste the tone and role guidance into the opening message of each new chat inside the project
options.explanation: Repeating guidance in every chat defeats the purpose of project instructions, which persist automatically across chats.

options.text: Set project instructions defining the tone and role, since these apply automatically to every chat
options.explanation: Project instructions are built specifically to establish behavioral guidelines, such as tone and role, that Claude applies to all chats within that project.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: Claude keeps quoting a superseded pricing sheet that someone uploaded to a shared Project several months ago. Which two actions address the cause?
question: Select two.

options.text: Remove the superseded pricing sheet from the Project's knowledge so it stops being used.
options.explanation: The stale document is the cause, so removing it from the knowledge base is what actually stops the wrong figures.

options.text: Switch the Project over to a deeper-reasoning tier so the wrong figures get caught in future.
options.explanation: A deeper tier reasons better over whatever it is given, and it is still being given the superseded sheet.

options.text: Upload the current pricing sheet so that the Project draws on the version now in force.
options.explanation: Replacing it with the current sheet gives the Project the right source, which is the other half of the same fix.

options.text: Add a line to every chat telling Claude to ignore any pricing figure that looks wrong.
options.explanation: Re-prompting cannot fix a wrong source document; Claude has no way to know which figure is out of date.

options.text: Start a brand new Project every month so that old uploads never have time to accumulate.
options.explanation: Discarding the workspace monthly throws away the accumulated context and still does not curate the sources.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
question: Which statement accurately reflects how a project's chat history relates to that project's workspace?

options.text: Chat history is automatically discarded at the end of every chat session within a project
options.explanation: Chat history is retained as part of the project workspace, not discarded automatically at session end.

options.text: Each project is a self-contained workspace that maintains its own chat history apart from other projects
options.explanation: Projects function as self-contained workspaces, each maintaining its own separate chat history and knowledge base distinct from other projects.

options.text: Chat history is stored globally across the account and is identical no matter which project it belongs to
options.explanation: Chat history is scoped per project rather than merged into one identical global history across all projects.

options.text: Chat history can only be viewed after re-uploading it to the project's knowledge base first
options.explanation: Chat history is viewable directly within the project without needing to be uploaded to the knowledge base.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: An analyst has connected her work Google Drive to Claude and asks for last quarter's regional sales file. Claude replies that it cannot find it, although she knows the file exists because a colleague showed it to her.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Rephrase the request repeatedly until Claude eventually locates the file on the connected drive.
options.explanation: Rewording cannot reveal a file the connected account has no permission to open in the first place.

options.text: Remove the connector and set it up again, as a broken connection is the usual cause of this.
options.explanation: Reconnecting does not widen access, and nothing here suggests the connection itself has failed.

options.text: Check whether that file is shared with her own account, since the connector uses her own access.
options.explanation: A connector reaches only what the connecting account can already open, so a file a colleague has not shared with her is simply outside its scope.

options.text: Ask her colleague to run the same request and paste his answer back into her conversation.
options.explanation: This works around the question without establishing whether she is entitled to the file at all.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A reorganisation has changed how a team's workflow runs, and a shared project's instructions no longer describe it.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Revise the project instructions; gather what changed in the process; tell the members; check the outputs against the revised rules.
options.explanation: The instructions are rewritten before anyone has established what actually changed.

options.text: Check the outputs against the revised rules; tell the members; revise the project instructions; gather what changed in the process.
options.explanation: Outputs are checked against rules that do not exist yet, and the change is investigated last.

options.text: Gather what changed in the process; revise the project instructions; check the outputs against the revised rules; tell the members.
options.explanation: Understand the change, encode it, confirm it produces the right output, then inform the people who rely on it.

options.text: Tell the members; check the outputs against the revised rules; gather what changed in the process; revise the project instructions.
options.explanation: Members are told about a change that has not been made, and the revision happens last.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: An employee keeps a connector to a shared team drive in place after moving to a completely different department.
question: What is the greatest concern?

options.text: The drive's files are duplicated into the employee's own personal account and count against their storage.
options.explanation: Connectors do not copy files into the individual's own storage.

options.text: Claude keeps reaching material the person no longer needs, so access is broader than their current role.
options.explanation: A connection left in place after a role change quietly extends access beyond what the job now requires.

options.text: The organisation's owner is blocked from enabling any further connectors until this one is removed.
options.explanation: One connection does not prevent others from being enabled.

options.text: The connector stops working entirely, so any project relying on it returns an error to every member.
options.explanation: A department move does not by itself break a connector.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user asks Claude, connected via the Drive connector, to save a report Claude just generated into a specific Drive folder.
question: What can Claude do?

options.text: Claude can save files to Drive only when code execution is separately turned on first.
options.explanation: Code execution is required for XLSX chat uploads, not for the Drive connector's save and folder features.

options.text: Claude can only save generated files to the root of Drive, not a folder.
options.explanation: Folder creation and organized saving are supported, not just root-level file placement.

options.text: Claude can create folders and save Claude-generated files directly into Drive itself.
options.explanation: The Drive connector supports creating folders and saving Claude-generated files, so the report can go into the requested folder.

options.text: Claude cannot save any files to Drive, only read files already there.
options.explanation: Saving generated files to Drive is an explicit connector capability beyond just reading existing files.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A researcher mentions in a chat that they prefer citations in APA format, but does not add this preference to the project knowledge base or project instructions. In a different chat within the same project, Claude does not apply APA formatting by default.
question: Why does this occur?

options.text: Claude supports only one citation style per account for the entire lifetime of that account
options.explanation: Citation style is not fixed for the lifetime of an account; it can be guided per project through instructions.

options.text: The researcher's current plan does not support citation formatting inside project chats at all
options.explanation: This behavior reflects how context persistence works, not a plan-based restriction on formatting styles.

options.text: Preferences mentioned only in a single chat are not shared across chats unless added to instructions
options.explanation: Context shared in one chat is not shared across chats within a project unless it is captured in project instructions or added to the knowledge base.

options.text: APA formatting is a feature that must be enabled separately in account-wide settings outside projects
options.explanation: There is no separate account-wide setting for citation style; persistence within a project is controlled through instructions or knowledge base content.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A user on a free Claude account has already created five projects and wants to start a sixth one for a new personal task.
question: What should they expect?

options.text: They can create a sixth project only after deleting the oldest chat from an existing project
options.explanation: Deleting a chat does not lift the five-project cap; the limit applies to the count of projects, not chats.

options.text: They can create unlimited projects because free accounts carry no cap on project count at all
options.explanation: Free accounts are capped at five projects; the cap is not unlimited.

options.text: They can create a sixth project but that project will have no knowledge base feature available
options.explanation: The limitation described is about the number of projects allowed, not about disabling the knowledge base feature on new ones.

options.text: They cannot create a sixth project because free accounts are limited to a maximum of five projects
options.explanation: Free Claude accounts can create a maximum of five projects, so a sixth would require removing or upgrading rather than simply creating a new one.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: An HR partner finds that a project is producing answers in the wrong tone for its audience.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Identify the rule that is vague or missing; read what the instructions currently say; rerun a typical request; revise that rule.
options.explanation: A rule cannot be identified as weak before the instructions have been read, and the fix comes last.

options.text: Revise that rule; rerun a typical request; read what the instructions currently say; identify the rule that is vague or missing.
options.explanation: Revising before reading means editing direction nobody has actually examined.

options.text: Rerun a typical request; revise that rule; read what the instructions currently say; identify the rule that is vague or missing.
options.explanation: The rule is revised before it has been identified, and the instructions are read last of all.

options.text: Read what the instructions currently say; identify the rule that is vague or missing; revise that rule; rerun a typical request.
options.explanation: Diagnose the existing direction, isolate the weak rule, fix it, then confirm with a real request.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: An HR project built eighteen months ago is still in daily use. Its benefits summary has since been superseded by a newer edition, and one uploaded policy was retired outright in a restructure. Which two actions should the project owner take?
question: Select two.

options.text: Remove the retired policy, because an obsolete document still gets used in answers.
options.explanation: and this is a different maintenance action on a different document: nothing replaces the retired policy, so it is removed rather than refreshed. Claude has no way to know a policy no longer applies unless it stops being available.

options.text: Ask Claude which uploaded documents are out of date and act on whatever it reports.
options.explanation: Claude can compare documents it has been given, but it cannot know which reflects current company reality. Delegating the currency judgment to the model is precisely the human review step that project maintenance requires.

options.text: Upload the current benefits summary and delete the superseded edition it replaces.
options.explanation: Refreshing the document is the fix for a superseded source, and deleting the old edition matters as much as adding the new one — left in place, it competes with the current figures and produces confidently wrong answers.

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to disregard any document older than twelve months.
options.explanation: Uploaded files do not carry a reliable age Claude can filter on, and the rule would be wrong in both directions — discarding accurate long-standing policies while keeping a recently uploaded document that is already superseded.

options.text: Keep both benefits editions in place so Claude can compare the old and new wording.
options.explanation: Two live editions of the same summary is the situation that causes staff to be quoted last year's benefits. If a historical version is genuinely needed, it belongs outside the project knowledge that answers everyday questions.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A manager asks Claude, connected via the Calendar connector, to find a time when five attendees are all free next week.
question: What can Claude do?

options.text: Claude can identify mutual availability across attendees using the connector directly.
options.explanation: The Calendar connector explicitly supports identifying mutual availability across attendees, finding a shared open slot for all five.

options.text: Claude can list each attendee's events but cannot compute their overlapping free time.
options.explanation: Computing mutual availability, not just listing separate events, is specifically supported.

options.text: Claude can only check the manager's own calendar, not the attendees' ones.
options.explanation: The connector is designed to view shared calendars and attendee availability, not just the manager's events.

options.text: Claude cannot access calendar data for anyone besides the account owner.
options.explanation: Access to shared calendars for availability checks is a core connector feature.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user has connected the Gmail connector and asks Claude to reply to a client email.
question: What happens once Claude has drafted the reply?

options.text: Claude holds the message for a workspace administrator to approve before anything leaves the account
options.explanation: The approval prompt goes to the person making the request, not to an administrator. Administrators control whether a connector is available at all, not individual messages.

options.text: Claude sends it straight away, because authorising a connector authorises every action that connector offers
options.explanation: Authorising a connector does not hand over unattended permission to act. Write actions are gated by an approval step by default, which is the point of that design.

options.text: Claude can send it, but by default it asks the user to approve the action before the message goes out
options.explanation: Sending, replying and forwarding are write actions the mail connector supports, and by default Claude asks for approval before each one. The user stays in control of what actually leaves the account without having to copy the draft out by hand.

options.text: Claude can only produce a draft, because a mail connector is limited to searching and reading messages
options.explanation: Mail connectors are not read-only. Alongside searching and reading, they support sending, replying to and forwarding messages.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A bid team on a Team plan is setting up a shared project for public-sector tender responses. Two writers will draft in it and four managers will review. Which two set-up choices are appropriate?
question: Select two.

options.text: Paste the tender house rules at the top of each new chat instead of storing them.
options.explanation: House rules that apply to every bid are exactly what project instructions are for. Re-pasting them into each chat means they get shortened, misremembered or forgotten, and different writers end up working to different rules.

options.text: Upload the approved boilerplate and the last three winning tenders as knowledge.
options.explanation: Project knowledge is where durable background belongs: uploading the boilerplate and past winning tenders makes that material available across every chat in the project, instead of being re-pasted per bid.

options.text: Have every writer make a personal copy of the project so nobody waits for anyone.
options.explanation: Personal copies destroy the shared context the project exists to provide: the separate knowledge bases drift apart, and every boilerplate update has to be repeated in each one. A shared project already lets people work at the same time.

options.text: Ask an administrator to lift the five-project limit that applies to the bid team.
options.explanation: The cap of five projects is a Free-account limit. This team is on a Team plan, which has no stated project limit, so there is no cap for an administrator to lift.

options.text: Share it with the two writers as "Can edit" and the four managers as "Can view".
options.explanation: and on a separate axis from knowledge: this is the access decision. Project sharing is a Team and Enterprise capability, and the creator grants specific members either "Can view" or "Can edit" — those are the two levels that exist.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A consultant is setting up a Claude Project for a client engagement she will work on every week for months. Which two things belong in that set-up?
question: Select two.

options.text: Project knowledge holding the client documents that each chat in the Project should draw on.
options.explanation: Project knowledge is where background documents live so Claude has them in every chat in that Project.

options.text: One chat for each client document, so every document keeps its own conversation thread.
options.explanation: Splitting one document per chat fragments the engagement and abandons the shared knowledge base a Project provides.

options.text: Project instructions covering the tone, role and house rules every chat there should follow.
options.explanation: Project instructions are the durable, project-scoped direction that shapes tone, role and house rules across every chat there.

options.text: A note asking Claude to remember these client details for later use in her unrelated Projects.
options.explanation: A Project is self-contained, so its context does not spread into other Projects, and asking for that does not create it.

options.text: One very long opening message that every later chat is expected to scroll back through.
options.explanation: A long opening message is a one-off prompt in one chat, not durable configuration for the Project.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A programme manager connects her Gmail account to a private Claude project so she can draft client status updates using recent correspondence. She writes a draft inside that project and then sends it in an email to an external partner agency the programme works with.
question: What is the greatest risk in this workflow?

options.text: The partner agency gains the same access to her mailbox the moment she sends the draft, because the connector automatically reaches everyone the email goes to.
options.explanation: Wrong. A connector is authorised for her own account and enforced at the user level; sending an email to the partner agency does not extend that authorisation to them, and the project she is working in was never shared with the partner because connectors are only available in private projects.

options.text: Details from messages unrelated to the update can surface in the draft, and she carries them outside the organisation when she sends it.
options.explanation: Claude can surface anything it finds relevant while searching her mailbox, so material from messages that have nothing to do with the update can end up woven into the draft. Once she emails that draft to the partner agency, whatever slipped in leaves the organisation with it.

options.text: Connecting her mailbox pulls every message into the project's knowledge base as if each one had been uploaded.
options.explanation: Wrong. Claude draws on a connected mailbox only when something in it is relevant to the request being handled, rather than importing every message wholesale into the project's knowledge base.

options.text: The mailbox connector stops working the moment she copies text out of the project chat into an email.
options.explanation: Wrong. The connector stays authorised on her account independently of what she does with the content it surfaces; copying text out of a project chat has no effect on the connection itself.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A weekly digest produced with help from a project turns out to have been based on a source that has since been found unreliable.
question: What should the person who publishes the digest do?

options.text: Tell the recipients which past digests are affected and correct the source before the next one.
options.explanation: Maintenance includes informing the people who already acted on the earlier output.

options.text: Add a standing disclaimer to all future digests saying that any figure in them may be inaccurate.
options.explanation: A permanent disclaimer neither corrects the past nor restores confidence in the future.

options.text: Stop producing the digest, since a source problem means the workflow can never be trusted again.
options.explanation: One bad source is a maintenance failure, not a reason to abandon a working process.

options.text: Quietly swap the source and let the correction show up in future digests without further comment.
options.explanation: Recipients keep relying on earlier digests they have no reason to doubt.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A team is about to connect a shared Google Drive to Claude for the first time. Which two considerations matter most before they do it?
question: Select two.

options.text: Whether organisational policy requires an approval before any data source is connected.
options.explanation: Most organisations require approval before a data source is connected, and that governance step precedes the technical one.

options.text: Whether connecting a drive turns the files it holds into Project instructions as well.
options.explanation: Connected files are a knowledge source; Project instructions are separate configuration that a person writes.

options.text: What the connection actually lets Claude see, so that the scope can be narrowed beforehand.
options.explanation: A connector is a permission-and-scope decision, so knowing and narrowing what Claude can reach comes first.

options.text: Whether connecting up the drive will permanently increase the size of the context window used.
options.explanation: A connector changes what Claude can reach, not the size of the context window, which is a property of the model.

options.text: Whether the connector removes the need to review the answers drawn from those files.
options.explanation: Material reaching Claude through a connector still needs the same scrutiny as any other source before it is relied on.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user has decided they no longer want Claude to be able to reach a connected service.
question: What should they do first?

options.text: Change the password on the service, which removes it from the connector list automatically.
options.explanation: A password change is not how a connection is managed, and it disrupts other tools too.

options.text: Disconnect the service in the connector settings so that Claude can no longer reach it.
options.explanation: Removing the connection is the direct control, and it takes effect for every conversation.

options.text: Delete the projects that used the service so that the connection has nothing left to read.
options.explanation: The connection remains live and reachable from any new conversation.

options.text: Ask Claude in each new chat to avoid using that service when it is answering questions.
options.explanation: A per-chat request depends on being remembered every time and leaves the access in place.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: An HR coordinator uploads a policy handbook to Project A's knowledge base, so the document resides only in that project. Later, the coordinator starts a new, unrelated 'Vendor Contracts' Project B without any further action.
question: What is the handbook's availability in Project B?

options.text: The handbook is not available in Project B, since each project's knowledge base is scoped to itself alone
options.explanation: Anthropic's Claude platform offers Projects as self-contained workspaces, each with its own knowledge base and chat history. Uploaded files like a handbook are confined to the project they were added to and are not automatically shared across other projects. This scoping ensures that Project B's knowledge base remains separate and only contains files explicitly added to it.

options.text: The handbook automatically appears in every new project the coordinator creates from that point on
options.explanation: There is no automatic propagation of files across projects. Each project's knowledge base is independent; files must be uploaded or shared explicitly if needed. This behavior prevents unintended data exposure and maintains clean separation between unrelated workstreams.

options.text: The handbook is deleted from Project A's knowledge base the moment a second project gets created
options.explanation: Creating a new project has no effect on existing projects or their knowledge bases. Files remain intact in Project A and are not automatically removed or transferred. Project B starts with an empty knowledge base until files are added to it directly.

options.text: The handbook becomes available only within projects sharing the same billing plan tier as Project A
options.explanation: Knowledge base scoping is determined by the project container, not by billing plan tier. While different plans may offer features like higher file limits or longer context windows, they do not alter the fundamental rule that each project has its own isolated set of reference files.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A regional team keeps the manual for a discontinued product in a project's knowledge base, on the grounds that someone may still ask about it one day.
question: What is the greatest concern?

options.text: Older files are read first, so any newer document uploaded after them is skipped in every answer.
options.explanation: Upload order does not determine which document is used to answer a question.

options.text: The manual counts twice against the project's limit, halving the space left for current documents.
options.explanation: Files do not count twice, and space is not the concern being raised.

options.text: Claude may answer current questions from material about a product the company no longer sells.
options.explanation: Retired material that is still loaded competes with current sources and produces wrong current answers.

options.text: Discontinued manuals cannot be stored in a project, so the whole knowledge base becomes unavailable.
options.explanation: There is no restriction on the age or status of an uploaded document.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A researcher pastes a forty-page methodology handbook into a project's instructions field instead of uploading it as a document.
question: What is the greatest concern with doing this?

options.text: Uploading is the only supported route, so pasting the handbook prevents the project from being saved at all.
options.explanation: Text can be typed into the instructions field; the problem is judgment, not a hard block.

options.text: Pasted text in the instructions is treated as a one-off prompt and is discarded when that chat ends.
options.explanation: Project instructions persist across chats; they are not discarded at the end of a conversation.

options.text: The instructions become a document rather than direction, so the real house rules are buried and applied unevenly.
options.explanation: Instructions are for concise standing direction; burying a handful of rules inside long reference text weakens them.

options.text: Project instructions can be read only by their author, so teammates in the project receive a different set of rules.
options.explanation: Instructions belong to the project, and members with access see the same ones.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project's knowledge base has grown to dozens of overlapping documents added by different people over time, and answer quality has fallen.
question: What is the best way to improve it?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to prefer whichever of the documents happens to be the longest.
options.explanation: Length is no indicator of currency or correctness.

options.text: Consolidate the material into a smaller set of current documents and remove the duplicates.
options.explanation: Curating down to current, non-overlapping sources removes the conflicts that degrade answers.

options.text: Add more documents covering the same topics so that the majority of the sources agree with one another.
options.explanation: Adding more overlapping material makes the conflict worse, not better.

options.text: Split the documents across several new projects so that each workspace holds only a handful of files.
options.explanation: Scattering stale duplicates across workspaces spreads the problem instead of resolving it.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user tries to upload an XLSX spreadsheet into a chat and the upload is rejected.
question: What must be enabled first for the upload to succeed?

options.text: The Google Drive connector must be connected before spreadsheets can be uploaded.
options.explanation: The Drive connector is a separate feature and is not required to upload a local XLSX file in chat.

options.text: Code execution must be turned on in account settings before XLSX files upload.
options.explanation: XLSX uploads require code execution to be enabled in account settings; without it, spreadsheets cannot be processed.

options.text: The account must be upgraded from Free to Pro before spreadsheets can upload.
options.explanation: Plan tier is not the blocker here; the specific requirement is enabling code execution.

options.text: The project knowledge base feature must be turned on for the account first.
options.explanation: Project knowledge being enabled is unrelated; XLSX support is gated by the code execution setting specifically.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A team is writing the instructions for a shared project that will be used for all of its customer communications.
question: Which direction belongs in the project instructions rather than in an individual chat?

options.text: Summarise the complaint from the Ashworth account that came in during yesterday afternoon.
options.explanation: This is a one-off task tied to a single conversation, not standing direction for the project.

options.text: Write at a reading level suited to customers, and never quote internal ticket references.
options.explanation: Project instructions carry durable, project-wide direction such as tone, audience and house rules, so they apply consistently to every chat in the project.

options.text: Draft this week's outage notice, keeping it to one paragraph for the status page.
options.explanation: A specific deliverable for this week belongs in the chat where it is being produced.

options.text: Compare the two apology drafts below and say which reads better for this customer.
options.explanation: A request about material pasted into one conversation cannot serve as project-wide direction.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A benefits administrator keeps last year's policy handbook in a project's knowledge base. Claude keeps quoting the old deductible, and the administrator has now rewritten the question five different ways.
question: What is the greatest concern here?

options.text: The answers are confidently wrong from an out-of-date source, and no amount of rephrasing will correct them.
options.explanation: When the uploaded source is stale, the output is wrong at the source and reprompting cannot repair it.

options.text: The project has run out of usage allowance, which causes older documents to be summarised inaccurately.
options.explanation: Usage allowance affects how much you can do, not the accuracy of a quoted figure.

options.text: The question is too short, so Claude fills in the gaps with figures drawn from general knowledge of benefits.
options.explanation: The wrong figure matches the superseded handbook, which points at the source rather than the prompt.

options.text: The handbook is too long for the project, so only the first pages are read and the remainder is dropped.
options.explanation: Length is not the issue; the figure being quoted is present in the document and simply out of date.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project's instructions state that refunds are approved within five working days, while an uploaded policy document says ten.
question: What should the project owner do first?

options.text: Establish which of the two figures is current, then correct whichever of the sources is wrong.
options.explanation: You cannot fix a contradiction without first determining which statement reflects the real process.

options.text: Add a line telling Claude to average the two figures whenever it answers questions about refunds.
options.explanation: Averaging two conflicting policy statements produces a figure that is in neither source.

options.text: Ask Claude which of the two figures it prefers, and then keep whichever source it says it uses.
options.explanation: Claude has no way to know which figure reflects the organisation's current process.

options.text: Delete the project instructions and rely on the uploaded policy document from now on instead.
options.explanation: This assumes the document is right, which is exactly what has not been established.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A project's instructions say "write for our executive committee". The same project is also used to produce customer-facing FAQ answers.
question: What is the greatest risk here?

options.text: The project can no longer hold uploaded documents, because an audience rule takes the place of the knowledge base.
options.explanation: Audience direction and uploaded knowledge are independent and coexist without issue.

options.text: Customer material inherits an executive register that is wrong for its readers, and the mismatch is easy to miss.
options.explanation: One durable audience rule silently mis-shapes every piece of work aimed at a different audience.

options.text: Every FAQ answer is saved as a separate project, since a second audience needs its own workspace to exist.
options.explanation: Nothing creates projects automatically; the workspace is unchanged by what is asked in it.

options.text: The instruction blocks any request that is not addressed to the executive committee, so the FAQ chats fail.
options.explanation: An audience instruction shapes style; it does not reject requests.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A writer wants one rule to apply everywhere she uses Claude, and a second rule to apply only inside one client Project. Which two placements are correct?
question: Select two.

options.text: Put both of the rules into the client Project's instructions, since those apply account-wide.
options.explanation: Project instructions apply inside that Project only, so putting the global rule there would not apply it everywhere.

options.text: Put the client-specific rule into that Project's instructions so it applies only inside it.
options.explanation: Project instructions are scoped to their Project, which is exactly the boundary the second rule needs.

options.text: Put the everywhere rule into her account-wide personalization settings so it always applies.
options.explanation: Account-wide personalization is the right home for direction that should apply across all of her Claude use.

options.text: Put both rules at the top of each new chat, since durable settings are for administrators.
options.explanation: Durable instruction settings are available to ordinary users, and re-typing rules per chat is what they replace.

options.text: Put the client rule into her account-wide settings too, so that it is never once missed.
