options.explanation: Account-wide settings apply to all her work, so a client-specific rule placed there would leak into unrelated chats.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A team uploads the new travel policy to a project but leaves the previous year's version in the knowledge base as well.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The older document is archived automatically, so the team loses the record of what the old rules were.
options.explanation: Nothing removes or archives an uploaded file on its own; that is the maintainer's job.

options.text: The project immediately rejects the newer file, because two documents cannot cover the same subject area at once.
options.explanation: There is no restriction preventing two documents on the same topic.

options.text: Both versions are available, so Claude may cite the superseded rules without anyone noticing the conflict.
options.explanation: Two live versions of the same policy make wrong answers look exactly as authoritative as right ones.

options.text: The project switches to retrieval mode, which stops Claude from quoting either policy document directly.
options.explanation: Retrieval relates to the size of project knowledge and still allows documents to be quoted.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A support team and a marketing team share one project. Support wants terse troubleshooting answers; marketing wants warm promotional copy. The project owner wants consistent quality for both.
question: What should the owner do first?

options.text: Keep one project and ask each person to restate their preferred tone at the start of every chat.
options.explanation: This abandons durable direction entirely and reintroduces the inconsistency being complained about.

options.text: Split the work into two projects, each with instructions written for that team's audience and purpose.
options.explanation: Durable direction only works when one workspace serves one audience and purpose.

options.text: Ask Claude to work out from each question whether the person is in support or marketing, and adapt.
options.explanation: Guessing the requester's team from the wording is unreliable and leaves no explicit standard.

options.text: Write one set of instructions listing both styles and let each person say which one they want in each chat.
options.explanation: This is a conflicting rule set that pushes the choice back into every individual conversation.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A team member is worried that connecting Google Drive will let colleagues read files they are not allowed to open.
question: What is accurate?

options.text: A connector requires every file to be made public in Drive before Claude is able to read any of them.
options.explanation: No change to a file's sharing settings is required to use a connector.

options.text: A connector gives everyone in the workspace the same view, so the file permissions no longer apply inside Claude.
options.explanation: Connectors do not flatten or override the permissions of the connected service.

options.text: A connector follows each person's existing permissions, so files they cannot open in Drive stay out of reach.
options.explanation: If someone cannot reach a file in the source system, the connector cannot reach it for them either.

options.text: A connector copies the files into a shared store, so anyone in the organisation can search them later.
options.explanation: Connectors read from the source system rather than duplicating files into a shared pool.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A campaign project has finished, but the team may want to look back at its material later in the year.
question: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Archive the project so it stays available for reference without sitting among the active workspaces.
options.explanation: Archiving preserves the material and its context while keeping the active list clean.

options.text: Share the project with the whole organisation so that anyone can look back at the campaign material.
options.explanation: Broad sharing is not a substitute for tidying up, and it widens access without a reason.

options.text: Strip out the instructions but keep the documents, so the project cannot produce any new answers.
options.explanation: Removing the direction leaves a half-configured workspace that will mislead whoever opens it.

options.text: Delete the project, since finished work should not be left in the account under any circumstances.
options.explanation: Deletion destroys material the team has said it may still need.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A quality lead wants Claude to stop producing figures that do not appear anywhere in the reports uploaded to a project.
question: Which addition to the project instructions best supports this?

options.text: Tell Claude to add a disclaimer to every answer noting that figures may not have been verified.
options.explanation: A blanket disclaimer shifts responsibility to the reader instead of preventing the problem.

options.text: Tell Claude to answer only from the uploaded reports and to say plainly when a figure is not in them.
options.explanation: This scopes the source and gives an explicit alternative to inventing a number.

options.text: Tell Claude to always give a numeric answer, choosing the closest available figure when none matches.
options.explanation: This actively instructs the behaviour the quality lead is trying to prevent.

options.text: Tell Claude that accuracy is extremely important and that mistakes are unacceptable in this project.
options.explanation: Emphasis without a rule gives no actionable behaviour to follow when a figure is missing.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A project's instructions tell Claude to "respond as our compliance officer and give final approval on vendor contracts".
question: What is the greatest risk in writing the instructions this way?

options.text: It assigns Claude a decision role a person must own, so drafts may be treated as approvals nobody reviewed.
options.explanation: Framing durable direction as decision authority invites colleagues to treat output as a sign-off.

options.text: It uses a job title that Claude cannot recognise, so the instruction is skipped and the default tone applies.
options.explanation: Role framing is understood; the danger is the authority it implies, not a failure to parse the title.

options.text: It prevents the project knowledge base from being used, since role rules take priority over uploaded files.
options.explanation: Instructions and uploaded knowledge work together; one does not switch the other off.

options.text: It makes the project visible to everyone in the organisation, because role rules imply shared ownership.
options.explanation: Instruction wording has no effect on who the project is shared with.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
question: After replacing three documents in a project's knowledge base, what is the most reliable way to confirm the refresh has worked?

options.text: Compare the total size of the knowledge base before and after the three files were replaced.
options.explanation: Size tells you nothing about which figures the answers now come from.

options.text: Confirm that the file names of the three new documents appear correctly in the project's knowledge list.
options.explanation: A file being listed does not prove the old content has stopped shaping answers.

options.text: Ask questions whose correct answers changed, and check the responses against the new documents.
options.explanation: Only a question with a changed answer distinguishes the new source from the old one.

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that it has read all of the newly uploaded documents in the project.
options.explanation: A self-report about reading files is not evidence that answers now reflect them.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A Project that a department has relied on for a year has never had its uploaded knowledge reviewed. Which two maintenance actions are appropriate?
question: Select two.

options.text: Schedule a regular review so outdated documents are found before they cause wrong answers.
options.explanation: Stale knowledge is a documented failure mode: Claude Academy's Projects guidance says outdated documents can lead to outdated responses, so a scheduled review is what catches that before it produces wrong answers.

options.text: Update or remove documents that no longer reflect current facts before they mislead Claude.
options.explanation: Claude Academy's Projects guidance says to review and update project knowledge periodically because outdated documents can lead to outdated responses - updating or removing the stale ones is what turns a review into an actual fix rather than just a diagnosis.

options.text: Leave every old document in place, since more background material always improves the answers.
options.explanation: Claude Academy's Projects guidance is explicit that outdated documents can lead to outdated responses, so accumulating background material without pruning it works against accuracy, not for it.

options.text: Replace the Project with a fresh one as soon as any single answer turns out to be wrong.
options.explanation: Rebuilding the whole workspace after one bad answer discards good context instead of curating the source at fault.

options.text: Ask Claude at the start of each chat to work out which uploaded documents are outdated.
options.explanation: Claude cannot tell which uploaded document has been superseded; that judgment depends on knowledge it does not hold.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A finance team's project instructions include a standing rule that every figure must be reported in euros, plus several directions that were only ever meant for individual past deliverables, and Claude's answers in the project have become inconsistent. Which two revisions would make those instructions work better as standing direction?
question: Select two.

options.text: Rewrite each rule as a longer, more formal paragraph so none of them is overlooked.
options.explanation: Length and formality do not resolve which rules still apply. A long list of stale directions becomes a longer list of stale directions, and dense instructions are harder for the team to review.

options.text: Add a line at the top of the list telling Claude to follow every rule carefully.
options.explanation: A generic exhortation to follow the rules adds no information about which directions still apply or which take priority. Emphasis is not specification, and the outdated entries keep pulling answers in their own direction.

options.text: Move the list out of the project and paste it into the first message of each chat.
options.explanation: This gives up the main advantage of project instructions, which is that durable direction applies automatically to every chat. Pasted instructions have to be maintained by hand and will vary between chats and between people.

options.text: Delete directions that were only ever meant for one particular past deliverable.
options.explanation: Standing instructions should hold for every chat in the project. One-off directions kept past their deliverable pull answers toward a job nobody is doing any more, which is a direct source of the inconsistency.

options.text: Give the reason behind the euro-only rule so Claude can apply it to new cases.
options.explanation: and for an unrelated reason: it improves a rule that stays rather than removing one that should go. Stating why figures must be in euros lets Claude extend the intent sensibly to situations the rule never named.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A marketer discusses a campaign brief with Claude in Chat A inside a project, but Claude does not recall those details when the marketer opens a new Chat B in the same project.
question: What most likely explains this?

options.text: The brief was only discussed in Chat A and was never added to the project's shared knowledge base
options.explanation: Context is not shared across chats in a project unless it has been added to the project knowledge base; discussion in one chat alone stays local to that chat.

options.text: The project has already reached its maximum allowed number of chats for the current billing cycle
options.explanation: There is no documented per-billing-cycle cap on the number of chats within a project that would explain this behavior.

options.text: Project instructions must be re-saved before any new chat can access prior chat conversations
options.explanation: Re-saving project instructions has no bearing on whether one chat's conversation content is visible to another chat.

options.text: The marketer's current account plan does not permit more than one chat inside each project
options.explanation: Plans do not restrict a project to a single chat; multiple chats within one project are expected and supported.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A consultant set account-wide instructions two years ago describing a role they no longer hold, and answers now carry the wrong framing.
question: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Mention the correct role at the start of each conversation and accept the extra step as normal.
options.explanation: Repeating a correction forever is the manual overhead durable configuration exists to remove.

options.text: Update the account-wide instructions so they describe the consultant's current role and the work they do now.
options.explanation: Personal configuration needs the same periodic refresh as any other durable direction.

options.text: Create a brand-new account so that the outdated preferences are all left behind with the previous configuration.
options.explanation: Abandoning an account to escape a stale setting loses all the history and other configuration with it.

options.text: Add a line to every project's instructions telling Claude to disregard the account-wide instructions.
options.explanation: This is a workaround that leaves the outdated configuration in place for all work outside projects.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: Using the Calendar connector, a user asks Claude to set up a team sync that repeats every Monday.
question: What can Claude do here?

options.text: Claude can draft the details, but an admin must go configure the recurrence separately.
options.explanation: No admin intervention is needed; the connector lets Claude set up recurrence directly.

options.text: Claude can create the event directly, since the connector supports recurring events.
options.explanation: The Calendar connector explicitly supports establishing recurring meetings, so a weekly Monday sync can be created directly.

options.text: Claude can view existing recurring events but cannot create new ones itself.
options.explanation: The connector supports both viewing and creating events, including recurring ones.

options.text: Claude can only create a single event with no way to set up recurrence.
options.explanation: Recurrence configuration is a documented capability, not a missing feature requiring a workaround.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A colleague reports that Claude gave them an incorrect answer inside a shared project.
question: What should the project owner do first?

options.text: Remove every document from the knowledge base and rebuild the project from current files.
options.explanation: Rebuilding everything is disproportionate before the cause is even known.

options.text: Rewrite the project instructions to add a rule that all answers must be double-checked by hand.
options.explanation: A blanket caution does not diagnose or fix whatever produced the wrong answer.

options.text: Advise the colleague to try the same question again in a new chat within the same project.
options.explanation: The same project knowledge is read again, so a retry rarely changes a source-driven error.

options.text: Ask which question was asked, then check the uploaded documents for the answer Claude gave.
options.explanation: Tracing the answer back to a source separates a stale document from a prompting or model problem.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A team repeatedly corrects Claude in chat because it keeps using the wrong report template.
question: What is the most durable fix?

options.text: Keep correcting Claude in chat, since each correction improves the answers for the whole team.
options.explanation: A correction inside one conversation does not change the behaviour for anyone else.

options.text: Put the template requirement into the project instructions so every chat starts with the right rule.
options.explanation: Making a repeated correction part of the configuration stops the team re-solving it every time.

options.text: Ask each person to paste the template into the first message of every conversation they start.
options.explanation: This keeps the manual step and simply moves it to the top of each chat.

options.text: Create a new project each month so that the wrong template does not carry over from any earlier work.
options.explanation: New workspaces without the rule will still default to the wrong template.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A project's instructions say "always write in plain language for non-specialists" and, further down, "use the full technical terminology our engineers expect". Team members report that outputs vary widely.
question: What is the greatest concern with these instructions as written?

options.text: Claude will merge the two rules into one style that always sits exactly halfway between the two audiences.
options.explanation: A predictable midpoint is not what happens; the observed symptom is inconsistency, not a stable compromise.

options.text: Instructions longer than a few lines are ignored, so only the very first rule in the list will ever be applied.
options.explanation: There is no such rule that only the opening line of project instructions is read.

options.text: The two rules conflict, so Claude has no reliable basis for choosing a register and results vary between chats.
options.explanation: Contradictory house rules are the direct cause: neither rule can be satisfied without breaking the other.

options.text: Conflicting rules cause the project knowledge base to be reindexed, which slows down every answer given.
options.explanation: Instruction wording does not trigger any reprocessing of uploaded documents.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A legal operations manager writes project instructions containing forty numbered rules intended to cover every request the team might ever make.
question: What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: Each numbered rule creates a separate chat history, so the project's conversations are split across rules.
options.explanation: Instructions do not create or partition chat histories in any way.

options.text: Numbered lists are not accepted in the instructions field, so only the first several rules are stored at all.
options.explanation: There is no restriction on numbered lists in project instructions.

options.text: Long instructions force the project into retrieval mode, which removes uploaded documents from answers.
options.explanation: Retrieval behaviour relates to the size of project knowledge, and it does not remove documents from answers.

options.text: Rules that rarely apply crowd out the few that always matter, so the key ones are followed less reliably.
options.explanation: Long, undifferentiated rule lists dilute the direction that actually matters for most requests.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A team lead grants "Can edit" access on a shared project to everyone who might ever open it, rather than giving most people "Can view".
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: The project's chat history becomes visible to the whole organisation regardless of the access levels granted.
options.explanation: Granting edit access to named people does not publish the project organisation-wide.

options.text: Only one editor can open the project at a time, so members are blocked whenever a colleague is in it.
options.explanation: There is no single-editor lock on a shared project.

options.text: Editors are billed separately for the project, so the department's costs rise with each person added.
options.explanation: Access levels within a project are not billed individually.

options.text: Anyone can change the instructions and the knowledge, so the shared setup can drift without anyone noticing.
options.explanation: Broad edit rights let the agreed direction and sources be altered silently by any of the members.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A Project's knowledge base has grown until it approaches the limit of what fits in the context window. Which two statements are accurate?
question: Select two.

options.text: The Project stays in retrieval mode permanently, even if its knowledge is reduced later.
options.explanation: The Project reverts to standard processing if the knowledge later drops back below the threshold.

options.text: The user has to switch retrieval on in the settings once the knowledge passes that threshold.
options.explanation: There is no setting to turn on; treating it as manual is the most common misunderstanding of this behaviour.

options.text: Claude switches over to retrieval automatically, with no configuration needed from the user.

options.text: Retrieval disables web search and the other features for every chat inside that Project.
options.explanation: Retrieval works alongside other Claude features, including web search, extended thinking and Research.

options.text: Retrieval lets the Project work with roughly ten times more content than it held before.
options.explanation: In retrieval mode a Project can hold up to about ten times more content than standard processing allows.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A grant writer wants every draft in a project written from the point of view of a programme officer assessing applications, so that weak arguments surface early.
question: What is the best way to set this up?

options.text: Upload sample funded applications to project knowledge and expect Claude to adopt a reviewer stance.
options.explanation: Examples of successful applications do not communicate an assessing point of view.

options.text: Name the perspective in the project title, since the title is what Claude reads first in each new chat.
options.explanation: A project title is a label; it is not where behavioural direction is configured.

options.text: Mention the reviewer's stance in whichever chats feel relevant, so the writer keeps control of when it applies.
options.explanation: This makes an intended default optional and easy to forget on the drafts that need it most.

options.text: State the perspective and its purpose in the project instructions so every chat adopts that stance.
options.explanation: A durable stance that should hold for all work in the workspace belongs in project instructions.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A consultant sets project instructions telling Claude to always respond as a financial advisor, then separately uploads quarterly earnings reports to the same project's knowledge base.
question: When the consultant opens a brand-new chat in that project, what should they expect?

options.text: Claude requires the consultant to manually re-enable the instructions and knowledge base for each chat
options.explanation: Neither instructions nor knowledge base content require manual re-enabling per chat; both are automatically active project-wide.

options.text: Claude applies the advisor persona but cannot access the reports until they are re-uploaded in that chat
options.explanation: Knowledge base files are available project-wide and do not need to be re-uploaded inside each individual chat.

options.text: Claude ignores the persona instructions in new chats but can still access the earnings reports fully
options.explanation: Project instructions apply to all chats in the project, not selectively to some and not others.

options.text: Claude applies the advisor persona and references the earnings reports, since both persist project-wide
options.explanation: Both project instructions and knowledge base uploads are designed to persist and apply automatically across every chat within the same project, including new ones.

options.explanation: A stable document is well suited to a one-time upload into Project knowledge, where it stays available to every chat.

options.text: Paste the whole handbook into every new chat, so the newest version is always present.
options.explanation: Re-pasting a whole handbook per chat is the manual work Project knowledge and connectors exist to remove.

options.text: Connect the Drive folder, so the weekly handbook changes are picked up from the source.
options.explanation: A connector reaches the live source, which is what a document that changes every week needs.

options.text: Upload a copy of the handbook just once and then rely on that copy for the rest of this year.
options.explanation: A one-time copy of a weekly-changing handbook goes stale fast and produces confidently outdated answers.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: An operations lead creates a project on an Enterprise plan and shares it with the whole organisation. To save time she uploads a complete team folder into the project knowledge, and that folder includes a spreadsheet of individual salary bands.
question: What is the greatest risk?

options.text: Anyone who opens the shared project can draw the salary details out through ordinary questions.
options.explanation: Project knowledge is background for every chat in the project, so sharing the project shares everything uploaded to it with everyone who can open it.

options.text: The extra documents will slow down every answer in the project until the folder has been trimmed back.
options.explanation: A larger knowledge base is a performance and tidiness concern, not the serious exposure here.

options.text: The salary spreadsheet can no longer be removed once other members have opened the project.
options.explanation: Documents can be removed from project knowledge at any time; the exposure is the real problem.

options.text: Claude will decline every request in the project while a salary document remains uploaded.
options.explanation: Claude does not refuse to work in a project because a sensitive file has been uploaded to it.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A developer wants Claude to have awareness of a project's coding conventions when answering questions in a dedicated 'Backend Refactor' project.
question: Which action correctly places that context so it applies across all chats in the project?

options.text: Star the coding convention files in a personal favorites list to make them available across project chats.
options.explanation: A personal favorites list is a user-specific bookmarking feature and does not inject content into Claude's context. Project knowledge base is the proper mechanism for providing shared documents across chats.

options.text: Ask Claude to memorize the coding conventions in a single chat to persist across project chats.
options.explanation: Memorization within a single chat does not persist to other chats. To share context across all project chats, you must upload the material to the project's knowledge base.

options.text: Rename each new chat to include the word 'conventions' so Claude infers the context across chats.
options.explanation: Chat names are only labels and do not convey document content or give Claude awareness of conventions. Only the project knowledge base can provide persistent context across chats.

options.text: Upload the convention docs to the project's knowledge base with the '+' button on the main page.
options.explanation: Uploading documents to the project's knowledge base with the '+' button injects them as context across all chats. This ensures Claude always has access to the coding conventions when answering in the 'Backend Refactor' project.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: At an Enterprise organization, no one has enabled connectors yet, and an employee tries to connect Google Drive.
question: What must happen before the employee can authenticate?

options.text: The employee must switch to a personal, non-organizational Claude account first.
options.explanation: Switching account types is irrelevant; the organization admin simply needs to enable the connector.

options.text: An Owner or Primary Owner must first enable the connector organization-wide.
options.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner or Primary Owner must enable connectors org-wide before members can authenticate their own accounts.

options.text: The employee must install a separate Workspace marketplace add-on before this.
options.explanation: No separate marketplace add-on installation is a prerequisite for the Drive connector.

options.text: The employee must contact Anthropic support to whitelist their Google account first.
options.explanation: There is no support-ticket whitelisting process; the control point is an org-level toggle set by an Owner or Primary Owner.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A marketing lead is writing the Project instructions for a Project her team will use every day. Which two choices make those instructions effective?
question: Select two.

options.text: Listing an answer to each specific question the team happened to ask Claude during the last month.
options.explanation: A list of past answers is a transcript, not direction, and it dates quickly as the team's questions change.

options.text: Stating the audience and the tone that every response inside that Project should be written for.
options.explanation: Audience and tone are exactly the durable direction Project instructions exist to hold, rather than being restated per chat.

options.text: Keeping the instructions vague, so that they never conflict with any individual chat request.
options.explanation: Vague instructions give no usable direction, so responses drift back to whatever each individual chat happens to say.

options.text: Repeating one rule several times in capital letters so it carries more weight than the others.
options.explanation: Emphasis and repetition are not what makes an instruction effective; clarity and stated intent are.

options.text: Giving the reason behind a house rule, so that Claude can apply it to unforeseen situations.
options.explanation: Giving the reason behind a rule lets Claude generalise it to cases the instructions never anticipated.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A user wants to know if they must upgrade from a free account just to try out the basic project feature with instructions and a small knowledge base.
question: What is true about project availability on free accounts?

options.text: Projects are available to free accounts too, though free users are capped at a maximum of five projects
options.explanation: Projects are available to all users including free accounts, though free users can create a maximum of five projects.

options.text: Free accounts can create projects but are never permitted to set project instructions at all
options.explanation: Setting project instructions is part of the core project feature available to free accounts, not blocked entirely.

options.text: Projects are an exclusive Team and Enterprise feature and are unavailable on any individual account
options.explanation: Projects are not restricted to Team and Enterprise; free and Pro individual accounts can use them too.

options.text: Free accounts can create projects but the knowledge base feature is entirely disabled for them
options.explanation: The knowledge base is part of the core project experience available on free accounts, subject to the five-project cap rather than being disabled.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A consultant works in a free Claude account and keeps a separate project for each client. She already has five projects and has just signed a sixth client whose material she wants to keep separate too.
question: What should she do first?

options.text: Ask an administrator to raise the project allowance on her account before she starts the work.
options.explanation: A personal free account has no administrator who can lift the cap; the plan defines the limit.

options.text: Review her five projects and retire or repurpose one, since a free account is capped at five projects.
options.explanation: Projects are available to everyone, but a free account is limited to five of them, so she has to free one up before a sixth client workspace can exist.

options.text: Create the sixth project as normal, since the cap on the number of projects applies only to shared ones.
options.explanation: The five-project cap on free accounts is not limited to shared projects; it covers her projects.

options.text: Keep this client in ordinary chats instead, since projects are only offered on the paid plans.
options.explanation: Projects are available to all users, including free accounts, so this misreads the constraint.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A new joiner inherits a shared project whose outputs do not match what their manager describes as the team standard.
question: What should the new joiner do first?

options.text: Ask Claude in a chat to explain which instructions it received and treat that answer as the record.
options.explanation: The configuration itself is the record; a conversational account of it is not a reliable substitute.

options.text: Start a fresh project of their own so the existing team workspace is left exactly as it was found.
options.explanation: This leaves the team's shared problem untouched and fragments where the work is done.

options.text: Read the project instructions already in place to understand the current direction before changing anything.
options.explanation: You cannot tell what is missing or wrong until you know what direction the project currently carries.

options.text: Clear the existing instructions and rewrite them from scratch to match the manager's description of good output.
options.explanation: Discarding direction the team relies on, before understanding it, risks losing rules that were deliberate.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A legal analyst wants Claude to reference a set of contract templates in every chat within a 'Contracts Review' project without re-uploading them each time.
question: What is the correct way to make these templates persistently available across all chats in that project?

options.text: Upload the contract templates once to the project's knowledge base so all chats can reference them
options.explanation: Files added to the project knowledge base are available as context across all chats within the project, avoiding repeated uploads.

options.text: Paste the full text of every contract template directly into the project instructions field
options.explanation: Project instructions are meant for behavioral guidance like tone and role, not for storing full reference documents; the knowledge base is the appropriate location for that.

options.text: Email the templates to Claude support so an agent can manually link them to the analyst's account
options.explanation: There is no support workflow for linking documents to an account this way; uploads go directly into the project's knowledge base.

options.text: Attach the templates only to the first chat and mark that chat as the project's default conversation
options.explanation: Attachments made within an individual chat are not automatically shared with other chats; only knowledge base uploads persist project-wide.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: Using the Gmail connector, a user asks Claude to summarize the contents of a PDF attached to an email.
question: What limitation should the user expect?

options.text: Claude can read the email metadata and body but cannot open the attachment's content.
options.explanation: The Gmail connector exposes metadata and body content but does not process attachment content, so the PDF's contents remain inaccessible.

options.text: Claude cannot access the email at all until the attachment is first removed.
options.explanation: Claude can still read the surrounding email even with an attachment present; only the attachment content is off-limits.

options.text: Claude can read the attachment content, but only when it stays under 10MB in size.
options.explanation: There is no documented size threshold that unlocks attachment reading; content stays inaccessible regardless of size.

options.text: Claude can read the attachment content, but only when the attachment is a PDF file type.
options.explanation: Attachment content is inaccessible for any file type, not just non-PDF formats.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A freelancer on a Pro plan has built a project with detailed instructions and reference documents, and now wants two collaborators to work inside the same project.
question: What should they expect?

options.text: Sharing becomes available once the project contains uploaded documents rather than instructions alone.
options.explanation: What a project contains has no bearing on whether it can be shared.

options.text: Sharing works on every plan, so the collaborators can simply be invited with view or edit access.
options.explanation: Personal plans do not offer project sharing with other people.

options.text: Sharing works only after the project has been archived, which makes it visible to other accounts.
options.explanation: Archiving tidies a project away; it does not publish it to anyone.

options.text: Project sharing is a Team and Enterprise capability, so on a Pro plan the project stays personal.
options.explanation: Sharing projects with named colleagues is available on Team and Enterprise plans only.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A Team account with fifteen members has just had the Gmail connector enabled by the Primary Owner.
question: How does each member gain access through the connector?

options.text: One member authenticates once, granting Gmail access to the whole team.
options.explanation: Authentication is per-user; one member's OAuth grant does not extend to teammates' inboxes.

options.text: The Primary Owner authenticates for everyone through a single shared service account.
options.explanation: There is no shared service account model; each user connects their own Google account individually.

options.text: Members share one OAuth token that IT distributes to the whole team.
options.explanation: Shared or distributed tokens are not how the connector works; per-user authentication keeps data separate.

options.text: Each member individually authenticates via OAuth with their own Google credentials.
options.explanation: Even after org-level enablement, each user authenticates through standard OAuth with their own credentials, keeping access per-person.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project shared with a Team plan workspace has just had its escalation matrix replaced with a new version.
question: What else should the project owner do?

options.text: Tell the members who use the project what changed, so they know earlier answers may no longer hold.
options.explanation: Maintaining shared configuration includes informing the people whose past work relied on the old source.

options.text: Ask each member to create their own copy of the project so everyone controls their own knowledge base.
options.explanation: Copies multiply the maintenance problem and guarantee that some members keep using the old matrix.

options.text: Delete the project's chat history, because past conversations would otherwise override the new material.
options.explanation: Old conversations do not override project knowledge, and deleting them destroys a useful record.

options.text: Leave a note in the project title, since members are prompted to read the title before each new chat.
options.explanation: A title is not a change log, and members are not prompted to read it before chatting.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A pricing analyst notices Claude quoting a discount tier that was retired at the last price review.
question: What should the analyst do first?

options.text: Check the project's uploaded documents to see whether the retired price list is still in the knowledge base.
options.explanation: Confirming whether a superseded source is still loaded is the cheapest way to explain the wrong answer.

options.text: Rewrite the project instructions to say that all of the pricing answers must be treated as provisional estimates.
options.explanation: This hides the symptom behind a disclaimer instead of removing the outdated source.

options.text: Ask Claude to search the web for the current price list and to use that instead of the uploaded material.
options.explanation: Public search is not a reliable source for internal pricing and leaves the stale file in place.

options.text: Start a new conversation, since long chats gradually drift away from the documents they started with.
options.explanation: A fresh chat still reads the same project knowledge, so the retired figures come back.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user pastes a Google Doc URL into a chat with the Drive connector enabled and asks about the document's contents.
question: What does Claude do?

options.text: Claude downloads the document as a PDF and stores a copy in project knowledge.
options.explanation: Accessing a document via the connector does not create a permanent copy in project knowledge.

options.text: Claude ignores the URL and asks the user to paste the document's text instead.
options.explanation: The connector is designed to retrieve the document automatically, so manual pasting is not required.

options.text: Claude requires the document to be shared publicly before it can read the link.
options.explanation: Public sharing is not required, since the connector authenticates to the user's own private Google account.

options.text: Claude accesses and processes the referenced document once the message is sent.
options.explanation: With the Drive connector, a pasted URL is accessed and processed when the message is sent, informing the response.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: An Enterprise organisation wants its members to use the Google Drive connector, but with read access only.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Members authenticate individually; the owner enables the connector; the team confirms the limits; the owner restricts it to read actions.
options.explanation: Members cannot authenticate before the owner has enabled the connector.

options.text: The owner enables the connector; the owner restricts it to read actions; members authenticate individually; the team confirms the limits.
options.explanation: Enablement and action restrictions are owner-level and come before individuals connect their own accounts.

options.text: The owner restricts it to read actions; the team confirms the limits; members authenticate individually; the owner enables the connector.
options.explanation: Restrictions are configured for a connector that has not been enabled yet.

options.text: The team confirms the limits; members authenticate individually; the owner restricts it to read actions; the owner enables the connector.
options.explanation: The limits are confirmed first and the connector is enabled last, which reverses the setup.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A finance approvals process has changed: purchases above a threshold now need two signatures instead of one. A project's instructions still describe the old single-signature rule.
question: What should the project owner do first?

options.text: Upload the email announcing the change so that Claude can work out the new rule from that announcement itself.
options.explanation: This leaves the contradicting instruction in place and asks Claude to reconcile the conflict.

options.text: Archive the project and rebuild it later once the finance team has finished documenting the change.
options.explanation: Removing a working project is disproportionate when a single rule needs rewriting.

options.text: Update the project instructions to describe the new two-signature rule before the project is used again.
options.explanation: Durable direction that contradicts the current process must be corrected at the source, and quickly.

options.text: Tell colleagues to mention the new rule in their prompts whenever they ask about purchase approvals.
options.explanation: This relies on every person remembering, while the wrong rule stays configured for everyone else.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A finance team's project instructions state: "never give a figure without naming the report it came from".
question: Which addition would most improve this instruction?

options.text: Adding the rule a second time at the end of the instructions, so it is less likely to be overlooked.
options.explanation: Duplication does not clarify the rule and lengthens the instructions for no benefit.

options.text: Adding why the rule exists, so Claude can apply the same care to cases the rule did not anticipate.
options.explanation: Stating the reason lets the intent generalise to situations the literal wording never covered.

options.text: Adding an instruction to repeat the rule at the top of every answer, so readers can see it was followed.
options.explanation: Restating the rule in the output adds noise without improving whether it is actually followed.

options.text: Adding the names of the three people who approved the rule, so Claude knows the rule is authoritative.
options.explanation: Approval provenance changes nothing about how the rule is applied to an answer.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: An operations manager has two things to add to a project: the team's two-page approved abbreviation list, and the rule that answers must never use abbreviations outside that list.
question: What is the best placement?

options.text: Put both the reference list and the rule into the project instructions so that the two are always read together.
options.explanation: Two pages of reference text in the instructions field buries the rule that is meant to stand out.

options.text: Upload both the reference list and the rule as documents in the project knowledge base, for consistency.
options.explanation: A behaviour rule stored as background material is far weaker than one stated as project direction.

options.text: Keep the reference list on the team wiki and paste the rule at the start of each chat that needs it.
options.explanation: This puts the reference out of reach and turns a standing rule back into manual repetition.

options.text: Upload the reference to project knowledge and put the rule about unapproved abbreviations in the instructions.
options.explanation: Reference material belongs in knowledge; the standing behaviour rule belongs in the instructions.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: An internal FAQ drafted with help from a project is about to be published to all staff.
question: Which maintenance step matters most before it goes out?

options.text: Confirm the FAQ is long enough to cover every question the team has ever received from staff.
options.explanation: Coverage is not the risk here; answers drawn from outdated sources are.

options.text: Check each answer against the current source documents and confirm none rely on superseded material.
options.explanation: Publication is the point at which a stale source turns into a broadly circulated wrong answer.

options.text: Ask Claude to review its own FAQ and to confirm that all of the answers it has written are accurate.
options.explanation: A self-review cannot detect that the underlying uploaded source was out of date.

options.text: Republish the FAQ every month so that errors in the current version are eventually replaced.
options.explanation: Scheduled republication does not stop the first version going out with wrong answers.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A team lead is setting up a new project that will be used for recurring quarterly business reviews.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Write the instructions; run a typical request; upload the reference documents; create the project and name its purpose.
options.explanation: The instructions and the test both precede the project they belong to.

options.text: Create the project and name its purpose; write the instructions; upload the reference documents; run a typical request.
options.explanation: Establish the workspace and its purpose, give it durable direction and background, then check it on real work.

options.text: Upload the reference documents; run a typical request; create the project and name its purpose; write the instructions.
options.explanation: Documents cannot be uploaded into a project that has not been created yet.

options.text: Run a typical request; upload the reference documents; write the instructions; create the project and name its purpose.
options.explanation: The setup is tested before any part of it exists.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A marketing associate's project instructions say "keep it short", yet the drafts Claude produces are still far longer than the team wants.
question: What should the associate do first?

options.text: Replace the vague rule with a specific limit, such as a stated word count and a section structure.
options.explanation: Vague direction is the root cause; the fix is to make the requirement concrete enough to follow.

options.text: Switch to a more capable model, since shorter writing needs stronger reasoning about relevance.
options.explanation: A stronger model does not repair an under-specified instruction.

options.text: Add capital letters and the word "must" to the existing rule so the instruction carries more weight.
options.explanation: Emphasis does not add the missing information about how short is short enough.

options.text: Move the rule into the project knowledge base, where longer background material is normally stored.
options.explanation: Moving a behaviour rule into reference material makes it less likely to shape every answer, not more.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
situation: A product manager is deciding whether onboarding guides, style docs, and roadmap notes for three unrelated products should live in one shared project or in three separate projects.
question: Which approach best matches how Claude Projects are intended to be used?

options.text: Store the documents outside any project and paste the relevant ones into each new chat manually
options.explanation: Manually pasting documents into every chat ignores the knowledge base feature that projects provide for persistent context.

options.text: Create one project per document type instead of per product, mixing all three products' content
options.explanation: Organizing by document type while mixing three unrelated products still blends unrelated context, the opposite of the intended focused workspace.

options.text: Combine everything into a single project so all three products share one unified context in every chat
options.explanation: Merging unrelated products into one project would mix contexts, working against the purpose of keeping conversations focused.

options.text: Create a separate project per product so each self-contained workspace keeps a focused knowledge base
options.explanation: Projects are designed as self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, so organizing by unrelated product keeps context focused and avoids cross-contamination.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user edits a Google Doc directly in Drive after Claude referenced it earlier in a conversation, then asks a follow-up question about the same document.
question: What should the user expect?

options.text: The user must re-upload the document as a new file for changes to appear.
options.explanation: Re-uploading is unnecessary because the connector already reads the live document from Drive.

options.text: Claude uses a cached snapshot from the first access and misses the new edits entirely.
options.explanation: There is no static cached snapshot behavior; the connector reflects the current Drive version instead.

options.text: Claude's view of the document reflects the latest Drive version, since it auto-syncs.
options.explanation: Documents accessed through the Drive connector sync automatically with their Drive versions, so the follow-up reflects the latest edits.

options.text: Claude only sees updates when the document is re-shared through a new link.
options.explanation: Generating a new share link is not required, since syncing happens automatically for the existing reference.

objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
question: Within a single Claude Project, what is the functional difference between project instructions and the project knowledge base?

options.text: Project instructions define behavioral guidance like tone or role, while the knowledge base supplies reference files
options.explanation: Project instructions establish behavioral guidelines such as tone or role applied to all chats, while the knowledge base holds uploaded documents, text, and code used as background context.

options.text: Project instructions and the knowledge base are simply two names for the same underlying feature
options.explanation: The two are distinct features serving different purposes: behavioral guidance versus reference content.

options.text: Project instructions apply to a single chat at a time, while the knowledge base applies to every project a user owns
options.explanation: Project instructions apply to every chat within the project, not just one, and the knowledge base is scoped to that project, not to all of a user's projects.

options.text: Project instructions store uploaded files, while the knowledge base only accepts text typed into a settings field
options.explanation: This reverses the roles; file uploads belong to the knowledge base, not the instructions field.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A team lead on a Team plan wants a shared project whose instructions the whole team relies on.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Save them as project instructions; share the project; agree the rules with the team; collect colleague feedback.
options.explanation: Writing the rules before the team has agreed them means the shared setup encodes one person's view.

options.text: Agree the rules with the team; save them as project instructions; share the project; collect colleague feedback.
options.explanation: Agree, encode, distribute, then learn from real use by the people who now depend on it.

options.text: Collect colleague feedback; agree the rules with the team; share the project; save them as project instructions.
options.explanation: Feedback is gathered before anything exists, and the instructions are saved only after sharing.

options.text: Share the project; collect colleague feedback; agree the rules with the team; save them as project instructions.
options.explanation: Colleagues are asked to review a project that has no agreed direction in it yet.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user wants Claude to find a spreadsheet they opened yesterday in Google Drive but does not remember its exact URL.
question: What can the Drive connector do?

options.text: Only retrieve a file when the exact URL is provided by the user first.
options.explanation: A URL is one option, not a requirement; recent-document search is also supported.

options.text: List every file in the Drive account without offering any search tool.
options.explanation: Search capability is part of the connector, not just a flat unsearchable file list.

options.text: Only access files explicitly shared with a separate Claude service account first.
options.explanation: There is no separate service account requirement; the connector uses the user's own authenticated Drive access.

options.text: Search through recently accessed documents in Drive to help find the file.
options.explanation: The Drive connector lets users search recently accessed documents, or paste a URL, so the file can be found without the exact link.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A communications team wants every press-release draft produced in a shared project to come out in the company's house voice, without anyone having to explain the voice again in each chat.
question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Ask Claude in each new chat to match the house voice, and then correct the tone in the follow-up messages each time.
options.explanation: This is the repeated one-off prompting the team is trying to escape, and it produces different results per person.

options.text: Write down the house voice rules and audience the team already applies, then put them in the project instructions.
options.explanation: The durable direction has to exist as agreed wording before it can be configured; defining what good looks like comes first.

options.text: Upload every press release published last year and let Claude infer the house voice on its own from them.
options.explanation: Samples are useful background, but they do not state the rules, and inference from mixed past work is unreliable.

options.text: Create a separate project for each writer so that every person can keep their own preferred tone settings.
options.explanation: This guarantees inconsistency, which is the opposite of the shared house voice the team asked for.

objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
situation: A user is hesitant to connect Gmail to Claude over privacy concerns.
question: Which statement accurately describes how Anthropic handles connector data?

options.text: Anthropic does not train models on connector data, and stores it securely.
options.explanation: Anthropic does not train on Gmail, Drive, or Calendar connector data, and retrieved data is stored on Anthropic servers with standard security.

options.text: Anthropic trains its models on connector data by default, unless the user opts out.
options.explanation: Model training on connector data does not occur, so no opt-out is needed in the first place.

options.text: Connector data is processed only in memory and never stored on any server.
options.explanation: Retrieved connector data is stored on Anthropic's servers rather than existing only transiently.

options.text: Connector data is shared with the user's Workspace admin for compliance review.
options.explanation: There is no described mechanism routing a user's connector data to their Workspace admin.

objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
situation: A project owner is adding a newly issued reference document to a project's knowledge base.
question: Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.text: Confirm it is the approved current version; upload it to project knowledge; record a review date; ask a test question.
options.explanation: Verify currency before it becomes a source, then schedule the next review and confirm it answers correctly.

options.text: Upload it to project knowledge; confirm it is the approved current version; ask a test question; record a review date.
options.explanation: The document becomes a live source before anyone has checked that it is the current version.

options.text: Ask a test question; upload it to project knowledge; record a review date; confirm it is the approved current version.
options.explanation: The test happens before the document exists in the project, and currency is checked last.

options.text: Record a review date; ask a test question; confirm it is the approved current version; upload it to project knowledge.
options.explanation: A review date is set for a document that has not been added, and the upload comes last.

objective: Create effective system-level instructions
situation: A consultant wants Claude to use British spelling and metric units in every conversation, no matter which piece of work it belongs to.
question: Where does that direction best belong?

options.text: In the account-wide instructions, since the preference applies to all conversations rather than one workspace.
options.explanation: Account-wide instructions are the place for direction that should hold across every conversation.

options.text: In the instructions of each project, repeated so that every workspace carries the same spelling rule.
options.explanation: This works only inside projects that were remembered, and every new project has to be updated by hand.

options.text: In the opening message of each chat, restated whenever the consultant begins any new piece of work.
options.explanation: Repeating it forever is exactly the manual overhead durable configuration is meant to remove.
